Dr. Amarendra Sharma is an economist with over two decades of teaching experience spanning Principles of Microeconomics and Macroeconomics, Intermediate Micro and Macro, International Trade, Money & Finance, Game Theory, Industrial Organization, Labor Economics, and Economics in Films. He is currently at Binghamton University (SUNY), and has previously taught at the University of Maryland Global Campus, American University, Ithaca College, the University of Tampa, Elmira College, and Miami University.

He earned his PhD in Economics from the University of Cincinnati and holds Master's degrees from Cincinnati and the Delhi School of Economics. His research spans Development, Public, and International Economics, Industrial Organization, and Labor Economics. He has been listed in Who's Who in the World and Who's Who in America.

This textbook is the derivatives volume of the MacroNations finance sequence. It follows Northwind Components, the manufacturer introduced in the MacroNations finance course, as the company hedges its commodity, currency, and interest rate exposures, and as investors trade options on its shares.

HOW TO USE THIS BOOK

The book is written to be read without an instructor. Every technical term is defined where it first appears, every result is followed by a numerical example, and every exercise has a worked solution. Most chapters open with a decision made on a live model; the theory then explains the outcome. Concept checks within the text give immediate feedback, interactive figures — several of them three-dimensional — allow each formula to be examined numerically, and each chapter closes with an auto-graded check that awards a chapter badge.

The core text requires algebra, elementary calculus, and introductory probability. Sections marked ★ contain derivations that may be omitted without loss of continuity; an MBA course may omit them, and an advanced undergraduate course may assign them. Chapters 1–2 and the Payoff Lab arena are open without a subscription.

Chapter 1 · Part I: Foundations

Derivative Markets and Instruments

The four basic contracts — forwards, futures, options, and swaps — the markets in which they trade, the participants who use them, and the no-arbitrage principle on which their valuation rests

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. define a derivative and identify its underlying asset, maturity, and notional amount;
  2. distinguish exchange-traded from over-the-counter markets and explain the function of a clearinghouse;
  3. write and graph the payoff and the profit of long and short positions in forwards, calls, and puts;
  4. explain how hedgers, speculators, and arbitrageurs use derivatives, and compute the outcome of each use;
  5. state the no-arbitrage principle and apply it to detect a mispriced forward contract.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

How much of Northwind's copper purchase should be hedged?

Northwind Components, a manufacturer, must purchase 500,000 pounds of copper six months from today. Copper trades today at $4.00 per pound. A bank offers a contract that fixes the price of copper for delivery in six months at $4.10 per pound; the contract costs nothing to enter. The price that will prevail in six months is unknown. Select the fraction of the purchase to cover with the contract, then examine the cost of the purchase across the range of possible copper prices.

Two features of the figure deserve attention before any terminology is introduced. First, the contract does not make copper cheaper in every outcome; its effect is to narrow the range of possible costs. Second, the protection is symmetric: the position that removes the loss from a price increase also removes the gain from a price decrease. The contract offered by the bank is a forward contract, the simplest derivative, and the decision just made is a hedging decision. Both are defined precisely below.

1.1  What a derivative is

A derivative is a financial contract whose value depends on the value of one or more other variables, called the underlying. The underlying is most often the price of a traded asset — a share of stock, a bond, a currency, a commodity such as copper or crude oil — but it may be any variable that can be observed and agreed upon: an interest rate, a stock index, the occurrence of a corporate default, or the temperature at a specified weather station. The contract is called a derivative because its value is derived from the underlying; it has no source of value independent of it.

The contract offered to Northwind illustrates the definition. Its underlying is the price of copper. If copper trades at $4.60 in six months, a contract to buy at $4.10 is valuable; if copper trades at $3.60, the same contract is a liability. Nothing about the contract changes between the two cases except the value of the underlying.

Key terms

Derivative: a contract whose value depends on the value of an underlying variable. Underlying: the asset, rate, index, or event on which the contract is written. Maturity (or expiration date): the date on which the contract is settled or ceases to exist. Notional amount: the quantity of the underlying to which the contract refers, used to compute the payments; for Northwind, 500,000 pounds of copper.

Every derivative specifies, at a minimum, the underlying, the notional amount, the maturity, and a rule that converts the value of the underlying into a payment. This rule is the payoff function. Much of this book concerns two questions about a given payoff function: what the contract is worth today, and how the risk of holding it can be managed. This chapter introduces the principal contracts and the reasoning that later chapters develop into quantitative methods.

Four contract types account for nearly all derivatives activity. A forward contract and a futures contract each commit two parties to a future transaction at a price fixed today. An option gives one party the right, without the obligation, to transact at a price fixed today. A swap commits two parties to exchange a series of cash flows. Sections 1.3 through 1.6 define each in turn.

1.2  Where derivatives trade

Derivatives trade in two kinds of markets, which differ in how contracts are designed and in who bears the risk that a party fails to perform.

Exchange-traded markets

A derivatives exchange is an organized market in which the contracts are standardized by the exchange. The exchange specifies the underlying, the contract size, the delivery dates, and the settlement procedure; the participants negotiate only the price. Standardization concentrates trading in a small number of contracts and so makes them liquid, meaning that they can be bought or sold quickly at a price close to the last traded price.

Each exchange operates or appoints a clearinghouse, an institution that becomes the legal counterparty to every trade: the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. A trader on an exchange is therefore exposed to the clearinghouse and not to the unknown party on the other side of the trade. The clearinghouse protects itself by requiring each participant to deposit collateral, called margin, and by settling gains and losses every day. Chapter 2 describes this mechanism in detail.

Over-the-counter markets

In the over-the-counter (OTC) market, two parties negotiate a contract directly, usually with a bank acting as dealer on one side. The terms can be tailored to the needs of the client: Northwind's contract can be written for exactly 500,000 pounds and exactly the date on which the copper is required. The cost of this flexibility is counterparty credit risk, the risk that the other party fails to make a required payment. Since the financial crisis of 2007–2009, regulators in most jurisdictions have required standardized OTC contracts to be cleared through a central counterparty (CCP), which performs for the OTC market the function that a clearinghouse performs for an exchange.

Table 1.1  Exchange-traded and over-the-counter markets compared
FeatureExchange-tradedOver-the-counter
Contract termsStandardized by the exchangeNegotiated by the two parties
CounterpartyThe clearinghouseThe other party, or a CCP if the contract is cleared
Credit riskSmall; controlled by margin and daily settlementPresent; controlled by collateral agreements or central clearing
LiquidityHigh in the actively traded contractsVaries with the contract; customized terms are costly to unwind
Typical instrumentsFutures; listed optionsForwards; swaps; customized options

The size of the market

The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) reports that the notional amount of OTC derivatives outstanding worldwide was $846 trillion at the end of June 2025. This figure is several times the value of world output, and it is frequently misread. The notional amount is the reference quantity from which payments are computed; for most contracts it is never exchanged. A more informative measure is the gross market value, the cost of replacing all outstanding contracts at current market prices, which the BIS reports as $21.8 trillion at the same date, or approximately 2.6 percent of the notional amount. Interest rate contracts form the largest category by a wide margin, followed by foreign exchange contracts.

Concept check 1.1

A corporation requires a contract on 37,500 barrels of jet fuel for delivery on a date that matches no listed contract. Which statement is correct?

1.3  Forward contracts

A forward contract is an agreement between two parties to buy or sell an asset at a specified future date for a price agreed today. The agreed price is the delivery price, denoted \(K\). No payment is made when the contract is entered; the delivery price is set so that the contract has zero value to both parties at inception. Forward contracts trade over the counter.

The party that agrees to buy the asset holds the long position; the party that agrees to sell holds the short position. These two terms recur throughout the book with the same meaning: a long position in any contract is the position of the buyer and gains when the price of the underlying rises; a short position is the position of the seller. Northwind, which agrees to buy copper, is long the forward; the bank is short.

By contrast, the spot price of an asset is its price for immediate delivery. Let \(S_T\) denote the spot price at the maturity date \(T\). The holder of the long position is obliged to pay \(K\) for an asset then worth \(S_T\). The payoff of a contract is the amount it delivers to its holder at maturity:

\[ \text{Payoff to long forward} = S_T - K, \qquad \text{Payoff to short forward} = K - S_T . \]

Both payoffs are stated per unit of the underlying. Two properties follow at once. The payoff may be positive or negative, since both parties are obliged to transact. And the two payoffs sum to zero for every value of \(S_T\): the gain of one party is the loss of the other. A contract with this property is a zero-sum contract.

Worked example 1.1 — Northwind's forward purchase
Northwind enters a long forward on 500,000 pounds of copper at \(K = \$4.10\). Find the payoff of the forward and the net cost of the copper if the spot price at maturity is (a) $4.60 and (b) $3.60.
1
Case (a). Payoff per pound is \(S_T - K = 4.60 - 4.10 = 0.50\). On 500,000 pounds the forward pays \(0.50 \times 500{,}000 = \$250{,}000\).
2
Northwind buys copper in the spot market for \(4.60 \times 500{,}000 = \$2{,}300{,}000\). Net cost: \(2{,}300{,}000 - 250{,}000 = \$2{,}050{,}000\).
3
Case (b). Payoff per pound is \(3.60 - 4.10 = -0.50\); the forward loses $250,000. Spot cost is \(3.60 \times 500{,}000 = \$1{,}800{,}000\). Net cost: \(1{,}800{,}000 + 250{,}000 = \$2{,}050{,}000\).
4
Conclusion. In both cases the net cost is \(4.10 \times 500{,}000 = \$2{,}050{,}000\). The forward fixes the cost at the delivery price whatever the spot price proves to be. In case (b) Northwind would have paid less without the contract; the forward removes favorable outcomes together with unfavorable ones.
Common error

A forward that ends with a negative payoff was not, for that reason, a poor decision. The purpose of Northwind's hedge is a known cost, and the hedge delivers a cost of $2,050,000 in every case. A hedge should be evaluated by the risk it removed and not by a comparison, available only after the fact, with the outcome of not hedging.

1.4  Futures contracts

A futures contract, like a forward, is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a future date for a price agreed today. It differs from a forward in three respects. It trades on an exchange. Its terms are standardized: a copper futures contract on the COMEX division of the CME Group, for example, covers 25,000 pounds of copper of a specified grade for delivery in a specified month. And its gains and losses are settled every trading day through the margin account of each party, a procedure known as daily settlement or marking to market, in place of a single settlement at maturity.

The price agreed in a futures contract is the futures price. At maturity the futures price converges to the spot price, and the total gain to a long position over the life of the contract equals the change in the futures price, as for a forward. Northwind could hedge with futures by taking a long position in 20 contracts, since \(20 \times 25{,}000 = 500{,}000\) pounds. Most futures positions are closed before maturity by entering the opposite trade, and the hedger then buys the physical commodity in the spot market in the usual way.

The economic content of futures and forwards is therefore the same, and for the purposes of this chapter the payoff \(S_T - K\) describes both. The institutional differences — margin, daily settlement, and the consequences of standardization for the quality of a hedge — are the subject of Chapters 2 and 5.

1.5  Options

A forward obliges both parties to transact. An option obliges only one of them. A call option gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying asset at a specified price on or before a specified date. A put option gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to sell the underlying asset at a specified price on or before a specified date. The specified price is the strike price or exercise price, denoted \(K\); the date is the expiration date. Using the right is called exercising the option.

A European option can be exercised only on the expiration date. An American option can be exercised at any time up to and including that date. The names describe the exercise rule and carry no geographic meaning; both kinds trade on every continent. Unless stated otherwise, the options in this chapter are European.

The party that buys an option holds the long position. The party that sells it holds the short position and is said to have written the option; this party is the writer. Because a right without an obligation cannot have negative value to its holder, the buyer must pay the writer for it. The price paid is the option premium. This is the essential difference from a forward: a forward costs nothing to enter and may end with a loss; an option costs the premium to acquire and can lose no more than that premium.

Payoffs at expiration

The holder of a call will exercise at expiration only if the asset is worth more than the strike price. If \(S_T > K\), exercising yields \(S_T - K\); otherwise the option expires unexercised and yields nothing. The holder of a put will exercise only if \(S_T < K\). The payoffs per unit of the underlying are therefore

\[ \text{Long call: } \max(S_T - K,\, 0), \qquad \text{Long put: } \max(K - S_T,\, 0). \]

The writer of each option receives the negative of these amounts: \(-\max(S_T - K, 0)\) for a short call and \(-\max(K - S_T, 0)\) for a short put. The profit of a position is its payoff adjusted for the premium: the buyer's profit is the payoff less the premium paid, and the writer's profit is the premium received less the amount paid out. For clarity of exposition this chapter ignores the interest that could be earned on the premium between purchase and expiration; later chapters account for it.

The stock price at which the profit of an option position is exactly zero is the breakeven price. For a call with premium \(c\) it is \(K + c\); for a put with premium \(p\) it is \(K - p\).

Table 1.2  The four basic option positions, per unit of the underlying (\(c\), \(p\) = call and put premiums)
PositionPayoff at expirationProfitMaximum gainMaximum loss
Long call\(\max(S_T-K,0)\)\(\max(S_T-K,0)-c\)Unlimited\(c\)
Short call\(-\max(S_T-K,0)\)\(c-\max(S_T-K,0)\)\(c\)Unlimited
Long put\(\max(K-S_T,0)\)\(\max(K-S_T,0)-p\)\(K-p\)\(p\)
Short put\(-\max(K-S_T,0)\)\(p-\max(K-S_T,0)\)\(p\)\(K-p\)

Worked example 1.2 — A call and a put on Northwind shares
Northwind shares trade at $28. A three-month European call with strike $30 costs $1.50 per share, and a three-month European put with strike $26 costs $1.20 per share. Each listed contract covers 100 shares. Find the profit on one contract of each if the share price at expiration is (a) $35 and (b) $22, and find each breakeven price.
1
Call, \(S_T = 35\). Payoff \(=\max(35-30,0)=5.00\). Profit per share \(=5.00-1.50=3.50\); per contract, \(3.50\times100=\$350\).
2
Call, \(S_T = 22\). Payoff \(=\max(22-30,0)=0\). The option expires unexercised; the loss is the premium, \(1.50\times100=\$150\).
3
Put, \(S_T = 35\). Payoff \(=\max(26-35,0)=0\). Loss \(=1.20\times100=\$120\).
4
Put, \(S_T = 22\). Payoff \(=\max(26-22,0)=4.00\). Profit per share \(=4.00-1.20=2.80\); per contract, $280.
5
Breakeven prices. Call: \(K+c=30+1.50=\$31.50\). Put: \(K-p=26-1.20=\$24.80\). The call buyer profits only if the share price rises by more than 12.5 percent from $28; a rise to $31 leaves the option exercised but the position at a loss of $0.50 per share.
Key terms — moneyness

An option is in the money if immediate exercise would produce a positive payoff (\(S > K\) for a call, \(S < K\) for a put), at the money if \(S = K\), and out of the money otherwise. Both options in Worked example 1.2 are out of the money when purchased.

Concept check 1.2

An investor writes one put contract (100 shares) with strike $40 for a premium of $3 per share. At expiration the share price is $34. What is the investor's profit?

1.6  Swaps

A swap is an agreement between two parties to exchange cash flows on a series of future dates according to a specified rule. In the most common form, the plain vanilla interest rate swap, one party pays interest at a fixed rate on a notional principal and receives interest at a floating rate, one that is reset each period to a market reference rate, on the same principal. Only the difference between the two interest amounts changes hands on each date, and the principal itself is never exchanged.

A swap can be understood as a portfolio of forward contracts, one for each payment date, and this observation is the basis of its valuation. A company with floating-rate debt that wishes to fix its interest cost can enter a swap to pay fixed and receive floating; the floating receipts offset the floating payments on the debt and leave a fixed net cost. Interest rate swaps are the largest single category of derivatives by notional amount. Chapter 7 treats swaps in full.

1.7  Why derivatives are traded: three kinds of participant

Participants in derivatives markets are conventionally divided into three groups according to their purpose. Hedgers use derivatives to reduce a risk that they already bear. Speculators use derivatives to take on risk in pursuit of profit, on the basis of a view about the future direction of a market variable. Arbitrageurs take offsetting positions in two or more instruments to lock in a profit without bearing risk. The same contract serves all three; what differs is the position the participant holds before the trade.

Hedging

Northwind's forward purchase of copper is a hedge: the company is exposed to an increase in the price of copper, and the long forward gains when that price rises. The general rule is that a hedge is a derivatives position whose gains occur in the circumstances in which the existing exposure produces losses. A firm that will buy an asset hedges with a long forward; a firm that will sell an asset hedges with a short forward.

Options provide a different kind of hedge. Consider an investor who owns 1,000 Northwind shares, worth $28,000, and fears a decline over the next three months. The investor may buy ten put contracts with strike $26 at $1.20 per share, for a total premium of $1,200. If the share price falls below $26, the puts are exercised and the shares are sold for $26,000; net of the premium the investor realizes no less than $24,800. If the share price rises, the puts expire unexercised and the investor retains the entire gain on the shares, less the $1,200 premium.

The comparison is fundamental. A forward hedge fixes the outcome and costs nothing at inception, but gives up the benefit of favorable price movements. An option hedge sets a limit on the adverse outcome while preserving the favorable one, and for this asymmetry the hedger pays a premium. An option used in this way is a form of insurance, and the premium is the price of that insurance.

Speculation and leverage

A speculator who expects Northwind shares to rise can buy the shares or buy call options. The two choices differ in leverage: the extent to which a given percentage change in the price of the underlying produces a larger percentage change in the value of the position.

Worked example 1.3 — Leverage in an option position
A speculator has $4,200 and expects Northwind, at $28, to rise within three months. Compare (i) buying shares with (ii) buying the $30-strike call at $1.50, if the share price at expiration is $35 and if it is $29.
1
Positions. (i) \(4{,}200/28=150\) shares. (ii) \(4{,}200/1.50=2{,}800\) calls, that is, 28 contracts.
2
\(S_T=35\). Shares: \(150\times(35-28)=\$1{,}050\), a return of 25 percent. Calls: payoff \(2{,}800\times5=14{,}000\); profit \(14{,}000-4{,}200=\$9{,}800\), a return of 233 percent.
3
\(S_T=29\). Shares: \(150\times1=\$150\), a return of 3.6 percent. Calls: the payoff is zero because \(29<30\); the loss is $4,200, a return of −100 percent.
4
Conclusion. The option position magnifies both outcomes. The speculator was correct about the direction of the price in both cases, yet in the second case lost the entire investment because the rise was too small. A view on direction is not sufficient for an option position to profit; the magnitude and the timing of the movement matter as well.

Arbitrage

An arbitrage opportunity is a trading strategy that requires no net investment, has no possibility of a loss, and has a positive probability of a gain. The simplest case involves the same asset trading in two markets. Suppose that a share trades at $28.00 in New York and at £22.00 in London when the exchange rate is $1.30 per pound. The London price is equivalent to \(22.00\times1.30=\$28.60\). A trader who simultaneously buys in New York and sells in London earns $0.60 per share, before transaction costs, without bearing any risk.

Such an opportunity cannot persist. Purchases in New York raise the price there, sales in London lower the price there, and the two prices converge until the remaining difference is no larger than the cost of trading. The proposition that two assets, or two portfolios, with identical future payoffs must have the same price today is the law of one price.

Principle 1.1 — No arbitrage

In a market in which participants can trade freely, prices adjust until no arbitrage opportunity remains. Consequently, if a portfolio of traded assets reproduces the payoff of a derivative in every future state, the value of the derivative today must equal the cost of that portfolio.

A portfolio that reproduces the payoff of a derivative is a replicating portfolio. Principle 1.1 is the foundation of the theory of derivatives valuation. It requires no forecast of the price of the underlying and no assumption about the attitudes of investors toward risk; it requires only that identical payoffs cannot sell at different prices. Every valuation formula in this book, from the forward price in Chapter 4 to the Black–Scholes–Merton formula in Chapter 12, is an application of this single principle. Section 1.9 presents the first such application.

Concept check 1.3

A grain exporter will receive 2 million euros in four months and will convert them to dollars. The exporter enters a forward contract today to sell 2 million euros in four months at $1.10 per euro. How should this trade be classified?

1.8  The value of a derivative before maturity

Payoff diagrams describe a contract at a single date, its maturity. Before maturity, the value of a derivative depends on the current price of the underlying and also on the time that remains. An option that is out of the money today is not worthless, because the price of the underlying may yet move through the strike. The value of an option can accordingly be separated into two parts. Its intrinsic value is the payoff it would have if it were exercised immediately, \(\max(S-K,0)\) for a call. Its time value is the excess of its market value over its intrinsic value.

Interactive figure 1.2 presents the value of the $30-strike call on Northwind shares as a surface over two variables: the share price and the time remaining to expiration. The surface is computed from the Black–Scholes–Merton model, derived in Chapter 12, with a risk-free interest rate of 5 percent and a volatility of 39 percent per year; at a share price of $28 with three months remaining, the model value is approximately $1.52, close to the premium used in the examples above. The model need not be understood at this stage. The purpose of the figure is geometric: as the time remaining falls to zero, the smooth surface descends onto the angular payoff diagram of Section 1.5.

1.9  ★ A first no-arbitrage valuation: the forward price of a stock

Optional section. Sections marked with a star present derivations that may be omitted on a first reading without loss of continuity. This section uses continuous compounding: an amount \(A\) invested at the continuously compounded annual rate \(r\) for \(T\) years grows to \(Ae^{rT}\). Chapter 3 develops compounding conventions in full.

Section 1.3 stated that the delivery price of a forward is set so that the contract has zero value at inception. The delivery price with this property is the forward price, denoted \(F_0\). Principle 1.1 determines it exactly.

Proposition 1.1 — Forward price of an asset that pays no income

Let \(S_0\) be the spot price of an asset that pays no dividends or other income before date \(T\) and that can be stored at no cost, and let \(r\) be the continuously compounded risk-free interest rate for maturity \(T\). If there are no arbitrage opportunities, the forward price for delivery at \(T\) is \[ F_0 = S_0\,e^{rT}. \]

Proof. Consider two strategies, each of which delivers one unit of the asset at date \(T\). Under strategy A, the investor enters a long forward at delivery price \(F_0\) and pays \(F_0\) at \(T\). Under strategy B, the investor borrows \(S_0\) today, buys the asset, holds it, and repays \(S_0e^{rT}\) at \(T\). Neither strategy requires a net outlay today, and each leaves the investor holding one unit of the asset at \(T\). By the law of one price, the payments at \(T\) must be equal.

To confirm that any other price permits arbitrage, suppose first that \(F_0 > S_0e^{rT}\). An arbitrageur borrows \(S_0\), buys the asset, and enters a short forward. At \(T\) the asset is delivered for \(F_0\) and the loan is repaid, leaving \(F_0 - S_0e^{rT} > 0\) with certainty and no initial investment. This strategy is a cash-and-carry arbitrage. Suppose instead that \(F_0 < S_0e^{rT}\). An arbitrageur sells the asset short — that is, borrows the asset and sells it, with an obligation to return it later — invests the proceeds \(S_0\) at the rate \(r\), and enters a long forward. At \(T\) the investment is worth \(S_0e^{rT}\), the asset is bought for \(F_0\) under the forward and returned, and \(S_0e^{rT} - F_0 > 0\) remains. This is a reverse cash-and-carry arbitrage. Since both inequalities admit arbitrage, \(F_0 = S_0e^{rT}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Worked example 1.4 — Detecting a mispriced forward
Northwind shares trade at $28 and will pay no dividend in the next six months. The six-month risk-free rate is 5 percent per year, continuously compounded. A dealer quotes a six-month forward price of $29.50. Is there an arbitrage opportunity?
1
No-arbitrage forward price. \(F_0 = 28\,e^{0.05\times0.5} = 28\times1.025315 = \$28.71\).
2
Comparison. The quoted price, $29.50, exceeds $28.71. The forward is overpriced; it should be sold, and the share bought.
3
Strategy today. Borrow $28 for six months; buy one share; enter a short forward at $29.50. Net cash flow today: zero.
4
In six months. Deliver the share and receive $29.50; repay \(28e^{0.025}=\$28.71\). Riskless profit: \(29.50-28.71=\$0.79\) per share, whatever the share price is on that date.

The proposition contains no expectation of the future spot price. Two investors who disagree entirely about the prospects of Northwind must nonetheless agree on its forward price, because that price is fixed by the cost of the replicating strategy. Chapter 4 extends the result to assets that pay income, to currencies, and to commodities with storage costs.

1.10  The risks of derivatives

The leverage that makes derivatives efficient instruments for hedging makes them equally efficient instruments for taking large risks, and a position that was established as a hedge can become a speculation if it is enlarged beyond the exposure it was meant to offset. Several of the largest trading losses on record arose in this manner or from positions that were not supervised adequately.

Barings Bank1995Nikkei 225 futures and options£827 millionUnauthorized speculation by a single trader who also controlled settlement
Long-Term Capital Management1998Swaps and other relative-value positions$4.6 billionExtreme leverage; positions that lost value together in a crisis
Société Générale2008Equity index futures€4.9 billionUnauthorized positions concealed by fictitious offsetting trades
American International Group2008Credit default swapsGovernment support of $182 billionUnhedged sale of credit protection; collateral calls as credit markets fell

The cases share common elements: positions large relative to capital, inadequate separation between those who trade and those who record and monitor the trades, and insufficient attention to the cash required to maintain a position before it matures. The final chapter of this book returns to these episodes with the analytical tools developed in the intervening chapters. The lesson to carry forward is that the purpose of a derivatives position must be defined before the position is taken, and its risk measured continuously thereafter.

Historical note

Contracts for future delivery are far older than modern finance. Rice merchants at the Dōjima exchange in Osaka traded standardized contracts on future rice deliveries from the early eighteenth century, and the shogunate recognized the market officially in 1730. The Chicago Board of Trade, founded in 1848, standardized grain contracts in the following decades to serve the farmers and merchants of the American Midwest.

Two events in the spring of 1973 mark the beginning of the modern market. The Chicago Board Options Exchange opened for trading in listed call options on sixteen stocks in April, and in the same year Fischer Black and Myron Scholes, and separately Robert Merton, published the valuation theory that bears their names. For this work Scholes and Merton received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1997; Black had died in 1995.

Summary

  • A derivative is a contract whose value depends on an underlying variable. Its payoff function converts the value of the underlying at maturity into a payment.
  • Derivatives trade on exchanges, where contracts are standardized and a clearinghouse stands between the parties, and over the counter, where contracts are negotiated and counterparty credit risk must be managed.
  • A forward or futures contract obliges both parties to transact at a price fixed today. The long position pays \(S_T-K\) and the short position \(K-S_T\).
  • An option gives its holder a right without an obligation, in exchange for a premium. A call pays \(\max(S_T-K,0)\) and a put \(\max(K-S_T,0)\); profit equals payoff adjusted for the premium.
  • Hedgers reduce an existing risk, speculators accept risk on the basis of a view, and arbitrageurs lock in riskless profit from mispricing.
  • The absence of arbitrage implies that a derivative is worth the cost of the portfolio that replicates it. For an asset that pays no income, the forward price is \(F_0=S_0e^{rT}\).

Exercises

1.1 An investor enters a short forward contract to sell 100,000 British pounds at $1.2700 per pound. What is the investor's gain or loss if the exchange rate at maturity is (a) $1.2500 and (b) $1.3000?

The short forward pays \(K-S_T\) per pound. (a) \((1.2700-1.2500)\times100{,}000=\$2{,}000\) gain. (b) \((1.2700-1.3000)\times100{,}000=-\$3{,}000\), a loss of $3,000.

1.2 A European call with strike $50 costs $2.50. Write the profit of the buyer as a function of \(S_T\), state the breakeven price, and state the range of \(S_T\) over which the option is exercised.

Profit \(=\max(S_T-50,0)-2.50\). Breakeven: \(50+2.50=\$52.50\). The option is exercised whenever \(S_T>50\). For \(50<S_T<52.50\) it is exercised at a net loss, because exercise recovers part of the premium.

1.3 An investor writes five put contracts (100 shares each) with strike $60 for a premium of $4 per share. Compute the profit if the share price at expiration is (a) $66, (b) $58, and (c) $50. What is the maximum possible loss?

Profit per share \(=4-\max(60-S_T,0)\), on 500 shares. (a) \(4\times500=\$2{,}000\). (b) \((4-2)\times500=\$1{,}000\). (c) \((4-10)\times500=-\$3{,}000\). The maximum loss occurs at \(S_T=0\): \((4-60)\times500=-\$28{,}000\).

1.4 A share trades at $40. A three-month call with strike $42 costs $2. A speculator has $8,000. Compare the dollar profit and the percentage return from buying shares and from buying calls if the share price in three months is (a) $48 and (b) $41.

Shares: 200. Calls: 4,000. (a) Shares: \(200\times8=\$1{,}600\) (20%). Calls: \(4{,}000\times6-8{,}000=\$16{,}000\) (200%). (b) Shares: \(200\times1=\$200\) (2.5%). Calls: payoff zero; loss $8,000 (−100%).

1.5 A United States importer must pay 50 million yen in three months. Describe a hedge using (a) a forward contract and (b) an option, stating in each case the position taken, and explain the difference between the two outcomes.

(a) A long forward to buy 50 million yen fixes the dollar cost at the forward rate, whatever the spot rate. (b) A call option on yen (the right to buy yen at a strike exchange rate) sets a maximum dollar cost equal to the strike plus the premium, while leaving the importer free to buy at the spot rate if the yen depreciates. The forward costs nothing at inception and removes both adverse and favorable outcomes; the option requires a premium and removes only the adverse outcomes.

1.6 Explain why the writer of an option, unlike the buyer, is normally required by an exchange to post margin.

After paying the premium, the buyer has no further obligation and so cannot default. The writer has an obligation to pay \(\max(S_T-K,0)\) or \(\max(K-S_T,0)\) on exercise, an amount that may be many times the premium received. Margin secures the performance of that obligation to the clearinghouse.

1.7 ★ A share that pays no dividend trades at $80. The one-year risk-free rate is 4 percent, continuously compounded. (a) Compute the one-year forward price. (b) A dealer quotes $82.00. Describe the arbitrage and compute the profit per share.

(a) \(F_0=80e^{0.04}=80\times1.040811=\$83.26\). (b) The quoted forward is below \(F_0\), so it is underpriced: enter a long forward, sell the share short for $80, and invest the proceeds. In one year the investment is worth $83.26; buy the share for $82.00 under the forward and return it. Profit: \(83.26-82.00=\$1.26\) per share (reverse cash-and-carry).

1.8 “The notional amount of derivatives outstanding exceeds world output several times over; the market is therefore a threat to the world economy of the same magnitude.” Evaluate this statement.

The inference is unsound. The notional amount is a reference quantity for computing payments and, for most contracts, is never exchanged; the amount at risk is far smaller. Gross market value, the replacement cost of outstanding contracts, was about 2.6 percent of notional at mid-2025, and netting and collateral reduce exposure further. The statement is correct only to the extent that notional amounts indicate the scale of activity and that concentrated, poorly collateralized exposures can transmit losses, as in 2008. The appropriate measures of risk are market value, exposure after netting and collateral, and the concentration of that exposure.

Chapter 1 Check — Derivative Markets and Instruments

8 questions · pass at 70%
Chapter 2 · Part I: Foundations

Mechanics of Futures and Forward Markets

How a futures contract is specified, how margin and daily settlement remove credit risk, how positions are closed or delivered, and how these arrangements differ from those of a forward contract

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. read a futures contract specification and compute the dollar value of a price change;
  2. explain why the futures price converges to the spot price at maturity;
  3. construct the daily record of a margin account, including margin calls;
  4. describe the role of the clearinghouse and of central counterparties in over-the-counter markets;
  5. distinguish closing out, physical delivery, and cash settlement, and interpret volume and open interest;
  6. compare the cash flows of a futures position with those of an otherwise identical forward.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

How much cash must Northwind hold in reserve to keep its hedge?

Northwind Components hedges its purchase of 500,000 pounds of copper, due in six months, with a long position in 20 copper futures contracts at $4.10 per pound. The exchange requires a deposit of $120,000 when the position is opened. Losses on the position are collected in cash each day, and if the deposit is depleted Northwind must replenish it at once or lose the position. Select the cash reserve, beyond the initial deposit, that the treasurer should set aside for this purpose. Any balance above the required deposit is returned to the reserve each day.

The simulation assumes daily price changes with a standard deviation of 1.4 percent and no trend. The hedge is sound in every simulated path: a loss on the futures is matched by a lower cost of copper at the end of the six months. The difficulty is one of timing. The futures losses must be paid in cash as they occur, while the offsetting saving arrives only when the copper is bought. A hedger who cannot meet a margin call loses the hedge at the moment it is most needed. This chapter explains the mechanism that produces these cash demands and the reason exchanges impose it.

2.1  The specification of a futures contract

Chapter 1 defined a futures contract as a standardized agreement, traded on an exchange, to buy or sell an asset at a future date for a price agreed today. Because the two parties to a futures trade do not negotiate with each other, the exchange must state in advance every term other than the price. This statement is the contract specification. It has five principal elements.

The underlying asset. For a financial asset such as a currency or a stock index, the asset is unambiguous. For a commodity, quality varies, and the exchange specifies the grades that may be delivered and any price adjustment for each. The copper contract of the COMEX division of CME Group, for example, calls for Grade 1 electrolytic copper cathodes.

The contract size. The contract size is the quantity of the asset to be delivered under one contract. It determines the notional value of a contract, equal to the futures price multiplied by the contract size. A copper futures price of $4.10 per pound and a contract size of 25,000 pounds give a notional value of \(4.10\times25{,}000=\$102{,}500\).

The delivery arrangements. The exchange specifies where and how delivery may be made. For many commodities the party with the short position may choose among several approved locations.

The delivery months. A contract is identified by its delivery month, such as the December copper contract. The exchange specifies which months are listed, the period within the month during which delivery may occur, and the last day on which the contract trades.

The price quotation and limits. The exchange specifies the units in which the price is quoted and the tick size, the smallest permitted price change. Multiplying the tick size by the contract size gives the tick value, the change in the value of one contract when the price moves by one tick. Many exchanges also set daily price limits, which halt or restrict trading when the price moves by more than a stated amount in one day, and position limits, which cap the number of contracts a single speculator may hold.

Table 2.1  Specifications of five actively traded CME Group futures contracts
ContractContract sizePrice quotationTick sizeTick valueSettlement
Copper (COMEX)25,000 poundsDollars per pound$0.0005$12.50Physical delivery
Gold (COMEX)100 troy ouncesDollars per ounce$0.10$10.00Physical delivery
WTI crude oil (NYMEX)1,000 barrelsDollars per barrel$0.01$10.00Physical delivery
E-mini S&P 500$50 × indexIndex points0.25 point$12.50Cash
Euro FX€125,000Dollars per euro$0.00005$6.25Physical delivery

The practical use of the specification is the conversion of a price change into a monetary gain or loss:

\[ \text{Gain on a long position} = (\text{change in futures price}) \times (\text{contract size}) \times (\text{number of contracts}). \]

The gain on a short position is the negative of this amount. If copper futures rise from $4.10 to $4.16, a long position of 20 contracts gains \(0.06\times25{,}000\times20=\$30{,}000\).

Concept check 2.1

A trader is short 8 E-mini S&P 500 contracts. The futures price rises from 5,812.50 to 5,830.00. What is the trader's gain or loss?

2.2  Convergence of the futures price to the spot price

As the delivery period of a futures contract approaches, the futures price converges to the spot price of the underlying asset, and during the delivery period the two are equal or very nearly so. The reason is an arbitrage argument of the kind introduced in Section 1.7.

Suppose that during the delivery period the futures price were above the spot price. A trader could sell a futures contract, buy the asset in the spot market, and make delivery, receiving the futures price for an asset bought at the lower spot price. The profit would be immediate and without risk. Traders exploiting it would sell futures and buy the asset until the difference disappeared. Suppose instead that the futures price were below the spot price. Any firm that intended to acquire the asset would buy futures and take delivery in preference to buying in the spot market, and this demand would raise the futures price. In either case the difference cannot persist.

The difference between the spot price and the futures price at any time is the basis:

\[ \text{Basis} = \text{Spot price} - \text{Futures price}. \]

Convergence is the statement that the basis approaches zero at maturity. Before maturity the basis may be positive or negative and it changes from day to day; Chapter 4 determines its theoretical value, and Chapter 5 examines the risk it creates for hedgers.

2.3  Margin accounts and daily settlement

Two parties who agree to trade at a future date each bear the risk that the other will not perform. A party whose position has lost value has an incentive to default, and may lack the means to pay. The exchange removes this risk by two devices used together: margin, and the daily settlement of gains and losses.

A trader who enters a futures position must deposit funds with a broker in a margin account. The amount required when the position is opened is the initial margin. It is a performance deposit and not a payment toward the asset; it remains the property of the trader. At the end of each trading day the exchange announces a settlement price for the contract, and every margin account is adjusted to reflect the day's gain or loss. This procedure is daily settlement, also called marking to market. If the futures price rose during the day, the accounts of traders with long positions are credited, and the accounts of traders with short positions are debited by the same total amount; if the price fell, the transfers run the other way.

To ensure that the balance never becomes negative, the exchange sets a maintenance margin, somewhat below the initial margin. If the balance falls below the maintenance margin, the trader receives a margin call and must deposit additional funds to restore the balance to the initial margin level, and not merely to the maintenance level. The amount deposited in response to a margin call is the variation margin. A trader who does not meet the call has the position closed by the broker. A trader may withdraw any balance in excess of the initial margin.

Key terms

Initial margin: the deposit required when a position is opened. Maintenance margin: the balance below which a margin call is issued. Margin call: a demand for additional funds. Variation margin: the funds deposited to return the balance to the initial margin. Settlement price: the price, set by the exchange at the close of each day, at which gains and losses are computed.

Worked example 2.1 — Northwind's margin account
Northwind takes a long position in 20 copper futures at $4.10. The initial margin is $6,000 per contract and the maintenance margin is $4,500 per contract. Settlement prices on the next five days are $4.08, $4.05, $4.03, $4.06, and $4.12. Construct the record of the margin account.
1
Set-up. The position covers \(20\times25{,}000=500{,}000\) pounds. Initial margin: \(20\times6{,}000=\$120{,}000\). Maintenance margin: \(20\times4{,}500=\$90{,}000\).
2
Day 1. The price falls by $0.02. Loss: \(0.02\times500{,}000=\$10{,}000\). Balance: $110,000, which is above $90,000; no call.
3
Day 2. The price falls by $0.03. Loss: $15,000. Balance: $95,000; no call.
4
Day 3. The price falls by $0.02. Loss: $10,000. Balance: $85,000, which is below $90,000. Margin call: \(120{,}000-85{,}000=\$35{,}000\). Balance after the deposit: $120,000.
5
Days 4 and 5. The price rises by $0.03 and then by $0.06. Gains: $15,000 and $30,000. Balances: $135,000 and $165,000. Northwind may withdraw up to $45,000.
6
Check. The futures price rose from $4.10 to $4.12 over the five days, a cumulative gain of \(0.02\times500{,}000=\$10{,}000\). Final balance: \(120{,}000+35{,}000+10{,}000=\$165{,}000\). The total gain depends only on the first and last prices; the path of prices determines the margin calls.
⚙ Interactive figure 2.1 — The margin account, day by day

Daily settlement of 20 copper futures

The table and figure reproduce Worked example 2.1. Change the side of the position, or generate a new ten-day path of settlement prices, and confirm each entry by hand: the daily gain, the test against the maintenance margin, and the size of each margin call.

Common error

A margin call restores the balance to the initial margin, not to the maintenance margin. In Worked example 2.1 the call on Day 3 is $35,000, the amount that returns the balance from $85,000 to $120,000. A deposit of $5,000, which would raise the balance only to the maintenance level of $90,000, does not satisfy the call.

Margin levels are set by the exchange with reference to the variability of the futures price: the more variable the price, the higher the margin. The initial margin is typically chosen to cover the loss on a position over one or two days with a high degree of confidence, and it is revised when market conditions change. Margin is commonly a small fraction of notional value, here \(6{,}000/102{,}500\), or about 5.9 percent, and this is the source of the leverage in futures positions discussed in Chapter 1. Most brokers pay interest on cash margin balances, and securities such as Treasury bills are usually accepted in place of cash at a discount to their market value, known as a haircut.

2.4  The clearinghouse and central clearing

The clearinghouse of an exchange stands between the two parties to every trade. Once a trade is matched, the clearinghouse becomes the buyer to the seller and the seller to the buyer, so that each party's contract is with the clearinghouse alone. Only clearing members, which are firms that meet the capital requirements of the clearinghouse, deal with it directly; a broker that is not a clearing member must clear its trades through a firm that is. The margin that a clearing member posts with the clearinghouse is clearing margin. It is settled daily in the same manner as a customer's account, with one difference: there is no maintenance level, and the balance is restored to the required amount every day.

The clearinghouse is protected by a sequence of resources, applied in order if a member defaults: the margin of the defaulting member; that member's contribution to a default fund (or guaranty fund) to which all members contribute; a portion of the clearinghouse's own capital; and the default fund contributions of the surviving members. This ordered sequence is the default waterfall. Its design gives every member an interest in the soundness of the others, and losses to customers from the failure of a major clearinghouse have been rare.

Central clearing in over-the-counter markets

Before the financial crisis of 2007–2009, most OTC derivatives were cleared bilaterally: the two parties dealt directly with each other under a master agreement, usually one published by the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA), with or without an annex requiring collateral. The failure of Lehman Brothers in September 2008, with a very large number of OTC contracts outstanding, showed how difficult it was to assess exposures in a bilateral market.

Regulation since then, including the Dodd–Frank Act in the United States and the European Market Infrastructure Regulation in the European Union, requires standardized OTC derivatives between financial institutions to be cleared through a central counterparty (CCP). A CCP performs the function of an exchange clearinghouse: it becomes the counterparty to both sides, collects initial margin, and settles variation margin daily. Contracts that remain bilateral are subject to rules that require most financial institutions to exchange both initial and variation margin. The OTC market has therefore moved substantially toward the arrangements long used for futures.

2.5  Closing out, delivery, and open interest

The great majority of futures contracts do not lead to delivery. A trader leaves the market by closing out the position, that is, by entering the opposite trade in the same contract. A trader who is long 20 December copper contracts sells 20 December copper contracts; the clearinghouse nets the two positions to zero, and the trader's total gain or loss is the difference between the price at which the contracts were sold and the price at which they were bought. A hedger such as Northwind normally closes out its futures shortly before the delivery month and purchases copper from its usual supplier; convergence ensures that the gain or loss on the futures offsets the change in the spot price it pays.

If a position is held to maturity, it is settled in one of two ways. Under physical delivery, the party with the short position delivers the asset and receives the settlement price; the exchange specifies the procedure, which begins when the short issues a notice of intention to deliver. Under cash settlement, used where delivery of the underlying is impractical, as with a stock index, all open positions are marked to a final settlement price based on the spot value of the underlying, and no asset changes hands.

Two statistics describe the activity in a contract. Trading volume is the number of contracts traded during a day. Open interest is the number of contracts outstanding at a point in time, which equals the total of all long positions and, equivalently, the total of all short positions. A trade changes open interest according to the positions of the two parties before it.

Table 2.2  Effect of one trade of one contract on open interest
BuyerSellerChange in open interest
Opens a new long positionOpens a new short positionIncreases by one
Opens a new long positionCloses an existing long positionNo change
Closes an existing short positionOpens a new short positionNo change
Closes an existing short positionCloses an existing long positionDecreases by one
Concept check 2.2

On a given day 3,000 contracts trade. In 1,800 of these trades both parties open new positions; in 700 both parties close existing positions; in the remaining 500 one party opens and the other closes. By how much does open interest change?

2.6  Orders and market participants

A trader communicates an intention to trade through an order. A market order is an instruction to trade at once at the best price available. A limit order specifies a price and may be executed only at that price or one more favorable to the trader; it guarantees the price but not execution. A stop order, or stop-loss order, becomes a market order when the price reaches a specified level that is less favorable than the current price, and is used to limit the loss on an existing position. Orders are valid for the trading day unless stated otherwise; an order that remains in force until executed or cancelled is a good-till-cancelled order.

Nearly all futures trading is now electronic: orders are entered into the exchange's matching system, which pairs buyers with sellers by price and then by time of entry. In reports published by regulators such as the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in the United States, participants are classified as commercial traders, who use futures in connection with a business in the underlying asset and are predominantly hedgers, and non-commercial traders, who are predominantly speculators.

2.7  Forward contracts and futures contracts compared

Table 2.3  Forward and futures contracts
FeatureForwardFutures
MarketOver the counterExchange
TermsNegotiated; any quantity and dateStandardized size, grade, and delivery months
Settlement of gains and lossesOnce, at maturity (unless collateral is exchanged)Daily, through the margin account
CounterpartyThe other party, or a CCP if clearedThe clearinghouse
Usual terminationDelivery or final cash settlementClosing out before maturity
Delivery dateA single specified dateUsually a range of dates in the delivery month

The total gain on a futures position held to maturity equals that on a forward with the same price and size. What differs is its timing. Had Northwind entered a forward at $4.10 in place of the futures in Worked example 2.1, it would have paid and received nothing during the five days; the futures position required a payment of $35,000 on Day 3 and stood $45,000 above the required balance on Day 5. The opening exercise of this chapter measured the consequence: a futures hedge must be supported by liquid funds that a forward hedge, in the absence of a collateral agreement, does not require. In exchange, the futures position carries almost no credit risk and can be closed at any time at a market price.

★ Optional note: are forward and futures prices equal? When interest rates are constant, the forward price and the futures price for the same asset and maturity are equal. When interest rates vary unpredictably, they can differ. Suppose that the price of the underlying asset tends to rise when interest rates rise. A long futures position then receives its daily gains when rates are high, so that the gains can be invested at high rates, and pays its daily losses when rates are low, so that they can be financed cheaply. A long forward has no such advantage, because it settles only at maturity. The futures contract is therefore the more attractive of the two, and its price is slightly higher. When the correlation is negative, the futures price is slightly lower. For contracts with maturities of a few months the difference is usually negligible, and it is ignored in this book except in the treatment of interest rate futures in Chapter 6.

Concept check 2.3

A company can hedge a purchase due in nine months with either a forward contract from its bank or exchange-traded futures. Which consideration favors the forward?

Historical note

In the nineteenth-century grain markets of Chicago, contracts for future delivery were settled between the parties themselves, and defaults followed every sharp movement in prices. The Chicago Board of Trade responded in stages: it standardized contract terms in 1865 and required margin deposits in the same period, and in 1925 it established the Board of Trade Clearing Corporation, which took the opposite side of every trade.

The episode of Metallgesellschaft in 1993, listed in Table 1.3, is the standard illustration of the liquidity demands of daily settlement. A subsidiary had sold long-term fixed-price contracts to supply petroleum products and hedged them with short-dated oil futures that were renewed as they matured. When oil prices fell, the futures produced immediate losses that had to be paid in cash, while the offsetting gains on the supply contracts would be received only over years. The parent company closed the positions at a loss of approximately $1.3 billion.

Summary

  • A futures contract specification fixes the asset, the contract size, the delivery arrangements and months, and the manner of price quotation. The gain on a long position is the price change multiplied by the contract size and the number of contracts.
  • Arbitrage between the spot and futures markets forces the futures price to converge to the spot price at maturity; the basis, spot minus futures, approaches zero.
  • Gains and losses are settled daily through margin accounts. A balance below the maintenance margin produces a margin call for the amount that restores the initial margin.
  • The clearinghouse is the counterparty to every trade and is protected by margin and by a default waterfall. Standardized OTC derivatives are now cleared through central counterparties in a similar way.
  • Most futures positions are closed out before maturity; the remainder are settled by physical delivery or in cash. Open interest counts the contracts outstanding; volume counts the contracts traded.
  • A futures position and a forward position produce the same total gain but different cash flows over time. Daily settlement removes credit risk and creates a need for liquidity.

Exercises

2.1 A trader buys 5 gold futures contracts at $2,640.00 per ounce and closes the position at $2,611.50. Using Table 2.1, compute the gain or loss.

Price change: \(2{,}611.50-2{,}640.00=-28.50\) per ounce. Loss: \(28.50\times100\times5=\$14{,}250\).

2.2 A trader takes a short position in 4 crude oil futures at $72.00 per barrel. The initial margin is $7,000 per contract and the maintenance margin is $5,500 per contract. At what futures price does the trader receive a margin call? How much could be withdrawn if the price fell to $70.00?

Initial margin $28,000; maintenance $22,000. A call occurs when losses exceed $6,000. A short position loses when the price rises: \(6{,}000/(4\times1{,}000)=\$1.50\) per barrel, so a call occurs if the settlement price is above $73.50. At $70.00 the gain is \(2.00\times4{,}000=\$8{,}000\); the balance is $36,000 and $8,000 may be withdrawn.

2.3 A trader is long 10 Euro FX futures entered at 1.1000. Initial margin is $2,800 per contract and maintenance margin $2,500 per contract. Settlement prices on the next four days are 1.0990, 1.0965, 1.0950, and 1.1010. Construct the margin account.

The position covers €1,250,000; initial margin $28,000; maintenance $25,000. Day 1: \(-0.0010\times1{,}250{,}000=-\$1{,}250\); balance $26,750. Day 2: \(-0.0025\times1{,}250{,}000=-\$3{,}125\); balance $23,625, below $25,000; margin call $4,375; balance $28,000. Day 3: \(-\$1{,}875\); balance $26,125. Day 4: \(+0.0060\times1{,}250{,}000=+\$7{,}500\); balance $33,625. Check: cumulative gain \(0.0010\times1{,}250{,}000=\$1{,}250\); \(28{,}000+4{,}375+1{,}250=\$33{,}625\).

2.4 Explain why the futures price cannot remain above the spot price during the delivery period. What would a trader do if it did?

A trader would sell futures, buy the asset in the spot market, and deliver it against the futures, receiving the futures price for an asset bought at the lower spot price. The profit is immediate and riskless. The selling of futures lowers the futures price and the buying of the asset raises the spot price until the two are equal, apart from the costs of delivery.

2.5 The initial margin on a stock index futures contract with a notional value of $290,000 is $14,500. (a) What percentage of notional value is the margin? (b) If the index falls by 2 percent in a day, what is the loss on a long position as a percentage of the margin deposited?

(a) \(14{,}500/290{,}000=5\) percent. (b) The loss is \(0.02\times290{,}000=\$5{,}800\), which is \(5{,}800/14{,}500=40\) percent of the margin. A margin of 5 percent implies leverage of twenty to one.

2.6 Open interest in a contract is 42,000 at the start of a day. During the day 9,000 contracts trade: in 4,000 trades both parties open positions, in 3,500 one party opens and one closes, and in 1,500 both close. What is open interest at the end of the day?

\(42{,}000+4{,}000-1{,}500=44{,}500\). The 3,500 trades in which one party opens and the other closes leave open interest unchanged.

2.7 Describe the default waterfall of a clearinghouse and explain why surviving members' contributions are placed last.

Losses from a member's default are met, in order, from that member's margin, that member's default fund contribution, a portion of the clearinghouse's own capital, and the default fund contributions of surviving members. Placing the defaulter's resources first ensures that each member bears the cost of its own risk; placing the clearinghouse's capital before the survivors' funds gives the clearinghouse an incentive to set margins prudently; mutualizing the remaining loss among survivors gives every member an interest in admission standards and in the monitoring of others.

2.8 A firm has sold a product forward to customers at fixed prices for delivery over five years and hedges with three-month futures that it renews each quarter. Identify the principal risk of this arrangement, with reference to the mechanics of this chapter.

The risk is a mismatch in the timing of cash flows. A fall in the price produces losses on the long futures that are settled in cash at once through margin calls, while the corresponding gains on the fixed-price sales are realized only as deliveries occur over five years. The firm must finance the margin calls in the interval. If it cannot, it must close the hedge at a loss and remain exposed on the supply contracts. This was the position of Metallgesellschaft in 1993.

Chapter 3 · Part I: Foundations

Interest Rates, Discounting, and Forward Rates

The measurement of interest rates, the conversion between compounding conventions, the zero curve and its construction, forward rates, and the sensitivity of bond prices to interest rates

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. identify the reference rates used in derivatives markets and the rate used as the risk-free rate;
  2. convert an interest rate from one compounding frequency to another, including continuous compounding;
  3. price a coupon bond from zero rates and compute its yield and par yield;
  4. construct a zero curve from bond prices by the bootstrap method;
  5. compute forward rates from zero rates and explain the relation between the two curves;
  6. compute the duration of a bond and use it to estimate the effect of a change in yield.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

Which bank offers Northwind the highest return?

Northwind's treasurer has $10,000,000 to deposit for one year and receives three quotations. The three banks are of equal credit quality. Select the deposit that produces the most interest.

Select a quotation.

3.1  Interest rates in derivatives markets

An interest rate is the amount a borrower promises to pay a lender for the use of money, expressed as a fraction of the amount lent per unit of time. Many interest rates are quoted in any currency at any time, and they differ chiefly in credit risk, the risk that the borrower will not pay as promised. The greater the credit risk, the higher the rate. Four kinds of rate are important in the valuation of derivatives.

Treasury rates are the rates at which a government borrows in its own currency by issuing bills and bonds. Because a government can ordinarily meet obligations in its own currency, these rates are regarded as free of credit risk.

Overnight reference rates are published daily and measure the cost of borrowing for one business day. Each major currency has one: the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) for the United States dollar, the Sterling Overnight Index Average (SONIA) for the pound, the Euro Short-Term Rate (€STR) for the euro, and the Tokyo Overnight Average Rate (TONA) for the yen. These rates have replaced the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR), which was based on estimates submitted by banks and not on transactions; publication of the principal dollar LIBOR rates on that basis ended in June 2023. Floating payments in swaps are now determined by compounding the overnight rate over each payment period.

Repo rates are rates on repurchase agreements, in which one party sells securities and agrees to repurchase them later at a slightly higher price. The transaction is in substance a loan secured by the securities, and the rate is correspondingly low. SOFR is computed from overnight repo transactions secured by Treasury securities.

The risk-free rate. The valuation of derivatives requires a risk-free rate, the rate earned on an investment with no credit risk. Market practice is to use rates derived from overnight indexed swaps (OIS), contracts in which a fixed rate is exchanged for the compounded overnight reference rate; Chapter 7 describes them. For the present it is sufficient to know that a term structure of risk-free rates can be observed in the market for every major currency. Throughout this book, \(r\) denotes the risk-free rate.

3.2  Measuring interest rates: compounding

A statement that an interest rate is 5 percent per year is incomplete. Its meaning depends on how often interest is added to the principal, which is the compounding frequency. If the rate \(R\) is compounded \(m\) times per year, an amount \(A\) invested for \(n\) years grows to

\[ A\left(1+\frac{R}{m}\right)^{mn}. \]

With \(m=1\) the rate is compounded annually; with \(m=2\), semiannually; with \(m=4\), quarterly. The effective annual rate is the rate with annual compounding that produces the same result: \((1+R/m)^m-1\). The opening exercise turned on this point. A rate of 4.92 percent compounded quarterly has an effective annual rate of \((1.0123)^4-1=5.0115\) percent, which exceeds 5.00 percent compounded annually.

Continuous compounding

As the compounding frequency \(m\) increases without limit, the terminal value approaches a limit. Because \(\lim_{m\to\infty}(1+R/m)^{m}=e^{R}\), where \(e=2.71828\ldots\) is the base of natural logarithms, an amount \(A\) invested for \(n\) years at a rate \(R\) with continuous compounding grows to

\[ A\,e^{Rn}. \]

Conversely, the value today of an amount \(A\) to be received in \(n\) years is \(A\,e^{-Rn}\). The operation of converting a future amount into its value today is discounting, and the factor \(e^{-Rn}\) is the discount factor. Continuous compounding is used throughout the theory of derivatives because it makes these two operations simple: compounding over successive periods adds the exponents, and discounting is multiplication by an exponential. For practical purposes it is nearly indistinguishable from daily compounding.

Conversion

Let \(R_c\) be a rate with continuous compounding and \(R_m\) the equivalent rate compounded \(m\) times per year. The two produce the same terminal value when \(e^{R_c}=(1+R_m/m)^m\), which gives

\[ R_c = m\,\ln\!\left(1+\frac{R_m}{m}\right), \qquad R_m = m\left(e^{R_c/m}-1\right). \]

Worked example 3.1 — Converting between conventions
(a) A bond yield is quoted as 6 percent with semiannual compounding. Find the equivalent continuously compounded rate. (b) A lender quotes 5 percent with continuous compounding on a loan with interest paid quarterly. Find the rate with quarterly compounding and the interest on $1,000,000 each quarter.
1
(a) \(R_c=2\ln(1+0.06/2)=2\ln(1.03)=2\times0.029559=0.059118\), or 5.912 percent.
2
(b) \(R_4=4\left(e^{0.05/4}-1\right)=4\times0.012578=0.050314\), or 5.031 percent.
3
Interest each quarter: \(1{,}000{,}000\times0.050314/4=\$12{,}578\).
4
Observation. For a given investment, the more frequent the compounding, the lower the quoted rate that describes it. A continuously compounded rate is always below the equivalent rate under any discrete convention.

3.3  Zero rates and the pricing of bonds

The \(n\)-year zero rate, also called the \(n\)-year spot rate, is the rate of interest earned on an investment that begins today and lasts \(n\) years, with all interest and principal paid at the end and nothing paid in between. It is the yield on a zero-coupon bond, a bond that makes a single payment at maturity. The relation between the zero rate and maturity is the zero curve, or the term structure of interest rates.

Most bonds pay coupons, periodic payments of interest, and repay the principal (also called the face value or par value) at maturity. A coupon bond is a collection of single payments at different dates, and each payment should be discounted at the zero rate for its own date. The price of the bond is the sum of the present values.

Table 3.1  Zero rates used in the examples of this section (continuous compounding)
Maturity (years)Zero rateDiscount factor
0.54.0%0.980199

1.54.7%0.931928
2.04.9%0.906649
Worked example 3.2 — Pricing a coupon bond from zero rates
A two-year bond with a principal of $100 pays a coupon of 5 percent per year, semiannually. Find its price using the zero rates of Table 3.1.
1
Cash flows. $2.50 at 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 years; $102.50 at 2.0 years.
2
Present values. \(2.50\times0.980199=2.4505\); \(2.50\times0.956954=2.3924\); \(2.50\times0.931928=2.3298\); \(102.50\times0.906649=92.9315\).
3
Price. \(2.4505+2.3924+2.3298+92.9315=\$100.10\).

Bond yield and par yield

The yield of a bond, or yield to maturity, is the single discount rate that, applied to every cash flow, gives the market price. For the bond of Worked example 3.2 the yield \(y\), with continuous compounding, solves

\[ 2.50\,e^{-0.5y}+2.50\,e^{-1.0y}+2.50\,e^{-1.5y}+102.50\,e^{-2.0y}=100.10 . \]

The equation has no algebraic solution and is solved by trial and error or by a numerical routine; the result is \(y=4.884\) percent. The yield is an average of the zero rates, weighted toward the two-year rate because most of the value of the bond lies in the final payment.

The par yield for a given maturity is the coupon rate that causes a bond to be priced at its principal, or at par. Let \(d_i\) denote the discount factor for the \(i\)th payment date, \(d_n\) the discount factor for maturity, \(A=\sum d_i\) the sum of the discount factors on all payment dates, and \(m\) the number of payments per year. A bond with principal 100 and annual coupon \(c\) is priced at par when \(100=(c/m)A+100\,d_n\), so that

\[ c=\frac{(100-100\,d_n)\,m}{A}. \]

With the rates of Table 3.1, \(A=0.980199+0.956954+0.931928+0.906649=3.775729\) and \(c=(100-90.6649)\times2/3.775729=4.945\). The two-year par yield is 4.945 percent with semiannual compounding. The coupon of 5 percent in Worked example 3.2 is slightly above this, which is why that bond is priced slightly above par.

3.4  Determining zero rates: the bootstrap method

Zero rates for short maturities can be observed directly from the prices of Treasury bills, which pay no coupon. For longer maturities few zero-coupon instruments trade, and the zero rates must be inferred from the prices of coupon bonds. The standard procedure, the bootstrap method, proceeds from the shortest maturity to the longest, using the zero rates already found to isolate one new rate at each step.

E2.00$5.50$101.004.923%
Worked example 3.3 — Bootstrapping the zero curve
Derive the zero rates in the last column of Table 3.2.
1
Bonds A, B, and C make a single payment of $100, so each price is a discount factor multiplied by 100. For bond A, \(100e^{-0.25R}=99.00\) gives \(R=-\ln(0.9900)/0.25=4.020\%\). Similarly \(R=-\ln(0.9790)/0.5=4.245\%\) for B and \(R=-\ln(0.9560)/1.0=4.500\%\) for C.
2
Bond D pays $2.50 at 0.5 and 1.0 years and $102.50 at 1.5 years. The first two payments are discounted with factors already known, 0.9790 and 0.9560: \(2.50\times0.9790+2.50\times0.9560=4.8375\).
3
The final payment must account for the rest of the price: \(102.50\,d_{1.5}=100.40-4.8375=95.5625\), so \(d_{1.5}=0.932317\) and \(R=-\ln(0.932317)/1.5=4.672\%\).
4
Bond E pays $2.75 at 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 years and $102.75 at 2.0 years. \(2.75\times(0.9790+0.9560+0.932317)=7.8851\). Then \(102.75\,d_{2}=101.00-7.8851=93.1149\), so \(d_2=0.906228\) and \(R=-\ln(0.906228)/2=4.923\%\).
5
Completion. Rates for maturities between those computed are obtained by interpolation, most simply by joining the computed points with straight lines.

3.5  Forward rates

A forward rate is the rate of interest, implied by today's zero rates, for a period of time that begins in the future. Suppose that the zero rate for maturity \(T_1\) is \(R_1\) and the zero rate for a longer maturity \(T_2\) is \(R_2\), both with continuous compounding. An investment for \(T_2\) years at \(R_2\) must produce the same result as an investment for \(T_1\) years at \(R_1\) followed by an investment from \(T_1\) to \(T_2\) at the forward rate \(R_F\); otherwise one of the two would be preferred by every investor. Hence \(e^{R_2T_2}=e^{R_1T_1}\,e^{R_F(T_2-T_1)}\), and

\[ R_F=\frac{R_2T_2-R_1T_1}{T_2-T_1}. \]

Table 3.3  Zero rates and the forward rates they imply (continuous compounding)
Year \(n\)Zero rate for an \(n\)-year investmentForward rate for year \(n\)
13.2%—
23.8%4.4%
34.2%5.0%
44.5%5.4%
54.7%5.5%

The forward rate for the second year is \((3.8\times2-3.2\times1)/(2-1)=4.4\) percent, and that for the fifth year is \((4.7\times5-4.5\times4)/1=5.5\) percent. The formula may be rewritten as

\[ R_F=R_2+(R_2-R_1)\frac{T_1}{T_2-T_1}, \]

which shows that when the zero curve slopes upward, so that \(R_2>R_1\), the forward rate exceeds both zero rates; when the zero curve slopes downward, the forward rate lies below them. The reasoning is that of averages: a zero rate is the average of the forward rates over its life, and for an average to rise the newest element must exceed it.

A forward rate is not merely a calculation. An investor can secure it today. Using Table 3.3, a company that borrows $100 for one year at 3.2 percent and invests the proceeds for two years at 3.8 percent has no net cash flow today, owes \(100e^{0.032}=\$103.25\) at the end of year 1, and receives \(100e^{0.076}=\$107.90\) at the end of year 2. It has arranged, today, to invest $103.25 during the second year at the rate \(\ln(107.90/103.25)=4.4\) percent. The contract that provides this result directly, the forward rate agreement, is treated in Chapter 6.

⚙ Interactive figure 3.2 — Zero curve and forward curve

The forward curve lies above a rising zero curve and below a falling one

Set the zero rate at the short end and the level that long-maturity rates approach. The solid line is the zero curve; the dashed line is the forward rate for a very short period beginning at each date. Make the curve flat, then inverted, and observe the position of the forward curve.

★ Optional: the instantaneous forward rate. Let \(R(T)\) be the zero rate for maturity \(T\). Setting \(T_1=T\) and \(T_2=T+\Delta T\) in the forward rate formula and letting \(\Delta T\) approach zero gives the forward rate for a very short period beginning at \(T\): \[ R_F(T)=\frac{d}{dT}\bigl[T\,R(T)\bigr]=R(T)+T\,\frac{dR}{dT}. \] The forward curve in Interactive figure 3.2 is computed from this expression. It exceeds the zero rate exactly where the zero curve has positive slope. Equivalently, if \(P(0,T)=e^{-R(T)T}\) is the price today of a zero-coupon bond paying 1 at \(T\), then \(R_F(T)=-\partial\ln P(0,T)/\partial T\), the form in which the forward rate appears in the interest rate models of advanced texts.

3.6  Discount factors in three dimensions

The discount factor \(e^{-RT}\) depends on two quantities, the rate and the maturity, and its behavior in the two together governs the valuation of every contract in later chapters. Interactive figure 3.3 presents it as a surface. Two features should be noted. For a short maturity the surface is almost level across rates: the value of a payment due soon is insensitive to the rate. For a long maturity the surface falls steeply as the rate rises: the value of a distant payment is highly sensitive to the rate. This observation is made precise by the concept of duration in the next section.
