Chapter 6 · Part II: Forwards, Futures, and Swaps

Interest Rate Futures and Forward Rate Agreements

Day count and quotation conventions, forward rate agreements, futures on overnight reference rates, Treasury bond futures and the cheapest-to-deliver bond, and hedging with duration

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. apply the principal day count conventions and compute accrued interest;
  2. compute the payoff and the value of a forward rate agreement;
  3. read the quotation of a three-month SOFR futures contract and use the contract to fix a borrowing or lending rate;
  4. convert a Treasury bond futures quotation into an invoice amount and identify the cheapest-to-deliver bond;
  5. compute a duration-based hedge and state its limitations.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

How many interest rate futures fix the cost of Northwind's loan?

In three months Northwind Components will borrow $20,000,000 for three months at the reference rate then prevailing. The futures market currently implies a rate of 4.40 percent for that period. A futures contract on the three-month rate is available: for each contract sold, the seller gains $25 for every 0.01 percentage point by which the rate rises above 4.40 percent, and loses $25 for every 0.01 point by which it falls below. Select the number of contracts to sell.

The cost is fixed with 20 contracts, one for each million dollars borrowed. The correspondence is not accidental: the contract is designed so that $25 is the interest on $1,000,000 for one quarter at 0.01 percent. Sections 6.2 and 6.3 present the two instruments, one over-the-counter and one exchange-traded, with which a future interest rate is fixed.

6.1  Day count and quotation conventions

Interest accrues over time, and a convention is needed for measuring the time between two dates. A day count convention is written \(X/Y\), where \(X\) defines how the number of days between two dates is counted and \(Y\) defines the number of days in the reference period. The interest earned between two dates is

\[ \frac{\text{number of days between the dates}}{\text{number of days in the reference period}}\times\text{interest earned in the reference period}. \]

Table 6.1  Principal day count conventions
ConventionDays between datesReference periodTypical use
Actual/actualActual calendar daysActual days in the coupon periodGovernment bonds in the United States and most other markets
30/360Each month counted as 30 days360 days per yearCorporate and municipal bonds in the United States
Actual/360Actual calendar days360 days per yearMoney market instruments and floating rates in dollars and euros
Actual/365Actual calendar days365 days per yearMoney market instruments and floating rates in sterling

Under actual/360, interest for a full year of 365 days is \(365/360\) times the quoted rate; a quoted rate of 4.40 percent produces 4.461 percent over a year. The difference matters in large transactions.

Worked example 6.1 — Accrued interest under two conventions
A bond with a principal of $100 pays a coupon of 6 percent per year on 1 March and 1 September. Find the interest accrued from 1 March to 3 July under (a) actual/actual and (b) 30/360.
1
(a) There are 184 actual days from 1 March to 1 September and 124 from 1 March to 3 July. Accrued interest: \((124/184)\times3.00=\$2.0217\).
2
(b) With 30-day months there are 180 days in the coupon period and \(4\times30+2=122\) days from 1 March to 3 July. Accrued interest: \((122/180)\times3.00=\$2.0333\).

Clean and dirty prices

The quoted price of a bond, called the clean price, excludes interest accrued since the last coupon. The amount a buyer actually pays, called the dirty price or cash price, is the quoted price plus accrued interest. The convention prevents the quoted price from falling abruptly each time a coupon is paid. Prices of United States Treasury bonds are quoted per $100 of principal in dollars and thirty-seconds of a dollar; a quotation of 104-16 means \(104\tfrac{16}{32}=\$104.50\). For clarity this chapter states prices in decimals.

6.2  Forward rate agreements

A forward rate agreement (FRA) is an over-the-counter contract that fixes the interest rate to apply to a specified principal for a specified future period. One party agrees to pay a fixed rate \(R_K\) and to receive the reference rate \(R_M\) that is observed in the market for the period; the other party takes the opposite side. No principal is exchanged. Only the difference in interest is paid.

Let the period run from \(T_1\) to \(T_2\), let \(L\) be the principal, and let \(\tau=T_2-T_1\). Both rates are expressed with a compounding period equal to \(\tau\), so that interest for the period is the rate multiplied by \(\tau\). For the party that pays fixed and receives the reference rate, the payoff valued at \(T_2\) is

\[ L\,(R_M-R_K)\,\tau . \]

This party gains when rates rise and is therefore the natural position for a future borrower; the opposite position suits a future lender or investor. An FRA is usually settled at \(T_1\), as soon as the reference rate is known, by payment of the present value of this amount, \(L(R_M-R_K)\tau/(1+R_M\tau)\).

Valuation

Section 3.5 showed that the forward rate \(R_F\) for a future period can be secured today at no cost. An FRA in which the fixed rate equals the forward rate therefore has zero value, and this is the rate at which FRAs are entered. For an existing FRA with fixed rate \(R_K\), the value is found by supposing that the reference rate will equal the forward rate and discounting the resulting payoff. With \(R_2\) the continuously compounded zero rate for maturity \(T_2\):

Result 6.1 — Value of a forward rate agreement

To the party that pays the fixed rate \(R_K\) and receives the reference rate, \[ V=L\,(R_F-R_K)\,\tau\,e^{-R_2T_2}, \] where \(R_F\) is the forward rate for the period, expressed with compounding period \(\tau\). To the other party the value is \(-V\).

The procedure — assume that forward rates are realized, then discount at the zero rates — is used again in Chapter 7 to value swaps. It does not assert that forward rates are forecasts. It is valid because each uncertain payment can be exchanged today, at no cost, for the payment computed at the forward rate.

Worked example 6.2 — Northwind's forward rate agreement
Northwind will borrow $20,000,000 for three months, beginning in six months. It has entered an FRA to pay 4.60 percent (quarterly compounding) on that principal for that period. Zero rates with continuous compounding are 4.20 percent for six months and 4.40 percent for nine months. (a) Find the forward rate and the value of the FRA today. (b) If the reference rate for the period proves to be 5.30 percent, find the settlement amount and Northwind's net cost of borrowing.
1
Forward rate, continuous compounding. \(R_F=(4.40\times0.75-4.20\times0.50)/0.25=4.800\%\).
2
Converted to quarterly compounding. \(4(e^{0.048/4}-1)=4.829\%\).
3
Value. \(V=20{,}000{,}000\times(0.04829-0.04600)\times0.25\times e^{-0.044\times0.75}=11{,}446\times0.967539=\$11{,}074\). The FRA has positive value to Northwind because the market's forward rate is now above the rate Northwind fixed.
4
(b) Settlement. Payoff valued at the end of the period: \(20{,}000{,}000\times(0.0530-0.0460)\times0.25=\$35{,}000\). Paid at the start of the period: \(35{,}000/(1+0.0530\times0.25)=\$34{,}542\), received by Northwind.
5
Net cost. Interest on the loan at 5.30 percent: \(20{,}000{,}000\times0.0530\times0.25=\$265{,}000\). Less the payoff of the FRA: \(265{,}000-35{,}000=\$230{,}000\), which is interest at 4.60 percent. The rate has been fixed.
⚙ Interactive figure 6.1 — Settlement of a forward rate agreement

The borrowing rate is fixed whatever the reference rate proves to be

Set the fixed rate of the FRA and the reference rate observed at the start of the period. The table shows the payoff, the amount actually settled, and the cost of the loan net of the FRA.

Concept check 6.1

A pension fund will receive $50,000,000 in four months and will invest it for six months. It wishes to fix the rate it will earn. Which position in an FRA is appropriate, and what happens if rates fall?

6.3  Futures on short-term interest rates

The exchange-traded counterpart of the FRA is the short-term interest rate futures contract. For three decades the principal contract was the Eurodollar futures contract of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, which was based on three-month dollar LIBOR. With the discontinuation of LIBOR it has been replaced by the three-month SOFR futures contract, and contracts of the same design are traded on SONIA in London and on €STR in Frankfurt.

The contract has four features.

  • Reference period. Each contract refers to a quarter that begins on the third Wednesday of March, June, September, or December. The contract is named for the month in which its reference quarter begins and ceases trading at the end of that quarter.
  • Final settlement. At the end of the reference quarter the contract is settled in cash at \(100-R\), where \(R\) is the overnight SOFR rate compounded daily over the quarter, expressed as an annual percentage rate.
  • Quotation. Before final settlement, the futures price is quoted as \(100-R\), where \(R\) is now the rate that the market implies for the reference quarter. A quotation of 95.60 implies a rate of 4.40 percent. The price therefore falls when rates rise.
  • Contract value. One basis point, defined as 0.01 percentage point, is worth $25 per contract. This is the interest on $1,000,000 for one quarter at 0.01 percent: \(1{,}000{,}000\times0.0001\times0.25=\$25\).

Because the price is \(100-R\), a short position gains when rates rise and a long position gains when rates fall. A future borrower, who is harmed by a rise in rates, hedges by selling contracts; a future lender hedges by buying them. The number of contracts required to hedge a three-month exposure is the principal divided by $1,000,000.

Worked example 6.3 — Fixing a borrowing rate with SOFR futures
Northwind will borrow $20,000,000 for the quarter beginning on the third Wednesday of June, at compounded SOFR. The June three-month SOFR futures price is 95.60. Northwind sells 20 contracts. Compounded SOFR for the quarter proves to be 5.10 percent. Find the result.
1
Rate fixed. \(100-95.60=4.40\) percent.
2
Futures. Final settlement price: \(100-5.10=94.90\). The price has fallen by 0.70, or 70 basis points. Gain on the short position: \(70\times25\times20=\$35{,}000\).
3
Loan. Interest at 5.10 percent: \(20{,}000{,}000\times0.0510\times0.25=\$255{,}000\).
4
Net cost. \(255{,}000-35{,}000=\$220{,}000\), which is interest at 4.40 percent: \(20{,}000{,}000\times0.0440\times0.25\). For simplicity the calculation treats the quarter as exactly one quarter of a year; in practice interest accrues on an actual/360 basis.

★ Optional: the convexity adjustment. The rate implied by a futures price is slightly higher than the forward rate for the same period. The futures contract is settled daily, and a party that is short gains when rates rise, when the gain can be invested at high rates, and loses when rates fall, when the loss can be financed cheaply. A short position in futures is therefore more favorable than the corresponding position in an FRA, and the futures rate must be higher to compensate. A standard approximation is \[ \text{Forward rate}=\text{Futures rate}-\tfrac12\sigma^{2}T_1T_2, \] where \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) are the times to the start and end of the reference period and \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the change in the short-term interest rate in one year, with both rates expressed with continuous compounding. With \(\sigma=0.012\), \(T_1=4\), and \(T_2=4.25\), the adjustment is \(0.5\times0.012^{2}\times4\times4.25=0.00122\), or about 12 basis points. For contracts maturing within a year it is less than one basis point and is usually ignored.

6.4  Treasury bond futures

The principal contracts on long-term interest rates are futures on government bonds: Treasury bond and Treasury note futures in Chicago, and contracts on German, British, and Japanese government bonds on their respective exchanges. The United States Treasury bond futures contract is described here; the others are similar in design.

The contract is on $100,000 of principal. The party with the short position may deliver any Treasury bond with between 15 and 25 years remaining to maturity. Since the eligible bonds differ in coupon and maturity, and therefore in price, the exchange adjusts the amount paid according to the bond delivered, by means of a conversion factor published for each bond. The conversion factor is approximately the price, per dollar of principal, that the bond would have if its yield were 6 percent with semiannual compounding. The cash received by the party making delivery is

\[ (\text{settlement futures price}\times\text{conversion factor})+\text{accrued interest}, \]

per $100 of principal. If the settlement price is 112.00, the conversion factor of the bond delivered is 0.9300, and accrued interest is $1.25, the cash received is \(112.00\times0.9300+1.25=\$105.41\) per $100 of principal, or $105,410 for one contract.

The cheapest-to-deliver bond

The conversion factor system does not make all bonds equally attractive to deliver. The party with the short position will choose the bond for which the cost of acquiring it, less the amount received for delivering it, is least. Accrued interest is both paid on purchase and received on delivery and so cancels. The bond chosen, the cheapest-to-deliver bond, is the one that minimizes

\[ \text{quoted bond price}-(\text{settlement futures price}\times\text{conversion factor}). \]

Worked example 6.4 — Cheapest to deliver
The settlement futures price is 112.00. Three bonds may be delivered: bond A, quoted at 118.50 with a conversion factor of 1.0500; bond B, quoted at 135.25 with a factor of 1.2000; and bond C, quoted at 104.75 with a factor of 0.9300. Which is cheapest to deliver?
1
Bond A. \(118.50-112.00\times1.0500=118.50-117.60=0.90\).
2
Bond B. \(135.25-112.00\times1.2000=135.25-134.40=0.85\).
3
Bond C. \(104.75-112.00\times0.9300=104.75-104.16=0.59\).
4
Conclusion. Bond C is cheapest to deliver. The futures price is determined by this bond, and the duration of the futures contract, required in the next section, is taken to be the duration of this bond at the maturity of the contract.

Which bond is cheapest to deliver depends on the level of yields. When yields are above 6 percent, the conversion factor system favors the delivery of bonds with low coupons and long maturities; when yields are below 6 percent, it favors bonds with high coupons and short maturities. The party with the short position also has some choice over the timing of delivery within the delivery month. These options are valuable to the short position, and the futures price is correspondingly a little lower than it would be without them.

6.5  Duration-based hedging

Section 3.7 established that the change in the value of a bond for a small change \(\Delta y\) in its yield is approximately \(-BD\,\Delta y\). Consider a portfolio of interest-sensitive assets with value \(V_P\) and duration \(D_P\) at the date the hedge is to be lifted, and a futures contract with value \(V_F\) and duration \(D_F\), the duration of the asset underlying the futures at the maturity of the contract. If all yields change by the same amount, \(\Delta V_P\approx-V_PD_P\,\Delta y\) and \(\Delta V_F\approx-V_FD_F\,\Delta y\). The number of contracts that makes the combined position insensitive to \(\Delta y\) is the duration-based hedge ratio:

Result 6.2 — Duration-based hedge ratio

\[ N^{*}=\frac{V_P\,D_P}{V_F\,D_F}. \] A holder of the portfolio hedges with a short position of \(N^{*}\) contracts; a party that will acquire the portfolio hedges with a long position.

Worked example 6.5 — Hedging a bond portfolio
A fund holds $10,000,000 of bonds with a duration of 6.8 years and wishes to protect their value over the next three months. Treasury bond futures are quoted at 110.00, and the cheapest-to-deliver bond will have a duration of 8.5 years at the maturity of the contract. Find the hedge, and verify it for a rise of 0.50 percentage points in all yields.
1
Contract value. \(V_F=110.00\times1{,}000=\$110{,}000\).
2
Number of contracts. \(N^{*}=(10{,}000{,}000\times6.8)/(110{,}000\times8.5)=72.7\). The fund sells 73 contracts.
3
Portfolio. \(\Delta V_P\approx-10{,}000{,}000\times6.8\times0.005=-\$340{,}000\).
4
Futures. Each contract falls in value by \(110{,}000\times8.5\times0.005=\$4{,}675\). Gain on 73 short contracts: \(73\times4{,}675=\$341{,}275\).
5
Net. \(-340{,}000+341{,}275=+\$1{,}275\), the effect of rounding to a whole number of contracts.
⚙ Interactive figure 6.2 — The limits of a duration hedge

A duration hedge protects against parallel shifts only

The first control changes the yield of the portfolio. The second sets the amount by which the yield underlying the futures changes by more or less than the yield of the portfolio, as happens when the yield curve changes shape. With the second control at zero the hedge of Worked example 6.5 holds; move it and observe the result.

The result rests on the assumption that the yield of the portfolio and the yield of the bond underlying the futures change by the same amount, a parallel shift of the yield curve. Short-term and long-term rates do not in fact move one for one, and a portfolio with a duration of 2 years hedged with a contract whose underlying bond has a duration of 8.5 years is exposed to any change in the difference between two-year and long-term yields. Two practices reduce the exposure: choosing a futures contract whose underlying duration is close to that of the portfolio, and hedging the exposure in each maturity range separately. The approximation also deteriorates for large changes in yield, when convexity becomes important.

Concept check 6.2

A three-month SOFR futures contract is quoted at 96.25. A trader buys 10 contracts, and the quotation moves to 96.05. What is the result?

Concept check 6.3

An insurer will receive $25,000,000 in two months and will invest it in bonds with a duration of 9 years. It fears that yields will fall before then. Bond futures have a contract value of $125,000 and a duration of 7.5 years. What position is appropriate?

Historical note

Interest rate futures were first traded in October 1975, when the Chicago Board of Trade introduced a contract on mortgage-backed certificates of the Government National Mortgage Association. Treasury bond futures followed in 1977 and became for many years the most actively traded futures contract in the world.

The Eurodollar futures contract, introduced by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange in 1981, was the first major contract to be settled in cash, since a three-month interbank deposit could not conveniently be delivered. At its height it had open interest of more than ten million contracts. Trading in its successor, the three-month SOFR contract, began in 2018, and in April 2023 the exchange converted the remaining Eurodollar positions into SOFR contracts.

Summary

  • Interest between two dates is computed under a day count convention; a bond's cash price is its quoted price plus accrued interest.
  • A forward rate agreement fixes the rate on a principal for a future period. The payer of the fixed rate receives \(L(R_M-R_K)\tau\) and is protected against a rise in rates. The value of an FRA is found by assuming that the forward rate is realized and discounting.
  • A three-month SOFR futures contract is quoted at 100 less the implied rate, and one basis point is worth $25. Borrowers sell contracts and lenders buy them, one contract for each $1,000,000 of a three-month exposure.
  • In a Treasury bond futures contract the short position chooses which bond to deliver and receives the settlement price multiplied by the bond's conversion factor, plus accrued interest. The cheapest-to-deliver bond minimizes the quoted price less the settlement price times the conversion factor.
  • The duration-based hedge ratio is \(N^{*}=V_PD_P/(V_FD_F)\). It protects against parallel shifts of the yield curve and not against changes in its shape.

Exercises

6.1 A deposit of $5,000,000 earns 4.80 percent on an actual/360 basis for 91 days. Find the interest. What rate on an actual/365 basis would give the same interest?

Interest: \(5{,}000{,}000\times0.048\times91/360=\$60{,}667\). Equivalent actual/365 rate: \(4.80\times365/360=4.867\) percent.

6.2 A Treasury bond with a coupon of 5 percent is quoted at 97.25. Coupons are paid on 15 February and 15 August. Find the cash price per $100 of principal on 15 May, on an actual/actual basis. (There are 181 days from 15 February to 15 August and 89 from 15 February to 15 May.)

Accrued interest: \((89/181)\times2.50=\$1.2293\). Cash price: \(97.25+1.2293=\$98.48\).

6.3 Zero rates with continuous compounding are 3.80 percent for one year and 4.10 percent for 1.5 years. A company has an FRA under which it receives a fixed rate of 5.00 percent with semiannual compounding on $10,000,000 for the six months beginning in one year. Find the value of the FRA to the company.

Forward rate: \((4.10\times1.5-3.80\times1.0)/0.5=4.70\) percent continuous, or \(2(e^{0.0235}-1)=4.756\) percent semiannual. The company receives fixed, so \(V=10{,}000{,}000\times(0.05000-0.04756)\times0.5\times e^{-0.041\times1.5}=12{,}217\times0.940353=\$11{,}488\).

6.4 In Exercise 6.3, the reference rate for the period proves to be 4.20 percent with semiannual compounding. What payment is made at the start of the period, and by whom?

Payoff to the receiver of fixed, valued at the end of the period: \(10{,}000{,}000\times(0.0500-0.0420)\times0.5=\$40{,}000\). Settled at the start: \(40{,}000/(1+0.0420\times0.5)=\$39{,}177\), paid to the company by its counterparty.

6.5 A bank will lend $45,000,000 for the quarter beginning in September at compounded SOFR. September three-month SOFR futures are quoted at 96.10. (a) What position fixes the bank's return, and at what rate? (b) If compounded SOFR for the quarter is 3.25 percent, verify the result.

(a) The bank is a lender and is harmed by a fall in rates; it buys 45 contracts, fixing \(100-96.10=3.90\) percent. (b) Final settlement: 96.75; the price has risen by 65 basis points. Gain: \(65\times25\times45=\$73{,}125\). Interest earned: \(45{,}000{,}000\times0.0325\times0.25=\$365{,}625\). Total: $438,750, which is \(45{,}000{,}000\times0.0390\times0.25\).

6.6 The settlement price of a Treasury bond futures contract is 108.50. Bond X is quoted at 99.00 with a conversion factor of 0.9050; bond Y is quoted at 121.75 with a conversion factor of 1.1150. (a) Which is cheaper to deliver? (b) If bond X is delivered with accrued interest of $0.80 per $100, what is received for one contract?

(a) X: \(99.00-108.50\times0.9050=99.00-98.1925=0.8075\). Y: \(121.75-108.50\times1.1150=121.75-120.9775=0.7725\). Bond Y is cheaper to deliver. (b) \(108.50\times0.9050+0.80=98.9925\) per $100; \(98.9925\times1{,}000=\$98{,}992.50\).

6.7 A portfolio of bonds is worth $40,000,000 and has a duration of 5.2 years. Bond futures are quoted at 115.00 on $100,000 of principal, and the cheapest-to-deliver bond has a duration of 8.0 years. (a) Find the hedge. (b) How many contracts reduce the duration of the portfolio to 3.0 years?

\(V_F=\$115{,}000\). (a) \(N^{*}=(40{,}000{,}000\times5.2)/(115{,}000\times8.0)=226.1\); short 226 contracts. (b) The duration to be removed is \(5.2-3.0=2.2\) years: \((40{,}000{,}000\times2.2)/(115{,}000\times8.0)=95.7\); short 96 contracts.

6.8 ★ A three-month SOFR futures contract whose reference quarter begins in six years is quoted at 95.20. The standard deviation of the change in the short rate in one year is 1.1 percent. Estimate the forward rate for the reference quarter with continuous compounding, treating the futures rate as continuously compounded.

Futures rate: 4.80 percent. Adjustment: \(0.5\times0.011^{2}\times6\times6.25=0.00227\), or 22.7 basis points. Forward rate: \(4.80-0.23=4.57\) percent.

Chapter 7 · Part II: Forwards, Futures, and Swaps

Swaps

The mechanics and uses of interest rate swaps, the comparative-advantage argument and its limits, the determination of swap rates, the valuation of interest rate and currency swaps, and the credit risk of a swap

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. set out the cash flows of a fixed-for-floating interest rate swap and use a swap to transform a liability or an asset;
  2. construct a swap that divides a comparative advantage between two borrowers and an intermediary, and assess the argument critically;
  3. compute the swap rate from a set of discount factors;
  4. value an interest rate swap after its inception;
  5. set out the cash flows of a fixed-for-fixed currency swap and value it;
  6. explain why the credit exposure of a swap is a small fraction of its notional principal.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

In which market should each company borrow?

Two companies each need $100,000,000 for five years. Alder Corporation, which has the higher credit rating, wants to pay a floating rate. Birch Corporation wants to pay a fixed rate. Lenders offer the terms below. Select the arrangement that gives the lower total cost.

Borrowing rates offered to the two companies
CompanyFixed rateFloating rateWants to pay
Alder Corporation4.00%SOFR + 0.20%Floating
Birch Corporation5.40%SOFR + 0.90%Fixed
Select an arrangement.

7.1  The mechanics of an interest rate swap

Chapter 1 defined a swap as an agreement between two parties to exchange cash flows on a series of future dates according to a specified rule. In an interest rate swap, one party pays interest at a fixed rate on a notional principal, and the other pays interest at a floating rate on the same principal, in the same currency, for a specified number of years. The principal is called notional because it is not exchanged; it serves only to determine the size of the interest payments. The party that pays the fixed rate is the fixed-rate payer; the other is the fixed-rate receiver, or floating-rate payer.

The floating rate in most swaps is now an overnight reference rate — SOFR, SONIA, or €STR — compounded daily over each payment period. A swap of a fixed rate for a compounded overnight rate is an overnight indexed swap (OIS). Because the compounded rate for a period is known only at the end of that period, the floating payment is determined, and paid, at the end of each period. Only the difference between the two interest amounts is paid, by whichever party owes the larger.

The fixed rate that makes a swap of a given maturity have zero value at inception is the swap rate for that maturity. Dealers quote a bid rate, the fixed rate they will pay in exchange for receiving floating, and a slightly higher offer rate, the fixed rate they require in exchange for paying floating. The swap rate is the average of the two, and the difference between them is the dealer's compensation.

An example: Northwind's swap

Northwind Components has a three-year bank loan of $50,000,000 on which it pays interest every six months at compounded SOFR plus 1.20 percent. It wishes to fix its interest cost. It enters a three-year swap with a notional principal of $50,000,000 under which it pays a fixed rate of 4.20 percent per year and receives compounded SOFR, with payments every six months. Northwind then has three sets of cash flows:

  • it pays SOFR + 1.20 percent to the bank under the loan;
  • it receives SOFR under the swap;
  • it pays 4.20 percent under the swap.

The two SOFR amounts cancel, and the net cost is \(4.20+1.20=5.40\) percent per year, fixed, whatever SOFR proves to be. The swap has transformed a floating-rate liability into a fixed-rate liability. Interactive figure 7.1 sets out the cash flows period by period; for simplicity each period is treated as exactly half a year.

⚙ Interactive figure 7.1 — Cash flows of a swap and a loan

A floating-rate loan and a pay-fixed swap produce a fixed cost

The table shows six semiannual periods. Generate a new path for SOFR and confirm, in each row, that the net receipt under the swap offsets the change in the interest on the loan, leaving a total of $1,350,000, which is 5.40 percent per year on $50,000,000.

A swap can equally transform an asset. An investor who holds a bond paying a fixed rate and who expects rates to rise can enter a swap to pay fixed and receive floating, converting the fixed income into a floating income. An investor holding a floating-rate asset can receive fixed and pay floating to obtain a fixed income.

Swaps are documented under the Master Agreement of the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA), which sets out the terms that apply to all transactions between two parties, including what happens if one of them defaults. The particular terms of each trade are recorded in a short confirmation.

Concept check 7.1

A company has issued a five-year bond paying a fixed rate of 5.0 percent. It now believes that rates will fall and wishes to pay a floating rate. Five-year swaps are quoted at 4.3 percent against SOFR. What should it do, and what will it pay?

7.2  The comparative-advantage argument

A long-standing explanation of the popularity of swaps is that of comparative advantage. A company is said to have a comparative advantage in the fixed-rate market if the premium it pays over a more creditworthy borrower is smaller in the floating-rate market than in the fixed-rate market, and conversely. In the opening exercise, Birch pays 1.40 percentage points more than Alder for fixed-rate funds and only 0.70 points more for floating-rate funds. Birch pays more in both markets, so Alder has an absolute advantage in both; but Birch's disadvantage is smaller in the floating-rate market, where it therefore has a comparative advantage, and Alder has a comparative advantage in the fixed-rate market.

Each company wants to borrow in the market in which it does not have a comparative advantage. The argument holds that each should borrow where its comparative advantage lies and then use a swap to obtain the kind of rate it wants. The total gain available is the difference between the two premiums:

\[ 1.40\%-0.70\%=0.70\%\ \text{per year.} \]

Worked example 7.1 — Designing the swap
A swap dealer stands between Alder and Birch and retains 0.10 percent per year. The remaining gain is divided equally. Design the swap.
1
Division of the gain. \(0.70-0.10=0.60\) percent, or 0.30 percent to each company. Alder's target cost is \((\text{SOFR}+0.20)-0.30=\text{SOFR}-0.10\) percent. Birch's target cost is \(5.40-0.30=5.10\) percent.
2
Borrowings. Alder borrows at the fixed rate of 4.00 percent. Birch borrows at SOFR + 0.90 percent.
3
Alder's swap. Alder pays SOFR to the dealer and receives a fixed rate \(X\). Its net cost is \(4.00+\text{SOFR}-X\), which equals \(\text{SOFR}-0.10\) when \(X=4.10\) percent.
4
Birch's swap. Birch receives SOFR from the dealer and pays a fixed rate \(Y\). Its net cost is \((\text{SOFR}+0.90)-\text{SOFR}+Y\), which equals 5.10 when \(Y=4.20\) percent.
5
The dealer. The dealer receives 4.20 percent from Birch and pays 4.10 percent to Alder, and passes SOFR from Alder to Birch: a net 0.10 percent per year, or $100,000 on $100,000,000. The dealer's bid is 4.10 and its offer 4.20.

Criticism of the argument

If such gains were freely available, the trading that exploited them would be expected to eliminate the difference between the two premiums. That the difference persists calls for an explanation, and the explanation shows that the gain is partly apparent.

The two premiums are not comparable, because the contracts are different. The fixed rates of 4.00 and 5.40 percent are fixed for five years. The floating rates are quoted as a spread over SOFR, and that spread is typically guaranteed only for a short period; the lender may review it, or decline to renew the loan, if the borrower's credit standing declines. A company with a lower rating is more likely to deteriorate over five years than over six months, which is why its premium for a five-year fixed commitment exceeds its premium for a short-term commitment. In the example, Birch obtains what appears to be a five-year fixed rate of 5.10 percent, but only so long as it can continue to borrow at SOFR + 0.90 percent. If its spread were to rise to SOFR + 2.00 percent, its cost would rise to 6.20 percent. It has fixed the level of interest rates and has not fixed its own credit spread. A direct fixed-rate loan at 5.40 percent would have fixed both.

7.3  Determining the swap rate

The swap rate can be computed from discount factors by the method used for the par yield in Section 3.3. Consider a swap with notional principal \(L\) and payment dates \(t_1,\dots,t_n\), spaced \(\tau\) years apart. Let \(d_i\) be the risk-free discount factor for date \(t_i\) and \(s\) the fixed rate.

The fixed leg. The fixed payments are \(Ls\tau\) on each date, and their present value is \(Ls\tau\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i\).

The floating leg. An amount \(L\) invested at the compounded overnight rate, with the interest withdrawn at the end of each period, produces exactly the floating payments of the swap and returns \(L\) at \(t_n\). The investment costs \(L\) today. The floating payments alone are therefore worth \(L\) less the present value of the principal returned: \(L-Ld_n=L(1-d_n)\).

Result 7.1 — The swap rate

Equating the values of the two legs, \[ s=\frac{1-d_n}{\tau\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i}. \] At inception a swap at this rate has zero value. At a later date, when \(n\) payments remain and the next floating period is about to begin, the value of the swap to the fixed-rate payer is \[ V=L\,(1-d_n)-L\,K\,\tau\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i, \] where \(K\) is the fixed rate of the swap and the discount factors are those then prevailing. The value to the fixed-rate receiver is \(-V\).

For the discount factors of Table 3.1 — 0.980199, 0.956954, 0.931928, and 0.906649 at six-month intervals — the two-year swap rate with semiannual payments is \((1-0.906649)/(0.5\times3.775729)=4.945\) percent, the same figure as the two-year par yield found in Section 3.3. The agreement is general: the swap rate is the par yield of the risk-free curve, because a fixed-rate receiver in a swap is in the position of an investor who owns a par bond and has financed it at the floating rate.

A swap can also be regarded as a portfolio of forward rate agreements, one for each period. Valuing each as in Result 6.1, by assuming that forward rates are realized, and summing gives the same value as Result 7.1. When the swap is entered, the sum is zero, although the individual FRAs are not: if the zero curve slopes upward, the fixed-rate payer expects to pay in the early periods and to receive in the later ones.

7.4  Valuing an interest rate swap

Worked example 7.2 — The value of Northwind's swap after eighteen months
Eighteen months after Northwind entered its swap, interest rates have risen. The swap has three semiannual payments remaining. Discount factors for six, twelve, and eighteen months are 0.9760, 0.9510, and 0.9255. Find the value of the swap to Northwind, which pays 4.20 percent on $50,000,000.
1
Floating leg. \(L(1-d_n)=50{,}000{,}000\times(1-0.9255)=\$3{,}725{,}000\).
2
Fixed leg. \(\sum d_i=0.9760+0.9510+0.9255=2.8525\). \(LK\tau\sum d_i=50{,}000{,}000\times0.042\times0.5\times2.8525=\$2{,}995{,}125\).
3
Value. \(V=3{,}725{,}000-2{,}995{,}125=+\$729{,}875\) to Northwind.
4
Interpretation. The current swap rate for eighteen months is \((1-0.9255)/(0.5\times2.8525)=5.2235\) percent. Northwind pays only 4.20 percent. The saving of 1.0235 percent per year on $50,000,000 for three half-year periods, discounted, is \(50{,}000{,}000\times0.010235\times0.5\times2.8525=\$729{,}883\), which agrees with the value found apart from rounding.
⚙ Interactive figure 7.2 — The value of a swap as rates change

A pay-fixed swap gains when rates rise

The figure values Northwind's swap, with eighteen months remaining, as all zero rates shift up or down from the levels of Worked example 7.2. Find the shift at which the swap has zero value, and compare the swap rate at that point with 4.20 percent.

Common error

The value of a swap is not its notional principal, nor any simple fraction of it. Northwind's swap has a notional principal of $50,000,000 and, after a substantial rise in rates, a value of about $730,000, or 1.5 percent of notional. At inception its value was zero. Statements about the size of the swap market that cite notional amounts should be read with this in mind, as Section 1.2 observed.

7.5  Currency swaps

A fixed-for-fixed currency swap is an agreement to exchange interest payments and principal in one currency for interest payments and principal in another. Unlike an interest rate swap, a currency swap involves the exchange of principal: at the start, the two parties exchange principal amounts that are equal in value at the spot exchange rate; during the life of the swap, each pays interest at a fixed rate on the principal it received; and at the end the principal amounts are exchanged back, at the original amounts.

Suppose that Northwind has borrowed $22,000,000 for three years in the United States at 4.5 percent but needs euros to build a plant in Germany, whose revenue will be in euros. The spot exchange rate is $1.10 per euro. Northwind enters a three-year currency swap with a bank under which it pays 3.0 percent per year on €20,000,000 and receives 4.5 percent per year on $22,000,000, with annual payments.

Table 7.1  Cash flows to Northwind under the currency swap (millions)
DateDollarsEurosNature
Start−22.00+20.00Exchange of principal
Year 1+0.99−0.60Interest
Year 2+0.99−0.60Interest
Year 3+0.99−0.60Interest
Year 3+22.00−20.00Re-exchange of principal

The dollars received under the swap service the dollar borrowing exactly. What remains is a liability to pay 3.0 percent on €20,000,000 and to repay €20,000,000 in three years, which the euro revenue of the plant will meet. The swap has transformed a dollar liability into a euro liability.

Valuation

To the party that receives dollars and pays the foreign currency, the swap is equivalent to owning a dollar bond and having issued a foreign-currency bond. If \(B_D\) is the value in dollars of the dollar cash flows remaining, \(B_F\) the value in the foreign currency of the foreign cash flows remaining, and \(S_0\) the spot price of the foreign currency in dollars, then

\[ V=B_D-S_0\,B_F . \]

Worked example 7.3 — Valuing the currency swap after one year
One year after the swap of Table 7.1 began, the exchange rate is $1.15 per euro. Risk-free rates are 4.0 percent in dollars and 2.5 percent in euros, with continuous compounding, for all maturities. Two annual payments remain. Find the value of the swap to Northwind.
1
Dollar leg. \(B_D=0.99e^{-0.04}+22.99e^{-0.08}=0.9512+21.2224=\$22.1736\) million.
2
Euro leg. \(B_F=0.60e^{-0.025}+20.60e^{-0.05}=0.5852+19.5953=\)€20.1805 million.
3
Value. \(V=22.1736-1.15\times20.1805=22.1736-23.2076=-\$1.0340\) million.
4
Interpretation. The euro has appreciated from $1.10 to $1.15, which raises the dollar value of the euros Northwind must pay. The loss on the swap is matched by the higher dollar value of the plant's euro revenue, which was the purpose of the arrangement.

The same value is obtained by treating the swap as a set of forward foreign exchange contracts, one for each remaining exchange, and valuing each at the forward rate \(S_0e^{(r-r_f)T}\) of Result 4.5. For the first exchange, the forward rate is \(1.15e^{0.015}=1.1674\); for the second, \(1.15e^{0.030}=1.1850\). Then \((0.99-0.60\times1.1674)e^{-0.04}+(22.99-20.60\times1.1850)e^{-0.08}=-\$1.0340\) million.

A currency swap has zero value at inception but is far more likely than an interest rate swap to acquire a large value, because the final exchange of principal is exposed to the whole of the movement in the exchange rate. Other forms exist: in a fixed-for-floating currency swap one of the two rates floats, and in a floating-for-floating currency swap, also called a cross-currency basis swap, both do.

Concept check 7.2

Under a currency swap a company receives 6 percent on 10 million pounds and pays 4 percent on 13 million dollars, with principal to be re-exchanged at maturity. If the pound depreciates sharply against the dollar during the life of the swap, the value of the swap to the company:

7.6  Credit risk and other swaps

A party to a swap is exposed to the default of its counterparty only when the swap has positive value to itself. If the counterparty defaults when the swap has negative value to the surviving party, that party still owes the value to the defaulter's estate and loses nothing. The potential loss is therefore the positive value of the swap, a small fraction of the notional principal for an interest rate swap, in which no principal is exchanged. The exposure of a currency swap is larger, because of the final exchange of principal.

Since 2009 this exposure has been reduced further. Standardized interest rate swaps between financial institutions are cleared through central counterparties, with initial margin and daily variation margin as described in Section 2.4. Swaps that are not cleared are generally subject to collateral agreements under which the party for which the swap has negative value posts collateral equal to that value.

The principle of a swap extends to any pair of cash-flow streams. An amortizing swap has a notional principal that declines on a schedule, to match a loan that is repaid in instalments. A basis swap exchanges one floating rate for another. In an equity swap, the total return on a share or an index, dividends and capital gains together, is exchanged for a fixed or floating rate of interest; the receiver of the equity return obtains the exposure of an investment in the shares without owning them. In a commodity swap, a fixed price for a quantity of a commodity is exchanged each period for the market price, which gives a producer or user the equivalent of a series of forward contracts at a single price. The credit default swap, in which periodic payments are exchanged for a payment contingent on a default, is the subject of Chapter 17. An option to enter a swap is a swaption.

Concept check 7.3

A bank is the fixed-rate receiver in an uncollateralized interest rate swap with a corporation. Interest rates have risen substantially since the swap began. If the corporation now defaults, the bank's loss on the swap is:

Historical note

The transaction usually identified as the first modern swap was a currency swap arranged by Salomon Brothers in 1981 between the World Bank and IBM. IBM had outstanding debt in Swiss francs and German marks and wished to convert it into dollars after those currencies had fallen against the dollar; the World Bank wished to borrow in those currencies, in which interest rates were low, but had reached the limit of what it could raise directly in those markets. The World Bank borrowed dollars and exchanged the obligations with IBM.

Interest rate swaps followed within a year. The market grew from a few billion dollars of notional principal in the early 1980s to become the largest of all derivatives markets: at the end of June 2025 the Bank for International Settlements reported that interest rate contracts made up the greater part of the $846 trillion of over-the-counter derivatives outstanding.

Summary

  • In an interest rate swap, a fixed rate is exchanged for a floating rate on a notional principal that is not itself exchanged. A pay-fixed swap converts a floating-rate liability into a fixed-rate liability; a receive-fixed swap does the reverse.
  • The comparative-advantage argument divides the difference between two borrowers' fixed-rate and floating-rate premiums. The gain is partly apparent, because a floating-rate spread is not guaranteed for the life of the swap.
  • The swap rate is \(s=(1-d_n)/(\tau\sum d_i)\), the par yield of the risk-free curve. The value of a swap to the fixed-rate payer is \(L(1-d_n)-LK\tau\sum d_i\).
  • A currency swap exchanges principal and interest in two currencies and is valued as the difference between two bonds, \(B_D-S_0B_F\), or as a set of forward exchange contracts.
  • The credit exposure of a swap is its positive value and not its notional principal; central clearing and collateral reduce it further.

Exercises

7.1 A company pays a fixed rate of 3.80 percent and receives compounded SOFR on a notional principal of $80,000,000, with semiannual payments. In a period in which compounded SOFR is 4.35 percent, what payment is made, and by whom?

\(80{,}000{,}000\times(0.0435-0.0380)\times0.5=\$220{,}000\), received by the company, since the floating rate exceeds the fixed rate it pays.

7.2 An investor holds $30,000,000 of a floating-rate note paying SOFR + 0.60 percent and wishes to earn a fixed rate for four years. Four-year swaps are quoted at 4.05 percent bid and 4.09 percent offer. Describe the swap and find the fixed rate earned.

The investor pays SOFR and receives fixed. A customer receiving fixed deals at the dealer's bid, 4.05 percent. Net income: \((\text{SOFR}+0.60)-\text{SOFR}+4.05=4.65\) percent.

7.3 Company X can borrow at a fixed rate of 5.0 percent or at SOFR + 0.4 percent. Company Y can borrow at a fixed rate of 6.6 percent or at SOFR + 1.2 percent. X wants a floating rate and Y a fixed rate. A dealer requires 0.2 percent. Design a swap that is equally attractive to both companies.

Fixed premium 1.6; floating premium 0.8; total gain 0.8; after the dealer's 0.2, each company gains 0.3. X borrows fixed at 5.0 and aims at SOFR + 0.1; Y borrows at SOFR + 1.2 and aims at 6.3. X pays SOFR and receives fixed \(X\): \(5.0+\text{SOFR}-X=\text{SOFR}+0.1\) gives \(X=4.9\). Y receives SOFR and pays fixed \(Y\): \(1.2+Y=6.3\) gives \(Y=5.1\). The dealer earns \(5.1-4.9=0.2\).

7.4 Discount factors for one, two, and three years are 0.9615, 0.9200, and 0.8763. Find the three-year swap rate with annual payments.

\(s=(1-0.8763)/(1\times(0.9615+0.9200+0.8763))=0.1237/2.7578=4.485\) percent.

7.5 A bank receives a fixed rate of 5.00 percent and pays compounded SOFR on $100,000,000, with annual payments and exactly two years remaining. Discount factors for one and two years are 0.9620 and 0.9230. Find the value of the swap to the bank.

Fixed leg: \(100{,}000{,}000\times0.05\times(0.9620+0.9230)=\$9{,}425{,}000\). Floating leg: \(100{,}000{,}000\times(1-0.9230)=\$7{,}700{,}000\). Value to the receiver of fixed: \(9{,}425{,}000-7{,}700{,}000=+\$1{,}725{,}000\). The current two-year swap rate is \(0.0770/1.8850=4.085\) percent, below the 5.00 percent the bank receives.

7.6 Explain why the swap rate for a given maturity equals the par yield for that maturity on the risk-free curve.

The floating leg together with a payment of the principal at maturity is worth the principal, \(L\). The fixed leg together with the principal at maturity is a fixed-rate bond with coupon \(s\). The swap has zero value when the two are equal, that is, when a bond with coupon \(s\) is worth \(L\): the definition of the par yield. Algebraically, \(L=Ls\tau\sum d_i+Ld_n\) gives \(s=(1-d_n)/(\tau\sum d_i)\).

7.7 Under a currency swap with three years remaining, a company pays 2.0 percent per year on 1,200 million yen and receives 5.0 percent per year on $10 million, with annual payments and a final exchange of principal. The exchange rate is 125 yen per dollar. Risk-free rates are 4.5 percent in dollars and 1.0 percent in yen, with continuous compounding. Find the value of the swap to the company in dollars.

Dollar leg: \(0.5e^{-0.045}+0.5e^{-0.09}+10.5e^{-0.135}=0.4780+0.4570+9.1740=\$10.1090\) million. Yen leg: \(24e^{-0.01}+24e^{-0.02}+1{,}224e^{-0.03}=23.761+23.525+1{,}187.825=1{,}235.111\) million yen, or \(1{,}235.111/125=\$9.8809\) million. Value: \(10.1090-9.8809=+\$0.2281\) million.

7.8 A company with a low credit rating borrows for five years at a floating rate, renewed every six months, and enters a five-year swap to pay fixed. State precisely which risks it has removed and which remain.

It has removed its exposure to the general level of interest rates: changes in the reference rate on the loan are offset by the swap. It retains (i) the risk that its own credit spread over the reference rate is increased at a renewal, which the swap does not offset; (ii) the risk that the lender declines to renew, leaving it with a swap and no loan; and (iii) counterparty risk on the swap whenever the swap has positive value to it, unless the swap is cleared or collateralized. A five-year fixed-rate loan would have removed (i) and (ii) as well, which is why it costs more.

Chapter 8 · Part III: Options

Option Markets and the Properties of Option Prices

How listed options are specified and traded, the six factors that determine an option's price, the bounds that arbitrage places on that price, put–call parity, and the conditions under which early exercise is optimal

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. describe the specification of a listed option and the adjustments made for stock splits and dividends;
  2. state the direction in which each of six factors affects the prices of calls and puts;
  3. derive the upper and lower bounds on option prices and construct the arbitrage when a bound is violated;
  4. derive put–call parity and use it to price one option from another or to identify an arbitrage;
  5. explain why an American call on a share that pays no dividend should not be exercised early, and why an American put sometimes should;
  6. modify the bounds and the parity relation for known dividends.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

A call option is offered at a low price. Is there a certain profit?

Northwind shares trade at $28.00 and will pay no dividend in the next six months. A European call with a strike price of $25.00 and six months to expiration is quoted at the price shown. Money can be borrowed or invested at 5 percent per year with continuous compounding. No model of the share price is available, and none is needed. Set the quote, select a strategy, and examine the result; then find the lowest quote at which no certain profit exists.

A call with a strike of $25 on a share worth $28 is worth at least $3: so much is evident. The exercise shows that it is worth at least $3.62, because the $25 need not be paid for six months. This chapter establishes what can be said about option prices from arbitrage alone, before any assumption is made about how share prices behave. The results hold in every model.

8.1  Option markets

Chapter 1 defined calls and puts, European and American exercise, the strike price, the expiration date, and the positions of buyer and writer. This section describes how options on shares are traded on exchanges. The largest markets are in the United States, where options on several thousand shares, on indices, and on exchange-traded funds are listed on exchanges including the Chicago Board Options Exchange; Eurex in Frankfurt and the exchanges of Asia operate on similar principles.

Specification

A listed option on a share is ordinarily American and covers 100 shares. Prices are quoted per share, so that a quoted premium of $1.50 means a payment of $150 for one contract. The exchange specifies the following.

Expiration dates. Standard options expire on the third Friday of the expiration month. Options are listed with expirations in the nearest months and in more distant months according to a fixed cycle; for actively traded shares there are also weekly expirations and long-dated options with up to about three years to run.

Strike prices. Strikes are set at regular intervals, typically $1, $2.50, or $5 according to the share price, on both sides of the current price. New strikes are added as the share price moves. All options of the same type (call or put) on a share form an option class; all options in a class with the same strike and expiration form an option series.

Moneyness. Section 1.5 defined an option as in the money, at the money, or out of the money according to whether immediate exercise would give a positive, zero, or negative payoff. The intrinsic value is \(\max(S-K,0)\) for a call and \(\max(K-S,0)\) for a put, and the remainder of the price is the time value.

Dividends and stock splits

Listed options are not adjusted for ordinary cash dividends. When a share goes ex-dividend, that is, begins to trade without the right to a dividend just declared, its price falls by approximately the amount of the dividend, and the terms of the option are unchanged. A dividend therefore reduces the value of a call and raises the value of a put.

Options are adjusted for stock splits and stock dividends. In an \(n\)-for-\(m\) split, the strike price is multiplied by \(m/n\) and the number of shares covered by \(n/m\). After a 2-for-1 split, a contract on 100 shares with a strike of $60 becomes a contract on 200 shares with a strike of $30, which leaves the positions of the buyer and the writer unchanged.

Trading, clearing, and margin

Most exchanges rely on market makers, who quote both a bid price, at which they will buy, and a higher ask price (or offer price), at which they will sell. The difference, the bid–ask spread, is their compensation and is a cost to other traders. Exchanges limit its size.

In the United States all listed options are cleared by the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC), which performs the function described in Section 2.4: it stands between buyer and writer and guarantees performance. When a holder exercises, the OCC assigns the exercise to a member with a short position in the same series, and the member assigns it to a client.

The buyer of an option pays the premium in full and has no further obligation. The writer has a potential liability and must post margin. A writer who does not hold an offsetting position in the share has written a naked option and must post margin equal to the premium received plus a percentage of the value of the underlying shares, adjusted for the amount by which the option is out of the money. A writer of a call who owns the shares has written a covered call and need post no further margin, since the shares can be delivered if the call is exercised.

Other options

Options on stock indices are settled in cash and are usually European. Large institutions trade options over the counter with terms of their own choosing. Three instruments issued by companies themselves resemble call options: warrants, which are calls issued by a company on its own shares; employee stock options, granted to staff as part of their remuneration; and convertible bonds, which may be exchanged for shares at a specified ratio. Unlike listed options, their exercise leads the company to issue new shares.

8.2  Factors affecting option prices

Six factors determine the price of an option on a share: the current share price \(S_0\); the strike price \(K\); the time to expiration \(T\); the volatility of the share price, \(\sigma\); the risk-free interest rate \(r\); and the dividends expected during the life of the option. Table 8.1 gives the effect on the option price of an increase in each factor with the others held fixed.

Table 8.1  Effect on the price of an option of an increase in one variable, the others unchanged
VariableEuropean callEuropean putAmerican callAmerican put
Share priceRisesFallsRisesFalls
Strike priceFallsRisesFallsRises
Time to expirationUncertainUncertainRisesRises
VolatilityRisesRisesRisesRises
Risk-free rateRisesFallsRisesFalls
DividendsFallsRisesFallsRises

Share price and strike price. A call pays the excess of the share price over the strike; it is worth more the higher the share price and the lower the strike. A put pays the excess of the strike over the share price, and the effects are reversed.

Time to expiration. The holder of an American option with a long life has every opportunity open to the holder of one with a short life, and more; the longer option cannot be worth less. For European options this need not hold. A European call that expires just before a large dividend may be worth more than one that expires just after it, and a deep in-the-money European put may be worth more with a short life, because the strike price is received sooner.

Volatility. The volatility of a share price, denoted \(\sigma\), is a measure of the uncertainty about its future movements; it is defined precisely in Chapter 12 as the standard deviation of the return on the share over one year, when the return is measured with continuous compounding. As volatility increases, very high and very low share prices both become more likely. The owner of a share is exposed to both and the effects offset. The owner of an option is not: the holder of a call gains from high prices and loses no more than the premium from low prices, and the holder of a put gains from low prices. Higher volatility therefore raises the value of both.

Risk-free rate. A higher interest rate lowers the present value of the strike price. The holder of a call will pay the strike and gains; the holder of a put will receive it and loses. The statement assumes that the share price itself is unchanged, although in practice a rise in rates is often accompanied by a fall in share prices.

Dividends. A dividend lowers the share price on the ex-dividend date, which reduces the value of a call and raises the value of a put.

Concept check 8.1

A company announces results that leave its share price unchanged but make its future prospects considerably more uncertain. What happens to the prices of calls and puts on its shares?

8.3  Upper and lower bounds

The following notation is used: \(c\) and \(p\) are the prices of a European call and a European put, and \(C\) and \(P\) the prices of the corresponding American options, all with strike \(K\) and time to expiration \(T\) on a share with current price \(S_0\) and price \(S_T\) at expiration. Dividends are assumed to be zero until Section 8.6. The assumptions are those of Section 4.1: no transaction costs, borrowing and lending at the risk-free rate \(r\), and the prompt removal of arbitrage opportunities.

Upper bounds

A call gives the right to buy one share, and cannot be worth more than the share: \(c\le S_0\) and \(C\le S_0\). If it were, an arbitrageur would buy the share and write the call. An American put gives the right to sell for \(K\), and cannot be worth more than \(K\): \(P\le K\). A European put will be worth at most \(K\) at expiration, and so at most its present value today: \(p\le Ke^{-rT}\).

Lower bound for a European call

Result 8.1 — Lower bounds for European options on a share paying no dividend

\[ c\ \ge\ \max\!\left(S_0-Ke^{-rT},\,0\right), \qquad p\ \ge\ \max\!\left(Ke^{-rT}-S_0,\,0\right). \]

Proof for the call. Compare two portfolios. Portfolio A consists of one European call and a zero-coupon bond that pays \(K\) at time \(T\); the bond costs \(Ke^{-rT}\) today. Portfolio B consists of one share. At time \(T\), if \(S_T>K\), the call is exercised using the proceeds of the bond, and portfolio A is worth \(S_T\); if \(S_T\le K\), the call expires and portfolio A is worth \(K\). Portfolio A is therefore worth \(\max(S_T,K)\), which is never less than the value \(S_T\) of portfolio B. A portfolio that is worth at least as much as another in every outcome cannot cost less today, so \(c+Ke^{-rT}\ge S_0\). Since a call cannot have negative value, \(c\ge\max(S_0-Ke^{-rT},0)\). \(\blacksquare\)

Proof for the put. Portfolio C consists of one European put and one share; portfolio D of a zero-coupon bond paying \(K\) at \(T\). At time \(T\) portfolio C is worth \(\max(S_T,K)\), which is never less than \(K\). Hence \(p+S_0\ge Ke^{-rT}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Worked example 8.1 — A violated lower bound
In the opening exercise, \(S_0=28\), \(K=25\), \(r=5\) percent, and \(T=0.5\), and the call is quoted at $3.20. Verify that the bound is violated and set out the arbitrage.
1
The bound. \(Ke^{-rT}=25e^{-0.025}=\$24.38\). Lower bound: \(28-24.38=\$3.62\). The quote of $3.20 is below it.
2
Today. Buy the call for $3.20 and sell the share short for $28.00: net receipt $24.80. Invest $24.38 for six months. Cash remaining: \(24.80-24.38=\$0.42\).
3
At expiration, \(S_T>25\). The investment has grown to $25.00. Exercise the call, pay $25.00, and return the share. Net cash flow: zero.
4
At expiration, \(S_T\le25\). Buy the share in the market for \(S_T\) and return it. Net cash flow: \(25-S_T\ge0\).
5
Conclusion. The arbitrageur receives $0.42 per share today and cannot owe anything at expiration. Purchases of the call raise its price until the bound is restored.
⚙ Interactive figure 8.1 — Bounds on option prices

The price of an option lies between two limits set by arbitrage alone

The dashed lines are the upper and lower bounds for a European option with a strike of $30. The solid line is the value given by the Black–Scholes–Merton model of Chapter 12, shown here only to locate the price between the bounds. Vary the time to expiration, the interest rate, and the volatility. The bounds do not depend on volatility; the price does.

8.4  Put–call parity

The two portfolios used in the proofs of Result 8.1 lead to the most important relation of this chapter. Portfolio A (a European call and a zero-coupon bond paying \(K\)) and portfolio C (a European put and a share) are each worth \(\max(S_T,K)\) at expiration. The options are European and cannot be exercised earlier. Two portfolios with identical values at \(T\) and no intermediate cash flows must have identical values today.

Result 8.2 — Put–call parity

For European options with the same strike price and expiration date on a share that pays no dividend, \[ c+Ke^{-rT}=p+S_0 . \]

Table 8.2  Values of the two portfolios at expiration
PortfolioComponent\(S_T>K\)\(S_T\le K\)
ACall\(S_T-K\)0
Zero-coupon bond\(K\)\(K\)
Total\(S_T\)\(K\)
CPut0\(K-S_T\)
Share\(S_T\)\(S_T\)
Total\(S_T\)\(K\)

Parity has three uses. It gives the price of a put from the price of a call with the same terms, or the reverse, so that only one of the two need be valued. It shows how any one of the four instruments — call, put, share, and bond — can be constructed from the other three; rearranged as \(c=p+S_0-Ke^{-rT}\), it states that a call is equivalent to a put together with a share financed in part by borrowing. And when market prices depart from it, it identifies an arbitrage.

Worked example 8.2 — Parity and its violation
Northwind shares trade at $28. A three-month European call with a strike of $30 costs $1.50, and the risk-free rate is 5 percent. (a) Find the price of the European put with the same terms. (b) The put is quoted at $2.60. Set out the arbitrage.
1
(a) \(Ke^{-rT}=30e^{-0.0125}=\$29.63\). \(p=c+Ke^{-rT}-S_0=1.50+29.63-28.00=\$3.13\).
2
(b) Diagnosis. At $2.60 the put is cheap relative to the call: \(p+S_0=30.60\), whereas \(c+Ke^{-rT}=31.13\). Buy the portfolio that is cheap and sell the one that is dear.
3
Today. Buy the put for $2.60 and the share for $28.00; write the call for $1.50. Net cost: \(2.60+28.00-1.50=\$29.10\), which is borrowed for three months.
4
At expiration. If \(S_T>30\), the call is exercised against the arbitrageur, who delivers the share for $30. If \(S_T\le30\), the arbitrageur exercises the put and sells the share for $30. In either case $30.00 is received.
5
Profit. Repay \(29.10e^{0.0125}=\$29.47\). Riskless profit: \(30.00-29.47=\$0.53\) per share.
⚙ Interactive figure 8.2 — Put–call parity

Any departure from parity is an arbitrage

Set the quoted prices of the three-month call and put with a strike of $30. The table compares the two portfolios, and the text sets out the trade and its profit. Find a pair of prices at which no profit remains.

Concept check 8.2

A share trades at $50 and pays no dividend. A one-year European put with a strike of $50 costs $3.00, and the risk-free rate is 4 percent with continuous compounding. What is the price of the one-year European call with the same strike?

8.5  Early exercise of American options

Calls on a share that pays no dividend

Result 8.3

It is never optimal to exercise an American call on a share that pays no dividend before the expiration date. Consequently \(C=c\).

An American call is worth at least as much as the European call, and by Result 8.1 the European call is worth at least \(S_0-Ke^{-rT}\). When \(r>0\) and \(T>0\) this exceeds \(S_0-K\), the amount obtained by exercising. A holder who no longer wishes to own the option does better to sell it than to exercise it.

Two economic reasons lie behind the result. First, exercise means paying the strike price now instead of at expiration, which forgoes interest on \(K\). Second, exercise gives up the protection that the option provides: after exercise the holder owns the share and bears the whole of any fall in its price, whereas the holder of the call can lose no more than its value. Even a holder who is certain that the share is overvalued should sell the call, or sell the share short against it, and should not exercise.

Puts

For a put the argument does not hold. Exercising a put means receiving the strike price now, and interest can be earned on it. Consider the extreme case of a share whose price has fallen almost to zero. Exercise yields almost \(K\) at once. Waiting can add almost nothing, since the share price cannot fall below zero, and it delays the receipt of \(K\). Exercise is optimal. More generally, an American put should be exercised early whenever the share price is sufficiently far below the strike. It follows that an American put is worth more than the corresponding European put, \(P>p\), and that a European put can be worth less than its intrinsic value, as Interactive figure 8.1 shows.

The share price below which exercise is optimal depends on the interest rate, the volatility, and the time remaining, and has no simple formula. Chapter 10 finds it numerically, and Interactive figure 10.3 displays it.

★ Optional: the relation between American call and put prices. Put–call parity is an equality only for European options. For American options on a share that pays no dividend, \[ S_0-K\ \le\ C-P\ \le\ S_0-Ke^{-rT}. \] Proof of the right-hand inequality. \(C=c\) and \(P\ge p\), so \(C-P\le c-p=S_0-Ke^{-rT}\). Proof of the left-hand inequality. Compare portfolio E, a European call and cash of \(K\) invested at the rate \(r\), with portfolio F, an American put and a share. If the put is not exercised early, F is worth \(\max(S_T,K)\) at \(T\) and E is worth \(\max(S_T,K)+Ke^{rT}-K\), which is larger. If the put is exercised at an earlier time \(\tau\), F is worth \(K\) at that time, while E is worth at least the invested cash, \(Ke^{r\tau}\ge K\). In every case E is worth at least as much as F, so \(c+K\ge P+S_0\); with \(c=C\) this is \(C-P\ge S_0-K\). \(\blacksquare\)

8.6  The effect of dividends

Let \(D\) denote the present value of the dividends that will be paid during the life of the option; for listed options, whose lives are short, these can be predicted with reasonable accuracy. A share that will pay dividends is worth \(D\) more than the claim to the share at time \(T\) alone. Replacing portfolio B of Section 8.3 by a share and portfolio A by a call together with cash of \(D+Ke^{-rT}\) gives the modified results:

\[ c\ge S_0-D-Ke^{-rT},\qquad p\ge D+Ke^{-rT}-S_0,\qquad c+D+Ke^{-rT}=p+S_0 . \]

When dividends are expected, Result 8.3 no longer holds. It can be optimal to exercise an American call immediately before an ex-dividend date, because the holder of the share receives the dividend and the holder of the call does not, and the share price will fall when the dividend is paid. Early exercise of a call is worth considering only at those dates, and only when the dividend is large relative to the interest forgone on the strike.

Worked example 8.3 — Parity with a dividend
A share trades at $28 and will pay a dividend of $0.40 in three months. A six-month European call with a strike of $28 costs $3.10. The risk-free rate is 5 percent for all maturities. Find the price of the six-month European put with the same strike.
1
Present value of the dividend. \(D=0.40e^{-0.05\times0.25}=\$0.395\).
2
Present value of the strike. \(28e^{-0.05\times0.5}=\$27.309\).
3
Put. \(p=c+D+Ke^{-rT}-S_0=3.10+0.395+27.309-28.00=\$2.80\).
Concept check 8.3

An investor holds an American call, deep in the money, on a share that pays no dividend, and is convinced that the share price is about to fall. What should the investor do?

Historical note

Put–call parity was known to option dealers long before it appeared in the academic literature. Russell Sage, a New York financier of the 1870s, used the relation to construct loans from options and shares at rates above those permitted by the usury laws of the time, and a description of the conversion of puts into calls appears in a handbook for traders published in London in 1902. The first formal statement in a journal is that of Hans Stoll in 1969.

The systematic derivation of bounds on option prices from the absence of arbitrage, without any assumption about the distribution of share prices, is due to Robert Merton, whose paper of 1973 established most of the results of this chapter, including the proposition that an American call on a share paying no dividend should not be exercised early.

Summary

  • Listed options on shares are American, cover 100 shares, expire on standard dates, and are adjusted for stock splits but not for cash dividends. Buyers pay the premium in full; writers post margin.
  • The price of an option depends on the share price, the strike, the time to expiration, the volatility, the risk-free rate, and dividends. Volatility raises the price of both calls and puts.
  • Arbitrage alone implies \(\max(S_0-Ke^{-rT},0)\le c\le S_0\) and \(\max(Ke^{-rT}-S_0,0)\le p\le Ke^{-rT}\).
  • Put–call parity, \(c+Ke^{-rT}=p+S_0\), links the prices of European calls and puts with the same terms; with dividends of present value \(D\), \(c+D+Ke^{-rT}=p+S_0\).
  • An American call on a share that pays no dividend should never be exercised early, so that \(C=c\). An American put should be exercised early when the share price is sufficiently low, so that \(P>p\).

Exercises

8.1 An investor holds two call contracts with a strike of $90 on a share. The company declares a 3-for-1 stock split. State the terms of the investor's position after the split.

The strike is multiplied by 1/3 and the number of shares by 3: each contract becomes a call on 300 shares with a strike of $30. The investor holds two such contracts, on 600 shares in total.

8.2 A share trades at $40 and pays no dividend. The risk-free rate is 6 percent. Find the lower bound for the price of (a) a four-month European call with a strike of $36 and (b) a four-month European put with a strike of $44.

(a) \(40-36e^{-0.06\times4/12}=40-35.287=\$4.71\). (b) \(44e^{-0.02}-40=43.129-40=\$3.13\).

8.3 A share trades at $22 and pays no dividend. A six-month European put with a strike of $26 is quoted at $2.50, and the risk-free rate is 5 percent. Is there an arbitrage? If so, describe it.

Lower bound: \(26e^{-0.025}-22=25.358-22=\$3.36\). The quote of $2.50 violates it. Borrow $24.50 for six months; buy the put for $2.50 and the share for $22.00. At expiration repay \(24.50e^{0.025}=\$25.12\). If \(S_T<26\), exercise the put and receive $26.00, for a profit of $0.88; if \(S_T\ge26\), sell the share for \(S_T\), for a profit of \(S_T-25.12\ge0.88\).

8.4 A share trades at $65. A six-month European call with a strike of $70 costs $2.85, and the risk-free rate is 4 percent. The share pays no dividend. Find the price of the six-month European put with a strike of $70.

\(p=c+Ke^{-rT}-S_0=2.85+70e^{-0.02}-65=2.85+68.614-65=\$6.46\).

8.5 In Exercise 8.4 the put is quoted at $7.00. Set out the arbitrage and compute the profit at expiration.

The put is dear. Write the put for $7.00, sell the share short for $65.00, and buy the call for $2.85: net receipt \(7.00+65.00-2.85=\$69.15\), invested for six months to give \(69.15e^{0.02}=\$70.55\). At expiration the share is bought for $70 in either case (by exercising the call if \(S_T>70\), or because the put is exercised against the arbitrageur if \(S_T\le70\)) and returned. Profit: \(70.55-70.00=\$0.55\) per share.

8.6 Explain why an American put on a share that pays no dividend is always worth at least its intrinsic value, whereas a European put may not be.

The holder of an American put can exercise at once and receive \(K-S_0\); the put cannot sell for less, or buying it and exercising would be an arbitrage. The holder of a European put cannot obtain \(K\) until expiration, and its lower bound is \(Ke^{-rT}-S_0\), which is below \(K-S_0\). When the share price is very low, the European put is worth little more than this bound, and so less than its intrinsic value.

8.7 A share trades at $50 and will pay a dividend of $1.00 in two months. A four-month European put with a strike of $50 costs $2.90, and the risk-free rate is 6 percent for all maturities. Find the price of the four-month European call with a strike of $50.

\(D=1.00e^{-0.06\times2/12}=0.990\). \(Ke^{-rT}=50e^{-0.02}=49.010\). \(c=p+S_0-D-Ke^{-rT}=2.90+50-0.990-49.010=\$2.90\).

8.8 ★ A share that pays no dividend trades at $31. The risk-free rate is 8 percent. An American call with a strike of $30 and three months to expiration costs $3.00. Find the range within which the price of the American put with the same terms must lie.

\(S_0-K\le C-P\le S_0-Ke^{-rT}\) gives \(31-30\le3.00-P\le31-30e^{-0.02}\), that is \(1.00\le3.00-P\le1.594\). Hence \(1.41\le P\le2.00\).
