Chapter 9 · Part III: Options

Trading Strategies with Options

Positions that combine options with the underlying share and with one another: covered calls and protective puts, spreads, combinations, and collars, with the profit, the cost, and the purpose of each

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. construct the profit diagram of any position composed of shares, calls, and puts;
  2. compute the cost, the maximum gain, the maximum loss, and the breakeven prices of a position;
  3. explain the relation between covered calls, protective puts, and single options by put–call parity;
  4. construct bull, bear, box, and butterfly spreads from calls or from puts;
  5. construct straddles, strangles, strips, and straps, and state the view each expresses;
  6. select a strategy that corresponds to a stated view on the direction and the variability of a share price.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

Which position profits from a large movement in either direction?

Northwind Components will announce the outcome of a major contract tender within three months. An investor believes that the share price, now $28, will move sharply when the result is known — upward if the contract is won, downward if it is lost — and has no view as to which. Three-month options with a strike of $28 cost $2.34 for the call and $1.99 for the put; the call with a strike of $30 costs $1.52. Select the position that corresponds to this view.

Select a position.

A share allows an investor to express one view: that the price will rise or, by a short sale, that it will fall. Options allow views on the size of a movement independently of its direction, views that the price will remain within a range, and views bounded on one side or both. Each view corresponds to a shape of profit diagram, and each shape can be assembled from calls and puts. This chapter is a catalogue of the principal shapes.

9.1  Method and data

The profit of a position at the expiration of its options is the sum of the profits of its components, computed as in Section 1.5. As there, the interest that could be earned on premiums between the purchase and the expiration is ignored, and all options are European with the same expiration date unless otherwise stated. For any position, four quantities should be computed:

  • the net cost: premiums and share prices paid, less premiums received;
  • the maximum gain and the maximum loss, over all possible share prices at expiration;
  • the breakeven price or prices: the share prices at which the profit is zero.

Because the profit of every component is a straight line between strike prices, the profit of the position is also a straight line between strikes, and it is sufficient to compute it at each strike and to note its slope beyond the lowest and highest strikes.

All the examples of this chapter use the prices of Table 9.1 for three-month options on Northwind shares, which trade at $28. The prices are consistent with one another and with put–call parity at a risk-free rate of 5 percent.

Table 9.1  Prices of three-month European options on Northwind shares (share price $28)
Strike$24$26$28$30$32
Call$4.84$3.45$2.34$1.52$0.94
Put$0.55$1.12$1.99$3.14$4.55

9.2  Positions in one option and the share

Covered call

A covered call consists of a long position in the share and a short position in a call. The share covers the writer against the obligation to deliver if the call is exercised. With the $30 call written at $1.52, the net cost is \(28.00-1.52=\$26.48\). If the share price at expiration is above $30, the call is exercised and the share is sold for $30, for a profit of \(30-26.48=\$3.52\), which is the maximum. If it is below $30, the investor keeps the share and the premium; the breakeven price is $26.48, and the maximum loss, if the share becomes worthless, is $26.48.

The writer of a covered call gives up the share's gains above the strike in exchange for the premium. The position is appropriate for an investor who intends to hold the share, expects its price to change little, and is prepared to sell at the strike.

Protective put

A protective put consists of a long position in the share and a long position in a put, as in the hedging example of Section 1.7. With the $26 put bought at $1.12, the net cost is \(28.00+1.12=\$29.12\). If the share price is below $26 at expiration, the put is exercised and the share is sold for $26; the loss is \(29.12-26=\$3.12\), which is the maximum. Above $26 the investor keeps the share. The breakeven price is $29.12, and the gain is unlimited.

The relation to single options

The profit diagram of a covered call has the shape of a written put, and that of a protective put has the shape of a purchased call. Put–call parity explains why. From Result 8.2,

\[ S_0-c=Ke^{-rT}-p \qquad\text{and}\qquad S_0+p=c+Ke^{-rT}. \]

The first states that a share with a written call is equivalent to a written put together with an investment of \(Ke^{-rT}\) at the risk-free rate; the second, that a share with a purchased put is equivalent to a purchased call together with the same investment. The reverse positions follow in the same way: a short position in the share combined with a purchased call has the shape of a purchased put, and a short position in the share combined with a written put has the shape of a written call.

Principal-protected notes

The second identity is the basis of a product widely sold to retail investors. A principal-protected note returns the investor's principal at maturity whatever happens, together with a share of any rise in an index. A bank can construct it from a zero-coupon bond and a call option. On a three-year note of $1,000 with a risk-free rate of 5 percent, the bond that returns $1,000 at maturity costs \(1{,}000e^{-0.05\times3}=\$860.71\), leaving $139.29 with which to buy call options on the index and to cover the bank's costs and profit. The investor is protected against a fall in the index and gives up, in exchange, the interest that the $1,000 would have earned.

Concept check 9.1

Using Table 9.1, an investor buys a Northwind share at $28 and writes the call with a strike of $28 for $2.34. What are the maximum gain and the breakeven price?

9.3  Spreads

A spread is a position in two or more options of the same type: all calls or all puts.

Bull spread

A bull spread is created by buying a call with strike \(K_1\) and writing a call with a higher strike \(K_2\). Since a call with a lower strike is the more valuable, the position requires an initial outlay. Buying the $26 call and writing the $30 call costs \(3.45-1.52=\$1.93\). At expiration the position is worth nothing if the share price is below $26, \(S_T-26\) between the strikes, and $4 above $30. The maximum loss is the cost, $1.93; the maximum gain is \(4-1.93=\$2.07\); and the breakeven price is \(26+1.93=\$27.93\).

A bull spread limits both the gain and the loss. An investor who expects a moderate rise gives up the gains above \(K_2\), which are thought unlikely, and reduces the cost of the position by the premium of the call written. A bull spread can also be created from puts, by buying the put with the lower strike and writing the put with the higher strike; it then produces an initial receipt.

Bear spread

A bear spread is created by buying a put with strike \(K_2\) and writing a put with a lower strike \(K_1\). Buying the $30 put and writing the $26 put costs \(3.14-1.12=\$2.02\). The position is worth $4 if the share price is below $26, \(30-S_T\) between the strikes, and nothing above $30. The maximum gain is \(4-2.02=\$1.98\), the maximum loss $2.02, and the breakeven price \(30-2.02=\$27.98\). It is the position of an investor who expects a moderate fall.

Box spread

A box spread combines a bull spread made from calls with a bear spread made from puts at the same two strikes. Its payoff is \(K_2-K_1\) whatever the share price, so that it is a risk-free investment and must cost \((K_2-K_1)e^{-rT}\). The bull and bear spreads above together cost \(1.93+2.02=\$3.95\), and \(4e^{-0.05\times0.25}=\$3.95\). A box spread whose price differs from this value is an arbitrage, but only if the options are European; with American options the written legs may be exercised early.

Butterfly spread

A butterfly spread uses three strikes, \(K_1<K_2<K_3\), with \(K_2\) midway between the others: buy one call at \(K_1\), buy one call at \(K_3\), and write two calls at \(K_2\). With strikes of $24, $28, and $32 the cost is \(4.84+0.94-2\times2.34=\$1.10\). The position is worth nothing if the share price at expiration is below $24 or above $32, and reaches its greatest value, $4, at $28. The maximum gain is \(4-1.10=\$2.90\); the maximum loss is the cost, $1.10; and the breakeven prices are \(24+1.10=\$25.10\) and \(32-1.10=\$30.90\).

A butterfly spread is the position of an investor who expects the share price to remain close to \(K_2\). It costs little and loses little if the expectation is wrong. The same position can be built from puts, at the same cost: with the puts of Table 9.1, \(0.55+4.55-2\times1.99=\$1.12\), which differs from $1.10 only through the rounding of the prices.

Calendar spread

In the spreads above, all options expire on the same date. A calendar spread uses options with the same strike and different expirations: write a call with a short life and buy a call with a longer life. Because the short-dated option loses time value more quickly, the position gains if the share price remains near the strike until the first expiration. Its profit at that date is a curve and not a set of straight lines, since the longer option still has time value, and it requires the valuation methods of Chapter 12.

Worked example 9.1 — Profit of a butterfly spread
Using Table 9.1, compute the profit of the butterfly spread with call strikes of $24, $28, and $32 at share prices of $22, $26, $28, $31, and $35.
1
Cost. \(4.84-2\times2.34+0.94=\$1.10\).
2
\(S_T=22\). All calls expire unexercised. Profit: \(0-1.10=-\$1.10\).
3
\(S_T=26\). The $24 call pays 2. Profit: \(2-1.10=\$0.90\).
4
\(S_T=28\). The $24 call pays 4; the others pay nothing. Profit: \(4-1.10=\$2.90\).
5
\(S_T=31\). The $24 call pays 7; the two written $28 calls cost \(2\times3=6\). Profit: \(7-6-1.10=-\$0.10\).
6
\(S_T=35\). Payoffs: \(11-2\times7+3=0\). Profit: \(-\$1.10\).

9.4  Combinations

A combination is a position that includes both calls and puts on the same share.

Straddle

A straddle is created by buying a call and a put with the same strike and expiration. It is the position selected in the opening exercise. With a strike of $28 the cost is \(2.34+1.99=\$4.33\). At expiration the position is worth \(|S_T-28|\). The maximum loss is the cost, incurred if the share price is exactly $28; the breakeven prices are \(28-4.33=\$23.67\) and \(28+4.33=\$32.33\); and the gain is unlimited on the upside and reaches $23.67 if the share becomes worthless.

A straddle profits from a large movement in either direction. Whether it is a sound investment depends on whether the movement the investor expects is larger than the movement already reflected in option prices. If the market as a whole expects a large movement, the options will be expensive, and the breakeven prices will be far apart. The straddle is therefore a position on volatility: it profits when the realized movement exceeds the movement implied by the prices paid. The reverse position, a written straddle, profits when the share price remains near the strike and carries an unlimited potential loss.

Strangle

A strangle is created by buying a put with strike \(K_1\) and a call with a higher strike \(K_2\). Buying the $26 put and the $30 call costs \(1.12+1.52=\$2.64\). The position is worth nothing between the strikes; its breakeven prices are \(26-2.64=\$23.36\) and \(30+2.64=\$32.64\). A strangle is cheaper than a straddle and loses less if the share price is unchanged, but the price must move further before it shows a profit.

Strips and straps

A strip consists of one call and two puts with the same strike and expiration, and a strap of two calls and one put. Both profit from a large movement in either direction. In a strip the investor considers a fall the more likely and gains twice as much per dollar of fall as per dollar of rise; in a strap the emphasis is reversed. With a strike of $28 a strip costs \(2.34+2\times1.99=\$6.32\) and a strap \(2\times2.34+1.99=\$6.67\).

Collar

A collar is a share held together with a purchased put at a strike \(K_1\) below the current price and a written call at a strike \(K_2\) above it. The put sets a minimum on the value of the holding and the call a maximum, and the premium received for the call pays for part or all of the put. With the $26 put and the $30 call the net cost is \(28.00+1.12-1.52=\$27.60\); the holding will be worth between $26 and $30 at expiration, so that the maximum loss is $1.60 and the maximum gain $2.40. A collar in which the two premiums are equal is a zero-cost collar. Collars are widely used by executives and founders who hold large positions in a single share and wish to limit their risk without selling.

An investor expects Northwind's share price to remain between $27 and $29 for the next three months and wishes to risk as little as possible. Which strategy of Table 9.2 is most suitable?

9.5  The value of a strategy before expiration

A profit diagram describes a position at a single date. Before that date the position has a market value equal to the sum of the values of its options, each of which exceeds or falls short of its payoff by its time value. Interactive figure 9.2 shows the value of three strategies as surfaces over the share price and the time remaining, computed from the Black–Scholes–Merton model with the volatility of 39 percent that underlies Table 9.1.

The figure makes visible a property that the profit diagrams conceal. A purchased straddle loses value with the passage of time at every share price: its holder pays, day by day, for the possibility of a large movement. A butterfly spread near its middle strike gains value with the passage of time: its holder is paid for bearing the risk of such a movement. A bull spread gains from the passage of time when the share price is near or above its higher strike and loses when the price is near or below its lower strike. The rate at which a position gains or loses value as time passes is its theta, and the positions of this chapter are examined again from this standpoint in Chapter 14.

⚙ Interactive figure 9.2 — Three-dimensional view

The value of a strategy as a function of the share price and the time to expiration

The dark line at the front edge is the payoff at expiration; the gold curve is the value at the selected time. Drag to rotate; scroll or pinch to zoom. Move the time slider toward zero with the share price at $28 and compare the three strategies.

Table equivalent of this figure

9.6  Other payoffs

The strategies of this chapter are those in common use, and they do not exhaust the possibilities. If European options were available at every strike price, any payoff that depends only on the share price at expiration could be constructed from them. A butterfly spread with strikes very close together pays a small amount if the share price finishes in a narrow interval and nothing otherwise; a sufficiently large number of such spreads, in suitable quantities, approximates any payoff function as closely as desired. This observation, which is due to Douglas Breeden and Robert Litzenberger, has an important consequence examined in Chapter 15: the prices of butterfly spreads at different strikes reveal the probabilities that the market assigns to different future share prices.

Concept check 9.3

A straddle with a strike of $50 costs $9. On the day before a company's results, an investor who expects “a large movement” of about $6 in the share price, in one direction or the other, considers buying it. What should the investor conclude?

Historical note

The vocabulary of this chapter is older than the listed options market. Straddles and spreads were traded in the over-the-counter market in puts and calls in New York and London in the nineteenth century; the terms appear in dealers' handbooks of the period, and the word straddle was in use on the New York Stock Exchange by the 1870s.

The best-known loss from the positions of this chapter is that of Barings Bank in 1995, listed in Table 1.3. Its trader in Singapore had written straddles on the Nikkei 225 index in large quantity, collecting premiums on the expectation that the index would remain within a narrow range. After the earthquake at Kobe in January 1995 the index fell sharply, and the trader's attempts to support it by buying futures multiplied the loss. A written straddle earns a small and regular income in exchange for an exposure to large movements that is, in principle, unlimited.

Summary

  • The profit of any position in shares, calls, and puts is the sum of the profits of its components and is linear between strike prices.
  • A covered call has the shape of a written put and a protective put the shape of a purchased call, as put–call parity requires.
  • Bull and bear spreads limit both gain and loss and express a view of a moderate rise or fall. A box spread is risk-free. A butterfly spread profits when the price remains near its middle strike.
  • Straddles, strangles, strips, and straps profit from large movements in either direction; they are positions on volatility, and profit only if the movement exceeds what option prices already reflect.
  • A collar confines the value of a shareholding between two strikes, the written call paying for the purchased put.
  • Before expiration, positions that have bought options lose value with the passage of time, and positions that have written them gain.

Exercises

Exercises 9.1 to 9.6 use the prices of Table 9.1.

9.1 An investor buys the share at $28 and the put with a strike of $28. Find the net cost, the maximum loss, and the breakeven price. Which single option has a profit diagram of the same shape?

Net cost: \(28.00+1.99=\$29.99\). The holding is worth at least $28, so the maximum loss is $1.99. Breakeven: $29.99. The shape is that of a purchased call with a strike of $28.

9.2 Construct a bull spread from the calls with strikes of $28 and $32. Find its cost, maximum gain, maximum loss, and breakeven price, and its profit if the share price at expiration is $30.50.

Buy the $28 call and write the $32 call: cost \(2.34-0.94=\$1.40\). Maximum gain: \(4-1.40=\$2.60\). Maximum loss: $1.40. Breakeven: \(28+1.40=\$29.40\). At $30.50: \(2.50-1.40=\$1.10\).

9.3 Construct a bull spread from the puts with strikes of $26 and $30. Find the initial cash flow and the maximum gain and loss, and compare the profit diagram with that of the bull spread made from calls with the same strikes.

Buy the $26 put and write the $30 put: initial receipt \(3.14-1.12=\$2.02\). Above $30 both expire: gain $2.02. Below $26 the position pays out $4: loss \(4-2.02=\$1.98\). The call spread has a maximum gain of $2.07 and a maximum loss of $1.93. The two diagrams have the same shape and differ by $0.05 at every share price, which is the interest on the difference in initial outlay, \(1.93+2.02=3.95\), over three months: \(3.95(e^{0.0125}-1)=0.05\).

9.4 An investor writes the straddle with a strike of $28. Find the range of share prices at expiration over which the position is profitable, and the loss if the share price is $38.

Premium received: $4.33. The position is profitable between $23.67 and $32.33. At $38 the call is exercised against the writer: \(4.33-10=-\$5.67\).

9.5 A founder holds Northwind shares worth $28 each and establishes a collar with the $24 put and the $32 call. Find the net cost per share and the range of values of the holding at expiration.

Net cost of the options: \(0.55-0.94=-\$0.39\), a net receipt. The holding will be worth between $24 and $32 per share; including the receipt, between $24.39 and $32.39.

9.6 A dealer offers a box spread with strikes of $24 and $32 for $7.80. Is it correctly priced? What should an investor do?

The box pays $8 at expiration with certainty and should cost \(8e^{-0.0125}=\$7.90\). At $7.80 it is cheap: buying it earns \(\ln(8/7.80)/0.25=10.1\) percent per year without risk, against a risk-free rate of 5 percent. From Table 9.1 its cost is \((4.84-0.94)+(4.55-0.55)=\$7.90\), which confirms the fair price.

9.7 A bank issues a five-year principal-protected note of $10,000 linked to a stock index. The five-year risk-free rate is 4 percent with continuous compounding. How much is available to purchase options and to cover the bank's costs?

The zero-coupon bond costs \(10{,}000e^{-0.20}=\$8{,}187.31\). The remainder, $1,812.69, is available for options and costs.

9.8 Three European calls on a share have strikes of $55, $60, and $65 and cost $10, $7, and $5 respectively. Find the cost of the butterfly spread and the range of share prices at expiration over which it loses money.

Cost: \(10+5-2\times7=\$1\). The maximum value is $5 at $60. Breakeven prices: \(55+1=\$56\) and \(65-1=\$64\). The spread loses money if the share price is below $56 or above $64.

Chapter 10 · Part IV: Valuation

The Binomial Model

The valuation of an option by replication on a one-step tree, risk-neutral valuation, trees with many steps, American options and early exercise, and the construction of a tree from the volatility of the share

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. value an option on a one-step binomial tree by constructing the portfolio that replicates it;
  2. state the principle of risk-neutral valuation and explain why the expected return on the share does not enter the price of an option;
  3. value European options on trees with two or more steps;
  4. value American options by testing for early exercise at each node;
  5. compute the delta of an option and explain why a hedge must be adjusted as the share price changes;
  6. construct a tree from the volatility of the share, and modify it for indices, currencies, and futures.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

How likely is a rise, and what is the call worth?

Northwind shares trade at $28. In three months the price will be either $32.20 or $25.20; no other outcome is possible. A European call with a strike of $28 expires on that date and will therefore pay either $4.20 or nothing. The risk-free rate is 5 percent per year with continuous compounding. Select the probability that the reader believes should be assigned to a rise, and observe the value that this belief implies for the call.

The value of the call does not depend on the probability of a rise. Two investors who disagree entirely about the prospects of Northwind must agree that the call is worth $1.87, because either of them can manufacture it for that amount. This result, which is the central idea of the theory of option valuation, is derived in Section 10.1. The probability at which the two lines cross, 45 percent, is not a forecast; Section 10.2 explains what it is.

10.1  A one-step binomial model

A binomial tree is a diagram of the paths that the price of a share may follow, on the assumption that in each short interval of time the price either rises by a given proportion or falls by a given proportion. The assumption is restrictive for a single interval, but when the life of an option is divided into many short intervals the tree approximates realistic behavior closely, as Section 10.6 shows. This section treats the opening exercise in detail.

Valuation by replication

The call pays $4.20 if the share price rises to $32.20 and nothing if it falls to $25.20. Consider a portfolio consisting of \(\Delta\) shares, financed in part by borrowing an amount \(B\) at the risk-free rate. The aim is to choose \(\Delta\) and \(B\) so that the portfolio is worth exactly the same as the call in both outcomes. After three months the loan requires repayment of \(Be^{0.05\times0.25}=1.012578B\), so the two conditions are

\[ 32.20\,\Delta-1.012578\,B=4.20, \qquad 25.20\,\Delta-1.012578\,B=0 . \]

Subtracting the second from the first gives \(7.00\,\Delta=4.20\), so \(\Delta=0.60\). The second equation then gives \(B=25.20\times0.60/1.012578=\$14.93\). A portfolio of 0.60 shares with borrowing of $14.93 is worth $4.20 if the share rises and nothing if it falls: it replicates the call. Its cost today is

\[ 0.60\times28.00-14.93=16.80-14.93=\$1.87 . \]

By Principle 1.1, the call must be worth $1.87. If it were quoted at $2.20, an arbitrageur would write the call, buy 0.60 shares, and borrow $14.93, receiving \(2.20-1.87=\$0.33\) today with no obligation in either outcome. If it were quoted at $1.50, the arbitrageur would buy the call, sell 0.60 shares short, and invest $14.93, receiving $0.37.

The number of shares, \(\Delta\), is the delta of the option: the change in the value of the option divided by the change in the price of the share between the two outcomes, \((4.20-0)/(32.20-25.20)=0.60\). The argument may be stated in the opposite direction. A portfolio that is long 0.60 shares and short one call is worth \(25.20\times0.60=\$15.12\) in both outcomes; it is riskless, and must therefore earn the risk-free rate. Its value today is \(15.12e^{-0.0125}=\$14.93\), so that \(16.80-c=14.93\) and \(c=\$1.87\).

Generalization

Let the share price be \(S_0\) and the life of the option \(T\). The price moves either up to \(S_0u\) or down to \(S_0d\), where \(u>1\) and \(d<1\), and the option then pays \(f_u\) or \(f_d\). The replicating portfolio holds \(\Delta\) shares, where

\[ \Delta=\frac{f_u-f_d}{S_0u-S_0d}. \]

Solving for the borrowing and computing the cost of the portfolio gives the value of the option:

Result 10.1 — One-step binomial valuation

\[ f=e^{-rT}\left[\,p\,f_u+(1-p)\,f_d\,\right], \qquad\text{where}\qquad p=\frac{e^{rT}-d}{u-d}. \]

In the example, \(u=32.20/28=1.15\), \(d=25.20/28=0.90\), and \(p=(1.012578-0.90)/(1.15-0.90)=0.4503\). Then \(f=0.987578\times(0.4503\times4.20+0.5497\times0)=\$1.87\), as before. The formula applies to any derivative whose payoff depends only on the share price at \(T\). For a put with a strike of $28, \(f_u=0\) and \(f_d=2.80\), and \(f=0.987578\times0.5497\times2.80=\$1.52\), which satisfies put–call parity: \(1.87+28e^{-0.0125}-28=\$1.52\).

Absence of arbitrage requires \(d<e^{rT}<u\). If the share were certain to earn more than the risk-free rate, or certain to earn less, one of the two assets would dominate the other. The condition ensures that \(p\) lies between 0 and 1.

Common error

The formula of Result 10.1 does not contain the probability that the share price rises. This is not an omission. The probability affects the price of the share, \(S_0\), which is taken as given; once \(S_0\) is known, nothing further about the probability is needed to value the option relative to the share. An investor who believes a rise to be very likely should regard both the share and the call as attractive at their present prices, and cannot conclude that the call is underpriced relative to the share.

10.2  Risk-neutral valuation

The quantity \(p\) in Result 10.1 has the form of a probability, and the expression \(pf_u+(1-p)f_d\) has the form of an expected payoff. The interpretation is exact in a particular sense. Suppose that the probability of a rise were \(p\). The expected share price at \(T\) would be

\[ p\,S_0u+(1-p)\,S_0d=S_0\left[p(u-d)+d\right]=S_0\,e^{rT}. \]

With probability \(p\), the share is expected to earn exactly the risk-free rate. A world in which every asset is expected to earn the risk-free rate is one in which investors require no compensation for bearing risk; it is called a risk-neutral world, and \(p\) is the risk-neutral probability of a rise.

Principle 10.1 — Risk-neutral valuation

The value of a derivative is its expected payoff in a risk-neutral world, discounted at the risk-free rate. To apply the principle: assume that the expected return on the underlying asset is the risk-free rate; compute the expected payoff of the derivative under that assumption; and discount it at the risk-free rate. The value obtained is correct in the real world, and not only in a risk-neutral one.

The principle does not assert that investors are indifferent to risk or that shares are in fact expected to earn the risk-free rate. It is a method of calculation whose validity rests on the replication argument of Section 10.1: because the option can be replicated, its value relative to the share is the same whatever investors' attitudes to risk, and it may therefore be computed under whichever attitude makes the computation simplest.

The real world

Suppose that investors in fact expect Northwind shares to return 12 percent per year. The real-world probability of a rise, \(q\), satisfies \(28e^{0.12\times0.25}=32.20q+25.20(1-q)\), which gives \(q=0.5218\). The expected payoff of the call in the real world is \(0.5218\times4.20=\$2.19\). To obtain the correct value of $1.87 from this figure, it would have to be discounted at the rate that solves \(1.87=2.19e^{-0.25k}\), namely \(k=64\) percent per year. The call is far riskier than the share, since it is equivalent to 0.60 shares financed largely by borrowing, and investors require a correspondingly higher return on it. That return is difficult to determine directly and, as later sections show, it changes from node to node. Risk-neutral valuation avoids the problem altogether.

Concept check 10.1

A share trades at $50. In six months it will be worth $55 or $45. The risk-free rate is 4 percent with continuous compounding. What is the value of a six-month European call with a strike of $50?

10.3  Two-step trees

The analysis extends to a tree with two steps by repeated use of Result 10.1, working backward from the expiration date. Let each step last \(\Delta t\) years, so that \(p=(e^{r\Delta t}-d)/(u-d)\) and the discount factor for one step is \(e^{-r\Delta t}\). The value at each node is computed from the values at the two nodes that follow it. This procedure is backward induction.

Worked example 10.1 — A European call on a two-step tree
Northwind shares trade at $28. In each of two three-month steps the price rises by 15 percent or falls by 10 percent. The risk-free rate is 5 percent. Value a six-month European call with a strike of $28.
1
Share prices. After one step: $32.20 or $25.20. After two: \(28\times1.15^{2}=\$37.03\); \(28\times1.15\times0.90=\$28.98\); \(28\times0.90^{2}=\$22.68\).
2
Payoffs at expiration. \(f_{uu}=37.03-28=9.03\); \(f_{ud}=28.98-28=0.98\); \(f_{dd}=0\).
3
Parameters. \(p=0.4503\); \(1-p=0.5497\); \(e^{-r\Delta t}=0.987578\).
4
Upper node ($32.20). \(f_u=0.987578\times(0.4503\times9.03+0.5497\times0.98)=\$4.548\).
5
Lower node ($25.20). \(f_d=0.987578\times(0.4503\times0.98+0.5497\times0)=\$0.436\).
6
Initial node. \(f=0.987578\times(0.4503\times4.548+0.5497\times0.436)=\$2.26\).

For a European option the intermediate nodes may be bypassed. The risk-neutral probabilities of reaching the three final nodes are \(p^{2}\), \(2p(1-p)\), and \((1-p)^{2}\), and

\[ f=e^{-2r\Delta t}\left[p^{2}f_{uu}+2p(1-p)f_{ud}+(1-p)^{2}f_{dd}\right], \]

which for the example gives \(0.975310\times(0.2028\times9.03+0.4951\times0.98)=\$2.26\).

Delta on the tree

The delta of the call differs from node to node. At the initial node, \(\Delta=(4.548-0.436)/(32.20-25.20)=0.587\). At the upper node after one step, \(\Delta=(9.03-0.98)/(37.03-28.98)=1.000\); at the lower node, \(\Delta=(0.98-0)/(28.98-22.68)=0.156\). A portfolio that replicates the call must therefore be adjusted after the first step: if the share price has risen, the holding is increased from 0.587 to 1.000 shares; if it has fallen, the holding is reduced to 0.156 shares. The adjustment requires no new money, because the value of the portfolio at each node equals the cost of the portfolio required for the next step. A strategy of this kind is self-financing, and the practice of adjusting a hedge as the share price changes is dynamic hedging, the subject of Chapter 14.

10.4  American options

The holder of an American option may exercise at any node. The value of the option at a node is therefore the greater of two amounts: the value obtained by exercising immediately, and the value of keeping the option for a further step, which is given by Result 10.1 and is called the continuation value. The procedure is again backward induction, with one additional comparison at each node:

\[ f=\max\!\left(\text{payoff from immediate exercise},\ \ e^{-r\Delta t}\left[p\,f_u+(1-p)\,f_d\right]\right). \]

Worked example 10.2 — An American put on a two-step tree
On the tree of Worked example 10.1, value a six-month put with a strike of $30, (a) if it is European and (b) if it is American.
1
Payoffs at expiration. \(f_{uu}=0\); \(f_{ud}=30-28.98=1.02\); \(f_{dd}=30-22.68=7.32\).
2
Upper node ($32.20). Continuation value: \(0.987578\times(0.4503\times0+0.5497\times1.02)=\$0.554\). Immediate exercise would yield \(30-32.20<0\). The put is not exercised: value $0.554 for both styles.
3
Lower node ($25.20). Continuation value: \(0.987578\times(0.4503\times1.02+0.5497\times7.32)=\$4.427\). Immediate exercise yields \(30-25.20=\$4.80\), which is greater. The European put is worth $4.427 at this node; the American put is exercised and is worth $4.80.
4
(a) European put. \(0.987578\times(0.4503\times0.554+0.5497\times4.427)=\$2.65\).
5
(b) American put. Continuation value at the initial node: \(0.987578\times(0.4503\times0.554+0.5497\times4.80)=\$2.85\). Immediate exercise yields \(30-28=\$2.00\), which is less; the put is held. Value: $2.85.
6
Conclusion. The right to exercise early is worth \(2.85-2.65=\$0.20\). It arises entirely at the lower node, where the holder gains more from receiving $30 at once than from waiting.

If the same procedure is applied to an American call on a share that pays no dividend, the continuation value exceeds the exercise value at every node, in accordance with Result 8.3, and the American and European values coincide.

Concept check 10.2

At a node of a binomial tree the share price is $36 and an American put has a strike of $42. The values of the put at the two following nodes are $2.40 (up) and $9.60 (down); \(p=0.6523\) and the one-step discount factor is 0.9704. What is the value of the put at this node?

10.5  Matching the tree to volatility

In the examples so far, the proportions \(u\) and \(d\) were given. In practice they are chosen to match the volatility of the share, \(\sigma\), introduced in Section 8.2. Volatility is defined so that the standard deviation of the return on the share over a short interval of length \(\Delta t\) is \(\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\); a volatility of 39 percent per year implies a standard deviation of return of \(0.39\times\sqrt{0.25}=19.5\) percent over three months.

Result 10.2 — The Cox–Ross–Rubinstein tree

A binomial tree with steps of length \(\Delta t\) matches a volatility of \(\sigma\) when \[ u=e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}},\qquad d=\frac1u=e^{-\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}},\qquad p=\frac{a-d}{u-d},\qquad a=e^{r\Delta t}. \]

Because \(d=1/u\), an upward movement followed by a downward movement returns the share price to its starting value, and the tree recombines: after \(n\) steps there are \(n+1\) distinct share prices and not \(2^{n}\). The choice of \(u\) and \(d\) does not involve the expected return on the share, in accordance with Section 10.2; the volatility of the share is the same in the real world and in the risk-neutral world, and only the probability of a rise differs between them.

With \(\sigma=0.39\) and \(\Delta t=0.25\): \(u=e^{0.195}=1.2153\), \(d=0.8228\), \(a=1.012578\), and \(p=(1.012578-0.8228)/(1.2153-0.8228)=0.4835\).

Share prices, option values, and early exercise at every node

The tree values a six-month option on Northwind shares (\(S_0=\$28\), \(r=5\) percent) with the parameters of Result 10.2. Select the type and style of option, the strike, the volatility, and the number of steps. Nodes at which an American option should be exercised are shaded. 10.6  Increasing the number of steps

A tree with one or two steps is a device for exposition. In practice the life of an option is divided into thirty or more steps, and often several hundred. With thirty steps there are 31 possible share prices at expiration and more than a thousand million paths by which they may be reached. As the number of steps increases, the distribution of the share price at expiration on the tree approaches a continuous distribution, and the value of a European option approaches a limit. That limit is the Black–Scholes–Merton formula, derived in Chapter 12.

Interactive figure 10.2 shows the approach. The binomial value does not converge smoothly: it oscillates as the number of steps alternates between odd and even, because the position of the strike price relative to the final nodes changes. A common remedy is to average the values obtained with \(n\) and \(n+1\) steps.

⚙ Interactive figure 10.2 — Convergence

The binomial value approaches a limit as the number of steps increases

The figure uses the option selected in Interactive figure 10.1. For a European option the dashed line is the Black–Scholes–Merton value; for an American option, for which no formula exists, it is the value from a tree with 400 steps.

The early-exercise region

With many steps, the tree identifies for each date the share price below which an American put should be exercised. Interactive figure 10.3 presents the result as a surface. Where the American surface lies above the plane of intrinsic value, the put should be held; where it coincides with that plane, the put should be exercised. The European surface, shown for comparison, dips below intrinsic value at low share prices, as Section 8.5 predicted.

⚙ Interactive figure 10.3 — Three-dimensional view

The value of a put, American and European, and the region of early exercise

The put has a strike of $30; the risk-free rate is 5 percent and the volatility 39 percent. The dark line at the front edge is the payoff at expiration. Select the style, then lower the share price with a year remaining until the readout reports that immediate exercise is optimal. Drag to rotate; scroll or pinch to zoom.

10.7  Options on other assets

The tree is easily adapted to underlying assets that provide income. In a risk-neutral world the total return on any asset is the risk-free rate \(r\). If the asset provides income at the rate \(q\), its price must grow at the rate \(r-q\), so that the expected price after one step is \(S_0e^{(r-q)\Delta t}\). The parameters \(u\) and \(d\) are unchanged, and Result 10.2 holds with a different value of \(a\).

Table 10.1  The growth factor \(a\) in \(p=(a-d)/(u-d)\)
Underlying asset\(a\)Reason
Share paying no dividend\(e^{r\Delta t}\)The price grows at the risk-free rate
Stock index with dividend yield \(q\)\(e^{(r-q)\Delta t}\)Part of the return is received as dividends
Currency with foreign rate \(r_f\)\(e^{(r-r_f)\Delta t}\)The holder of the currency earns the foreign rate
Futures contract\(1\)A futures position requires no investment, so its expected gain is zero

In every case the option is discounted at the risk-free rate \(r\). For an index with a volatility of 20 percent and a dividend yield of 2 percent, with \(r=5\) percent and steps of three months, \(u=e^{0.20\times0.5}=1.1052\), \(d=0.9048\), \(a=e^{0.03\times0.25}=1.007528\), and \(p=(1.007528-0.9048)/(1.1052-0.9048)=0.5126\).

Concept check 10.3

Two analysts value the same option on a binomial tree with the same volatility. One believes that the share will return 6 percent per year, the other 16 percent. How do their valuations of the option compare?

Historical note

The binomial model was published in 1979 by John Cox, Stephen Ross, and Mark Rubinstein, six years after the Black–Scholes–Merton formula, and independently in the same year by Richard Rendleman and Brit Bartter. The authors credit the idea to William Sharpe, who is said to have proposed it as a way of explaining option valuation without the mathematics of continuous time. The model proved to be more than an expository device: because it values American options, for which no formula exists, it became and remains one of the principal numerical methods in practice.

The principle of risk-neutral valuation was stated by John Cox and Stephen Ross in 1976. Its mathematical basis, the existence of a set of probabilities under which the discounted price of every traded asset is its expected future value, was established by Michael Harrison and David Kreps in 1979, and it is in that form that the principle appears in advanced texts.

Summary

  • On a one-step tree, a portfolio of \(\Delta=(f_u-f_d)/(S_0u-S_0d)\) shares and risk-free borrowing replicates any option, and the value of the option is the cost of that portfolio.
  • Equivalently, \(f=e^{-rT}[pf_u+(1-p)f_d]\) with \(p=(e^{rT}-d)/(u-d)\): the expected payoff in a risk-neutral world, discounted at the risk-free rate. The probability of a rise in the real world and the expected return on the share do not enter.
  • Trees with several steps are valued by backward induction. For an American option, the value at each node is the greater of the exercise value and the continuation value.
  • Delta changes from node to node, so that a replicating portfolio must be adjusted as the share price moves; the adjustment is self-financing.
  • A tree matches a volatility of \(\sigma\) when \(u=e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}\) and \(d=1/u\). As the number of steps increases, the value of a European option converges to the Black–Scholes–Merton value.
  • For an asset with income at rate \(q\), \(a=e^{(r-q)\Delta t}\) replaces \(e^{r\Delta t}\) in the probability; for a futures contract, \(a=1\).

Exercises

10.1 A share trades at $50. In six months it will be worth $55 or $45. The risk-free rate is 4 percent. Value a six-month European call with a strike of $50 by constructing the replicating portfolio, and verify the result with Result 10.1.

\(\Delta=(5-0)/(55-45)=0.5\). The portfolio of 0.5 shares must be worth 0 when the share is $45, so the loan repayment is \(0.5\times45=22.50\) and the amount borrowed \(22.50e^{-0.02}=\$22.05\). Cost: \(0.5\times50-22.05=\$2.95\). Check: \(p=(e^{0.02}-0.9)/0.2=0.6010\); \(f=e^{-0.02}\times0.6010\times5=\$2.95\).

10.2 On the tree of Exercise 10.1, value a six-month European put with a strike of $52 and verify put–call parity against the call with the same strike.

Put: \(f_u=0\), \(f_d=7\); \(f=e^{-0.02}\times0.3990\times7=\$2.74\). Call with strike $52: \(f_u=3\), \(f_d=0\); \(f=e^{-0.02}\times0.6010\times3=\$1.77\). Parity: \(c+Ke^{-rT}-S_0=1.77+52e^{-0.02}-50=1.77+50.97-50=\$2.74\).

10.3 A share trades at $40. In each of two six-month steps it rises by 10 percent or falls by 10 percent. The risk-free rate is 6 percent. Value a one-year put with a strike of $42 (a) if European and (b) if American.

\(p=(e^{0.03}-0.9)/0.2=0.6523\); discount factor \(e^{-0.03}=0.9704\). Final prices: 48.40, 39.60, 32.40; payoffs 0, 2.40, 9.60. Upper node ($44): \(0.9704\times0.3477\times2.40=0.810\); exercise value negative. Lower node ($36): continuation \(0.9704\times(0.6523\times2.40+0.3477\times9.60)=4.759\); exercise value 6.00. (a) European: \(0.9704\times(0.6523\times0.810+0.3477\times4.759)=\$2.12\). (b) American: \(0.9704\times(0.6523\times0.810+0.3477\times6.00)=\$2.54\), which exceeds the immediate exercise value of $2.00.

10.4 In Worked example 10.1, describe the replicating portfolio at the initial node and show that, if the share price rises in the first step, the portfolio is worth exactly the amount required to establish the replicating portfolio for the second step.

At the initial node \(\Delta=0.587\) and the call is worth $2.259, so the portfolio holds 0.587 shares (\(0.5874\times28=\$16.448\)) financed by borrowing \(16.448-2.259=\$14.189\). After a rise, the shares are worth \(0.5874\times32.20=\$18.915\) and the debt is \(14.189e^{0.0125}=\$14.367\); the portfolio is worth \(18.915-14.367=\$4.548\), which is \(f_u\). At that node \(\Delta=1.000\): the portfolio must hold one share ($32.20) with borrowing of \(32.20-4.548=\$27.652\). The additional 0.4126 shares cost \(0.4126\times32.20=\$13.285\), which is exactly the increase in borrowing, \(27.652-14.367\). No new money is required.

10.5 A share has a volatility of 30 percent. The risk-free rate is 5 percent. Find \(u\), \(d\), and \(p\) for a tree with steps of one month.

\(\Delta t=1/12\). \(u=e^{0.30\sqrt{1/12}}=e^{0.0866}=1.0905\); \(d=0.9170\); \(a=e^{0.05/12}=1.004175\); \(p=(1.004175-0.9170)/(1.0905-0.9170)=0.5024\).

10.6 In the opening exercise of the chapter, the call is quoted at $2.40. Set out the arbitrage and show the result in both outcomes.

The call is dear. Write the call for $2.40, buy 0.60 shares for $16.80, and borrow $14.93: net receipt today \(2.40-16.80+14.93=\$0.53\). If the share rises: shares worth \(0.60\times32.20=19.32\); call costs 4.20; loan requires 15.12; net \(19.32-4.20-15.12=0\). If it falls: shares worth 15.12; call expires; loan requires 15.12; net 0. The arbitrageur keeps $0.53 with no obligation.

10.7 A futures price is 80 and its volatility 25 percent. The risk-free rate is 4 percent. Using a one-step tree of six months with the parameters of Result 10.2 and Table 10.1, value a six-month European call on the futures with a strike of 80.

\(u=e^{0.25\sqrt{0.5}}=e^{0.17678}=1.1934\); \(d=0.8380\); \(a=1\); \(p=(1-0.8380)/(1.1934-0.8380)=0.4559\). \(F_u=95.47\), payoff 15.47; \(F_d=67.04\), payoff 0. \(f=e^{-0.02}\times0.4559\times15.47=\$6.91\).

10.8 “Risk-neutral valuation assumes that investors do not care about risk, which is false; the prices it gives are therefore unreliable.” Evaluate this statement.

The statement misdescribes the principle. The value of an option is established by replication: the option is worth the cost of a portfolio of the share and risk-free borrowing that reproduces it, and that cost is the same whatever investors' attitudes to risk, since those attitudes are already reflected in the price of the share. Because the value does not depend on attitudes to risk, it may be computed under any assumed attitude, and the assumption of risk neutrality is chosen for convenience: expected returns all equal the risk-free rate and discounting is at that rate. The result is the correct price in the real world. The principle would fail only where replication fails, for example if the share could not be traded.

Chapter 11 · Part IV: Valuation

Stochastic Processes and Itô's Lemma

The Markov property, the Wiener process, geometric Brownian motion as a model of share prices, Itô's lemma, the lognormal distribution of future share prices, and the estimation of volatility

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. state the Markov property and its relation to the efficiency of markets;
  2. describe a Wiener process and a generalized Wiener process, and compute the mean and standard deviation of a change over any interval;
  3. write the process assumed for a share price and simulate it over a short interval;
  4. use the lognormal distribution to compute the expected value, the median, and a confidence interval for a future share price;
  5. distinguish the expected return on a share from its expected continuously compounded return;
  6. estimate volatility from a series of historical prices;
  7. ★ state Itô's lemma and apply it to a function of a share price.
A note on this chapter. The binomial model of Chapter 10 treats time as a sequence of steps. This chapter describes the behavior of a share price when the steps become indefinitely short. Sections 11.1 to 11.5 and 11.7 use only the normal distribution and are required for Chapter 12. Section 11.6, which is marked ★, presents Itô's lemma and may be omitted; readers who omit it should accept Result 11.3 as stated.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

Is a share more likely to finish above its expected price, or below?

Northwind shares trade at $28. Investors expect a return of 12 percent per year, so that the expected price in one year is \(28e^{0.12}=\$31.57\). The volatility is 39 percent. The figure shows the distribution of the price in one year under the model of this chapter. Before the expected price is marked on it, select the statement that is correct.

Select a statement.

11.1  The Markov property

A variable whose value changes over time in an uncertain way is said to follow a stochastic process. The process is discrete-time if the value can change only at certain fixed dates, as on a binomial tree, and continuous-time if it can change at any moment. It is a discrete-variable process if only certain values are possible and a continuous-variable process if any value within a range is possible. Share prices are in reality quoted in discrete units and change only when the market is open, but a continuous-variable, continuous-time process describes them well and is far more convenient mathematically.

A Markov process is a stochastic process in which only the current value of the variable is relevant for predicting its future. The past history of the variable, and the path by which the present value was reached, add nothing. Share prices are assumed to follow a Markov process. The assumption is the weak form of market efficiency: the present price of a share already reflects all the information contained in the record of its past prices. If it did not, traders who studied past prices could earn more than a fair return, and their trading would remove the pattern on which they relied.

The Markov property concerns probabilities and not certainties. It asserts that the probability distribution of the price at any future date depends only on the price today.

11.2  The Wiener process

Consider a variable that follows a Markov process and whose change over one year is normally distributed with a mean of zero and a variance of 1. What is the distribution of its change over two years? The change over two years is the sum of two changes of one year each, and by the Markov property the two are independent. The mean of the sum is zero, and the variances of independent variables add, so the variance is 2 and the standard deviation \(\sqrt2\). By the same argument the change over six months has a variance of 0.5, and the change over any interval of length \(T\) has a variance of \(T\) and a standard deviation of \(\sqrt{T}\).

This is the essential arithmetic of uncertainty over time. Variances are proportional to time; standard deviations are proportional to the square root of time. Uncertainty over four years is twice, and not four times, uncertainty over one year.

The process just described is a Wiener process, also called Brownian motion. A variable \(z\) follows a Wiener process if it has two properties.

Definition 11.1 — Wiener process

Property 1. The change \(\Delta z\) during a short interval of length \(\Delta t\) is \[ \Delta z=\varepsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}, \] where \(\varepsilon\) is a random draw from the standard normal distribution, which has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
Property 2. The values of \(\Delta z\) for any two different short intervals are independent.

Property 1 implies that \(\Delta z\) is normally distributed with mean zero and standard deviation \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\). Property 2 is the Markov property. Together they imply that the change in \(z\) over any interval of length \(T\) is normal with mean zero and standard deviation \(\sqrt{T}\).

In the limit as \(\Delta t\) approaches zero, the change is written \(dz\). The path of a Wiener process is continuous but extremely irregular: because \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\) is much larger than \(\Delta t\) when \(\Delta t\) is small, the variable changes direction incessantly, and the length of the path it traces in any interval is infinite.

11.3  The generalized Wiener process

A Wiener process has an expected change of zero and a variance of 1 per year. A generalized Wiener process allows any constant expected change and any constant variance. A variable \(x\) follows a generalized Wiener process if

\[ dx=a\,dt+b\,dz, \]

where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants. The term \(a\,dt\) states that \(x\) is expected to increase by \(a\) per unit of time; \(a\) is the drift rate. The term \(b\,dz\) adds variability equal to \(b\) times a Wiener process; \(b^{2}\) is the variance rate. Over a short interval \(\Delta t\),

\[ \Delta x=a\,\Delta t+b\,\varepsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}, \]

and over any interval of length \(T\) the change in \(x\) is normally distributed with mean \(aT\) and standard deviation \(b\sqrt{T}\).

Worked example 11.1 — A generalized Wiener process
The cash balance of a company, in millions of dollars, follows a generalized Wiener process with a drift rate of 20 per year and a variance rate of 900 per year. The balance is now 50. Find the distribution of the balance in six months and in one year.
1
Parameters. \(a=20\); \(b=\sqrt{900}=30\).
2
Six months. Mean: \(50+20\times0.5=60\). Standard deviation: \(30\sqrt{0.5}=21.2\). The balance is normally distributed with mean 60 and standard deviation 21.2.
3
One year. Mean: \(50+20=70\). Standard deviation: \(30\sqrt{1}=30\).
4
Observation. Doubling the horizon doubles the expected change, from 10 to 20, but multiplies the standard deviation only by \(\sqrt2\), from 21.2 to 30.

A further generalization allows the drift and variance rates to depend on the value of the variable and on time. A process of the form

\[ dx=a(x,t)\,dt+b(x,t)\,dz \]

is an Itô process. Over a short interval the change is \(\Delta x=a(x,t)\Delta t+b(x,t)\varepsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}\), on the assumption that the drift and variance rates remain at their values at the start of the interval.

11.4  The process for a share price

A generalized Wiener process with constant drift and variance would be a poor model of a share price. It would imply that the expected change in the price is the same whether the price is $10 or $100, whereas investors require the same expected percentage return whatever the price; and it would permit the price to become negative. The appropriate assumption is that the expected return and the variability of the return are constant.

Result 11.1 — Geometric Brownian motion

The price \(S\) of a share that pays no dividend is assumed to follow the process \[ dS=\mu S\,dt+\sigma S\,dz, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad \frac{dS}{S}=\mu\,dt+\sigma\,dz, \] where \(\mu\) is the expected rate of return on the share per year and \(\sigma\) is the volatility of the share price per year. Over a short interval, \[ \frac{\Delta S}{S}=\mu\,\Delta t+\sigma\,\varepsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}. \]

This process is geometric Brownian motion. The return \(\Delta S/S\) over a short interval is normally distributed with mean \(\mu\,\Delta t\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\). The model is the limit of the binomial tree of Result 10.2 as the length of the step approaches zero: on that tree the return in each step is \(+\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\) or \(-\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\), approximately, and the sum of a large number of such steps is normally distributed.

Worked example 11.2 — One week of Northwind's share price
Northwind shares trade at $28, with \(\mu=0.12\) and \(\sigma=0.39\). Find the distribution of the change in the price over one week, and the change that results from a random draw of \(\varepsilon=-1.20\).
1
Interval. \(\Delta t=1/52=0.01923\); \(\sqrt{\Delta t}=0.13868\).
2
Return. Mean: \(0.12\times0.01923=0.00231\). Standard deviation: \(0.39\times0.13868=0.05408\).
3
Price change. Mean: \(28\times0.00231=\$0.065\). Standard deviation: \(28\times0.05408=\$1.514\).
4
A particular outcome. \(\Delta S=28\times(0.00231+0.05408\times(-1.20))=28\times(-0.06259)=-\$1.75\); the price falls to $26.25.
5
Observation. Over one week the standard deviation of the change is more than twenty times its mean. Over short intervals the behavior of a share price is dominated by its volatility; the expected return becomes visible only over years.

Repeating the calculation of step 4 week after week, each time with a new random draw and the price reached in the previous week, produces a simulated path of the share price. This procedure is Monte Carlo simulation, and Chapter 16 uses it to value derivatives. Interactive figure 11.1 displays twenty such paths.

⚙ Interactive figure 11.1 — Simulated paths of a share price

Twenty paths of geometric Brownian motion

Each grey line is one possible future of a share now priced at $28, simulated in weekly steps. The solid line is the expected price, the dashed line the median, and the dotted lines the limits within which the price lies with a probability of 95 percent. Vary the expected return and the volatility, and generate new paths. Observe which of the two parameters governs the appearance of the paths.

11.5  The lognormal distribution of share prices

Result 11.1 describes the change in the price over a short interval. For the valuation of options the distribution of the price at a future date \(T\) is required. The following result is derived in Section 11.6.

Result 11.2 — The lognormal property

If a share price follows geometric Brownian motion, the natural logarithm of the price at time \(T\) is normally distributed: \[ \ln S_T\ \sim\ \phi\!\left[\,\ln S_0+\left(\mu-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\right)T,\ \ \sigma^{2}T\,\right], \] where \(\phi[m,v]\) denotes a normal distribution with mean \(m\) and variance \(v\).

A variable whose logarithm is normally distributed has a lognormal distribution. A lognormal variable can take any value between zero and infinity, and its distribution is skewed: the mean, the median, and the most likely value are all different, as the opening exercise showed. From the properties of the lognormal distribution,

\[ E(S_T)=S_0\,e^{\mu T}, \qquad \text{median}(S_T)=S_0\,e^{(\mu-\sigma^{2}/2)T}, \qquad \operatorname{var}(S_T)=S_0^{2}\,e^{2\mu T}\left(e^{\sigma^{2}T}-1\right). \]

The expected price grows at the rate \(\mu\), in accordance with the definition of \(\mu\) as the expected return. The median grows at the lower rate \(\mu-\sigma^{2}/2\). For Northwind over one year, the expected price is \(28e^{0.12}=\$31.57\) and the median is \(28e^{0.12-0.07605}=28e^{0.04395}=\$29.26\). The probability that the price exceeds its expected value is \(N(-\sigma\sqrt{T}/2)=N(-0.195)=42.3\) percent, where \(N(x)\) denotes the probability that a standard normal variable is less than \(x\).

Worked example 11.3 — A confidence interval for the share price
For Northwind (\(S_0=28\), \(\mu=0.12\), \(\sigma=0.39\)), find the 95 percent confidence interval for the share price in six months, and the probability that the price will then exceed $30.
1
Mean of \(\ln S_T\). \(\ln28+(0.12-0.39^{2}/2)\times0.5=3.3322+0.04395\times0.5=3.3542\).
2
Standard deviation of \(\ln S_T\). \(0.39\sqrt{0.5}=0.2758\).
3
Interval for \(\ln S_T\). A normal variable lies within 1.96 standard deviations of its mean with a probability of 95 percent: \(3.3542\pm1.96\times0.2758\), that is, from 2.8137 to 3.8947.
4
Interval for \(S_T\). \(e^{2.8137}=\$16.67\) to \(e^{3.8947}=\$49.14\). The interval is not symmetric about the current price: it extends $11.33 below and $21.14 above.
5
Probability of exceeding $30. \(\ln30=3.4012\). The number of standard deviations above the mean is \((3.4012-3.3542)/0.2758=0.1704\), and \(1-N(0.1704)=43.2\) percent.

The distribution of the rate of return

Let \(x\) be the continuously compounded rate of return per year realized between time 0 and time \(T\), defined by \(S_T=S_0e^{xT}\), so that \(x=\ln(S_T/S_0)/T\). From Result 11.2,

\[ x\ \sim\ \phi\!\left[\,\mu-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2},\ \ \frac{\sigma^{2}}{T}\,\right]. \]

The expected continuously compounded return is \(\mu-\sigma^{2}/2\) and not \(\mu\). For Northwind it is \(0.12-0.07605=4.4\) percent per year, against an expected return of 12 percent. Both statements are correct, and they answer different questions. The quantity \(\mu\) is the expected return over a very short period, expressed per year; it is the arithmetic average of the returns over many short periods. The quantity \(\mu-\sigma^{2}/2\) is the return, compounded over the whole period, that an investor should expect to realize; it corresponds to the geometric average. The geometric average of a set of unequal numbers is always below the arithmetic average. A share that rises by 50 percent and then falls by 50 percent has an arithmetic average return of zero and has lost a quarter of its value.

The standard deviation of \(x\), \(\sigma/\sqrt{T}\), declines as the period lengthens: the average annual return over twenty years is known with far greater confidence than the return over one year.

A share has a volatility of 30 percent per year. What is the standard deviation of its return over one trading day, taking a year to contain 252 trading days?

11.6  ★ Itô's lemma

Optional section. The price of a derivative is a function of the price of the underlying asset and of time. Itô's lemma gives the process followed by such a function. This section uses partial derivatives: \(\partial G/\partial x\) denotes the rate of change of a function \(G\) with respect to \(x\) when its other arguments are held fixed.

Result 11.3 — Itô's lemma

Suppose that \(x\) follows the Itô process \(dx=a(x,t)\,dt+b(x,t)\,dz\), and let \(G\) be a function of \(x\) and \(t\). Then \(G\) follows the process \[ dG=\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}\,a+\frac{\partial G}{\partial t}+\frac12\,\frac{\partial^{2}G}{\partial x^{2}}\,b^{2}\right)dt+\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}\,b\,dz, \] in which \(dz\) is the same Wiener process as in the process for \(x\).

Outline of the derivation. In ordinary calculus a small change in \(G\) is approximated by \(\Delta G\approx(\partial G/\partial x)\Delta x+(\partial G/\partial t)\Delta t\), the terms of higher order being negligible. For an Itô process this is not sufficient. Expanding to the second order,

\[ \Delta G=\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}\Delta x+\frac{\partial G}{\partial t}\Delta t+\frac12\frac{\partial^{2}G}{\partial x^{2}}(\Delta x)^{2}+\cdots \]

With \(\Delta x=a\,\Delta t+b\,\varepsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}\), the square is \((\Delta x)^{2}=b^{2}\varepsilon^{2}\Delta t+\text{terms of higher order in }\Delta t\). This term is of the same order as \(\Delta t\) and cannot be neglected. Moreover, the variance of \(\varepsilon^{2}\Delta t\) is of order \((\Delta t)^{2}\), so that as \(\Delta t\) approaches zero the term ceases to be random and equals its expected value, \(b^{2}\Delta t\), because \(E(\varepsilon^{2})=1\). Substituting \((\Delta x)^{2}=b^{2}\,dt\) and \(\Delta x=a\,dt+b\,dz\) into the expansion gives the lemma. The essential point is expressed in the rule \((dz)^{2}=dt\): the square of the random term is not negligible, and it is not random.

For a share price, \(a=\mu S\) and \(b=\sigma S\), and the lemma becomes

\[ dG=\left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial S}\,\mu S+\frac{\partial G}{\partial t}+\frac12\,\frac{\partial^{2}G}{\partial S^{2}}\,\sigma^{2}S^{2}\right)dt+\frac{\partial G}{\partial S}\,\sigma S\,dz . \]

Both \(S\) and \(G\) are driven by the same source of uncertainty, \(dz\). This fact is the basis of the derivation of the Black–Scholes–Merton equation in Section 12.3: a portfolio of the share and the derivative can be formed in which the two random terms cancel.

Worked example 11.4 — Two applications of Itô's lemma
A share price follows \(dS=\mu S\,dt+\sigma S\,dz\). Find the process followed by (a) the forward price \(F=Se^{r(T-t)}\) of Result 4.1 and (b) \(G=\ln S\).
1
(a) Derivatives. \(\partial F/\partial S=e^{r(T-t)}\); \(\partial^{2}F/\partial S^{2}=0\); \(\partial F/\partial t=-rSe^{r(T-t)}\).
2
(a) Process. \(dF=\left[e^{r(T-t)}\mu S-rSe^{r(T-t)}\right]dt+e^{r(T-t)}\sigma S\,dz=(\mu-r)F\,dt+\sigma F\,dz\). The forward price follows geometric Brownian motion with the same volatility as the share and an expected growth rate of \(\mu-r\): the excess of the expected return over the risk-free rate.
3
(b) Derivatives. \(\partial G/\partial S=1/S\); \(\partial^{2}G/\partial S^{2}=-1/S^{2}\); \(\partial G/\partial t=0\).
4
(b) Process. \(dG=\left[\dfrac1S\,\mu S-\dfrac12\,\dfrac{1}{S^{2}}\,\sigma^{2}S^{2}\right]dt+\dfrac1S\,\sigma S\,dz=\left(\mu-\dfrac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\right)dt+\sigma\,dz\).
5
Conclusion. \(\ln S\) follows a generalized Wiener process with constant drift \(\mu-\sigma^{2}/2\) and constant variance rate \(\sigma^{2}\). By Section 11.3, its change between 0 and \(T\) is normal with mean \((\mu-\sigma^{2}/2)T\) and variance \(\sigma^{2}T\). This is Result 11.2. The term \(-\sigma^{2}/2\), which distinguishes the median from the mean, arises from the second derivative in the lemma.

11.7  Estimating volatility from historical data

The volatility of a share can be estimated from a record of its past prices observed at regular intervals: daily, weekly, or monthly. Let \(S_0,S_1,\dots,S_n\) be \(n+1\) successive prices, and \(\tau\) the length of the interval between observations, in years. The procedure is as follows.

  1. Compute the continuously compounded return in each interval: \(u_i=\ln(S_i/S_{i-1})\), for \(i=1,\dots,n\).
  2. Compute the standard deviation of the \(u_i\): \(s=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(u_i-\bar u)^{2}}\), where \(\bar u\) is their mean.
  3. By Result 11.2, the standard deviation of \(u_i\) is \(\sigma\sqrt{\tau}\). The estimate of the volatility is therefore \(\hat\sigma=s/\sqrt{\tau}\).

The standard error of the estimate is approximately \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{2n}\). More observations give greater precision, but volatility changes over time and data from the distant past may no longer be relevant; a common compromise is to use daily closing prices for the most recent 90 to 180 days. When daily data are used, \(\tau\) is taken as \(1/252\), the reciprocal of the number of trading days in a year, and not as \(1/365\). Evidence shows that volatility is far higher when markets are open than when they are closed, so that it is trading days and not calendar days that should be counted. If a dividend is paid during an interval, the return for that interval is computed as \(\ln[(S_i+D)/S_{i-1}]\).

Worked example 11.5 — Estimating volatility from weekly prices
The closing price of a share on eleven successive Fridays is $28.00, 28.90, 27.60, 28.40, 29.90, 29.10, 30.60, 29.80, 28.50, 29.70, and 30.40. No dividend was paid. Estimate the volatility.
1
Returns. \(u_1=\ln(28.90/28.00)=0.03164\); the ten returns are 0.03164, −0.04603, 0.02857, 0.05147, −0.02712, 0.05026, −0.02649, −0.04460, 0.04124, and 0.02330.
2
Sums. \(\sum u_i=0.08224\), so \(\bar u=0.008224\). \(\sum u_i^{2}=0.014782\).
3
Standard deviation. \(s=\sqrt{\dfrac{0.014782-10\times0.008224^{2}}{9}}=\sqrt{0.0015673}=0.03959\) per week.
4
Volatility. \(\hat\sigma=0.03959/\sqrt{1/52}=0.03959\times7.2111=0.2855\), or 28.5 percent per year.
5
Precision. Standard error: \(0.2855/\sqrt{20}=0.064\). With ten observations the estimate is imprecise: the true volatility could plausibly lie anywhere between 16 and 41 percent.

The expected return \(\mu\) cannot be estimated in this way with any useful precision. Section 11.5 showed that the average realized return over \(T\) years has a standard deviation of \(\sigma/\sqrt{T}\); with a volatility of 39 percent, even fifty years of data leave a standard deviation of 5.5 percentage points. It is one of the most fortunate facts in the theory of derivatives that, as Chapter 10 showed and Chapter 12 confirms, the value of an option does not depend on \(\mu\) at all.

Concept check 11.2

A share has an expected return of 15 percent and a volatility of 40 percent. What continuously compounded return per year should an investor expect to realize over a long holding period?

Concept check 11.3

The standard deviation of the change in a variable that follows a Wiener process is 2.0 over one year. What is it over four years?

Historical note

The irregular motion of pollen grains suspended in water was described by the botanist Robert Brown in 1827. The first mathematical model of such motion was constructed not by a physicist but by a student of finance: Louis Bachelier, in a doctoral thesis on the Paris bond market submitted in 1900, five years before Albert Einstein's paper on the same subject. Bachelier assumed that price changes, and not returns, were normally distributed, so that his model permitted negative prices; the replacement of the price by its logarithm was proposed by Paul Samuelson in 1965 and gives the geometric Brownian motion of this chapter.

The rigorous theory of the process is due to Norbert Wiener, in 1923, and the calculus that bears his name was developed by Kiyosi Itô in Japan in the 1940s. Itô regarded his work as pure mathematics and is reported to have been surprised, late in his life, to learn that it had become the working tool of financial markets.

Summary

  • Share prices are assumed to follow a Markov process: the distribution of future prices depends only on the present price.
  • A Wiener process has changes that are independent and normal with mean zero and variance equal to the length of the interval. Variance is proportional to time and standard deviation to its square root.
  • A share price is assumed to follow geometric Brownian motion, \(dS=\mu S\,dt+\sigma S\,dz\): over a short interval the return is normal with mean \(\mu\,\Delta t\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\).
  • The price at a future date is lognormal: \(\ln S_T\) is normal with mean \(\ln S_0+(\mu-\sigma^{2}/2)T\) and variance \(\sigma^{2}T\). The expected price is \(S_0e^{\mu T}\) and the median \(S_0e^{(\mu-\sigma^{2}/2)T}\).
  • The expected continuously compounded return is \(\mu-\sigma^{2}/2\), which is below the expected return \(\mu\).
  • Volatility is estimated as the standard deviation of the logarithmic returns divided by the square root of the interval between observations, in years.
  • ★ Itô's lemma gives the process followed by a function of a variable that follows an Itô process; its distinctive term is \(\tfrac12(\partial^{2}G/\partial x^{2})b^{2}\).

Exercises

11.1 A variable follows a generalized Wiener process with a drift rate of 4 per year and a variance rate of 25 per year. Its present value is 30. Find the probability that it is below 30 after two years.

After two years the variable is normal with mean \(30+8=38\) and standard deviation \(5\sqrt2=7.071\). The value 30 is \((30-38)/7.071=-1.131\) standard deviations from the mean; \(N(-1.131)=12.9\) percent.

11.2 A share trades at $60, with an expected return of 10 percent and a volatility of 25 percent. Find the mean and standard deviation of the change in its price over one trading day (1/252 of a year).

Mean: \(60\times0.10/252=\$0.024\). Standard deviation: \(60\times0.25\times\sqrt{1/252}=60\times0.015749=\$0.945\).

11.3 For the share of Exercise 11.2, find the expected price, the median price, and the 95 percent confidence interval for the price in two years.

Expected: \(60e^{0.20}=\$73.28\). Mean of \(\ln S_T\): \(\ln60+(0.10-0.03125)\times2=4.0943+0.1375=4.2318\); median \(e^{4.2318}=\$68.84\). Standard deviation of \(\ln S_T\): \(0.25\sqrt2=0.3536\). Interval: \(e^{4.2318\pm1.96\times0.3536}\), from \(e^{3.5388}=\$34.43\) to \(e^{4.9248}=\$137.66\).

11.4 For the share of Exercise 11.2, find the probability that a one-year European call with a strike of $70 will be exercised.

\(\ln S_T\) is normal with mean \(4.0943+0.06875=4.1631\) and standard deviation 0.25. \(\ln70=4.2485\), which is \((4.2485-4.1631)/0.25=0.3416\) standard deviations above the mean. Probability: \(1-N(0.3416)=36.6\) percent. This is the probability in the real world; the risk-neutral probability, which enters the valuation of the option, replaces \(\mu\) by \(r\).

11.5 A share's volatility is 32 percent. An analyst states that the standard deviation of its return over one month is \(32/12=2.7\) percent. Correct the statement.

Standard deviations scale with the square root of time: \(0.32\sqrt{1/12}=0.32\times0.2887=9.2\) percent. Dividing by 12 would be correct for the variance: \(0.32^{2}/12=0.00853\), whose square root is 9.2 percent.

11.6 Daily closing prices of a share on six successive trading days are $50.00, 50.60, 49.90, 50.40, 51.50, and 51.00. Estimate the volatility per year.

Returns: 0.011929, −0.013931, 0.009970, 0.021591, −0.009756. Mean: 0.003961. Sum of squared deviations: \(0.000997-5\times0.003961^{2}=0.000919\). \(s=\sqrt{0.000919/4}=0.01515\) per day. \(\hat\sigma=0.01515\times\sqrt{252}=0.241\), or 24.1 percent. With five observations the standard error is \(0.241/\sqrt{10}=7.6\) percentage points.

11.7 A fund reports that over ten years its annual returns averaged 9.0 percent with a standard deviation of 20 percent. Approximately what compounded annual return did an investor realize, and why does it differ from 9.0 percent?

Approximately \(0.09-0.20^{2}/2=7.0\) percent. The reported figure is an arithmetic average. The realized compounded return corresponds to the geometric average, which is lower by about half the variance, because gains and losses of equal percentage size do not offset: a loss of 20 percent requires a gain of 25 percent to recover.

11.8 ★ A share price follows \(dS=\mu S\,dt+\sigma S\,dz\). Use Itô's lemma to find the process followed by \(G=S^{2}\), and state the expected growth rate and volatility of \(G\).

\(\partial G/\partial S=2S\); \(\partial^{2}G/\partial S^{2}=2\); \(\partial G/\partial t=0\). \(dG=\left[2S\,\mu S+\tfrac12\times2\times\sigma^{2}S^{2}\right]dt+2S\,\sigma S\,dz=(2\mu+\sigma^{2})G\,dt+2\sigma G\,dz\). \(G\) follows geometric Brownian motion with an expected growth rate of \(2\mu+\sigma^{2}\) and a volatility of \(2\sigma\). Ordinary calculus would give a growth rate of \(2\mu\); the additional \(\sigma^{2}\) is the contribution of the second-derivative term.

Further reading

  • Bachelier, L. (1900). Théorie de la spéculation. Annales Scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure, 17, 21–86.
  • Hull, J. C. (2022). Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (11th ed.). Pearson. Chapters 14–15.
  • Itô, K. (1951). On stochastic differential equations. Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society, 4, 1–51.
  • Neftci, S. N. (2000). An Introduction to the Mathematics of Financial Derivatives (2nd ed.). Academic Press.
  • Samuelson, P. A. (1965). Rational theory of warrant pricing. Industrial Management Review, 6(2), 13–31.
