Chapter 12 · Part IV: Valuation

The Black–Scholes–Merton Model

The assumptions of the model, the differential equation that every derivative must satisfy, the formulas for European calls and puts and their interpretation, implied volatility, and the treatment of dividends

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. state the assumptions on which the Black–Scholes–Merton model rests;
  2. compute the prices of European calls and puts from the Black–Scholes–Merton formulas;
  3. interpret \(N(d_1)\) and \(N(d_2)\) and relate the formula to the replicating portfolio of Chapter 10;
  4. define implied volatility and compute it from a market price;
  5. adjust the formulas for known dividends and explain the limits of the model for American options;
  6. ★ derive the Black–Scholes–Merton differential equation from a riskless portfolio.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

Is the call cheap or dear?

A three-month European call on Northwind shares with a strike of $30 trades at $1.52. The share price is $28 and the risk-free rate is 5 percent. A colleague who has studied the company states that the volatility of its shares is 25 percent per year. If the colleague is right, how should the market price of the call be regarded?

Select an assessment.

12.1  Assumptions

The model of Fischer Black, Myron Scholes, and Robert Merton values a European option on a share by the argument of Chapter 10, applied to a share price that changes continuously and not in steps. It rests on the following assumptions.

  1. The share price follows the geometric Brownian motion of Result 11.1, with constant expected return \(\mu\) and constant volatility \(\sigma\).
  2. Short selling is permitted, and the proceeds are available in full.
  3. There are no transaction costs or taxes, and securities are perfectly divisible.
  4. The share pays no dividends during the life of the option.
  5. There are no riskless arbitrage opportunities.
  6. Trading in securities is continuous.
  7. The risk-free rate \(r\) is constant and the same for all maturities.

Several of these can be relaxed. Section 12.7 allows for dividends; the rate \(r\) may be a known function of time; and the volatility may be a known function of time, in which case \(\sigma^{2}\) in the formulas is replaced by its average over the life of the option. The first assumption is the one of substance. Chapter 15 examines the evidence against it and the adjustments that practitioners make.

12.2  The idea of the model

Chapter 10 showed that on a binomial tree an option can be replicated by a portfolio of \(\Delta\) shares and risk-free borrowing, adjusted at each node. The Black–Scholes–Merton argument is the same, with adjustment at every instant. Over a very short interval the price of an option and the price of the share are perfectly correlated, because both are driven by the single source of uncertainty in the share price. A portfolio that is short one option and long the appropriate number of shares is therefore riskless over that interval and must earn the risk-free rate. This single requirement determines the price of the option.

Two consequences should be noted before the formula is stated. The expected return on the share, \(\mu\), does not appear in the price of the option, for the reason given in Section 10.2: it is already reflected in the price of the share. And because \(\mu\) does not appear, the option may be valued by the principle of risk-neutral valuation, Principle 10.1: assume that the share is expected to earn the risk-free rate, compute the expected payoff, and discount at the risk-free rate.

12.3  ★ The Black–Scholes–Merton differential equation

Optional section. This section requires Itô's lemma, Result 11.3. Readers who omitted Section 11.6 may proceed to Section 12.4.

Let \(f\) be the price of a derivative that depends on the share price \(S\) and on time \(t\). The share price follows \(dS=\mu S\,dt+\sigma S\,dz\). By Itô's lemma,

\[ df=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial S}\mu S+\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+\frac12\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial S^{2}}\sigma^{2}S^{2}\right)dt+\frac{\partial f}{\partial S}\sigma S\,dz . \]

Form a portfolio that is short one derivative and long \(\partial f/\partial S\) shares. Its value is

\[ \Pi=-f+\frac{\partial f}{\partial S}S, \]

and the change in its value over a short interval is \(d\Pi=-df+(\partial f/\partial S)\,dS\). Substituting the two processes, the terms in \(dz\) cancel, and so do the terms in \(\mu\):

\[ d\Pi=\left(-\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}-\frac12\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial S^{2}}\sigma^{2}S^{2}\right)dt . \]

The portfolio is riskless over the interval, and in the absence of arbitrage it must earn the risk-free rate: \(d\Pi=r\Pi\,dt\). Hence

\[ \left(-\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}-\frac12\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial S^{2}}\sigma^{2}S^{2}\right)dt=r\left(-f+\frac{\partial f}{\partial S}S\right)dt, \]

which rearranges to the following.

Result 12.1 — The Black–Scholes–Merton differential equation

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+rS\frac{\partial f}{\partial S}+\frac12\sigma^{2}S^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial S^{2}}=rf . \]

The equation holds for every derivative whose value depends only on the price of a share that pays no dividend and on time. Different derivatives are distinguished by their boundary conditions, which specify the value at the boundaries of the possible values of \(S\) and \(t\). For a European call the condition is \(f=\max(S-K,0)\) when \(t=T\); for a European put, \(f=\max(K-S,0)\) when \(t=T\). The simplest solution is that for a forward contract with delivery price \(K\), \(f=S-Ke^{-r(T-t)}\) from Section 4.5: here \(\partial f/\partial t=-rKe^{-r(T-t)}\), \(\partial f/\partial S=1\), and \(\partial^{2}f/\partial S^{2}=0\), so the left-hand side is \(-rKe^{-r(T-t)}+rS=rf\), as required.

The portfolio is riskless only for an instant. As \(S\) and \(t\) change, so does \(\partial f/\partial S\), and the number of shares held must be adjusted continually. The equation contains \(S\), \(t\), \(\sigma\), and \(r\), none of which depends on the risk preferences of investors. The expected return \(\mu\), which does depend on them, has disappeared. This is the formal justification of risk-neutral valuation.

12.4  The pricing formulas

Result 12.2 — The Black–Scholes–Merton formulas

The prices of a European call and a European put on a share that pays no dividend are \[ c=S_0N(d_1)-Ke^{-rT}N(d_2), \qquad p=Ke^{-rT}N(-d_2)-S_0N(-d_1), \] where \[ d_1=\frac{\ln(S_0/K)+(r+\sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}, \qquad d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt{T}, \] and \(N(x)\) is the probability that a variable with a standard normal distribution is less than \(x\).

The function \(N(x)\) is the cumulative standard normal distribution. It is available in every spreadsheet and statistical program; a few values are given in Table 12.1. By symmetry, \(N(-x)=1-N(x)\).

Table 12.1  Selected values of the cumulative standard normal distribution
\(x\)−2.0−1.5−1.0−0.500.51.01.52.0
\(N(x)\)0.02280.06680.15870.30850.50000.69150.84130.93320.9772

The two formulas are consistent with put–call parity. Substituting \(N(-d_1)=1-N(d_1)\) and \(N(-d_2)=1-N(d_2)\) in the formula for the put gives \(p=c+Ke^{-rT}-S_0\), which is Result 8.2. The formulas satisfy the differential equation of Result 12.1 and its boundary conditions, and they are the limit of the binomial value of Chapter 10 as the number of steps increases, as Interactive figure 10.2 showed.

Worked example 12.1 — The Northwind options
Northwind shares trade at $28 and have a volatility of 39 percent. The risk-free rate is 5 percent. Find the prices of three-month European options with a strike of $30.
1
Preliminaries. \(\ln(28/30)=-0.06899\); \(\sigma^{2}/2=0.07605\); \(\sigma\sqrt{T}=0.39\times0.5=0.195\); \(Ke^{-rT}=30e^{-0.0125}=29.6273\).
2
\(d_1\). \(\dfrac{-0.06899+(0.05+0.07605)\times0.25}{0.195}=\dfrac{-0.06899+0.03151}{0.195}=-0.1922\).
3
\(d_2\). \(-0.1922-0.195=-0.3872\).
4
Normal probabilities. \(N(-0.1922)=0.4238\); \(N(-0.3872)=0.3493\).
5
Call. \(c=28\times0.4238-29.6273\times0.3493=11.866-10.349=\$1.52\).
6
Put. \(p=29.6273\times(1-0.3493)-28\times(1-0.4238)=19.278-16.134=\$3.14\). These are the prices of Table 9.1, and \(1.52+29.63=3.14+28.00\) to within rounding.

Interpretation

Each term of the formula for the call has a meaning. The call pays \(S_T-K\) if \(S_T>K\) and nothing otherwise. Its value is the discounted risk-neutral expected value of this payoff, which may be separated into the amount received and the amount paid.

  • \(N(d_2)\) is the probability, in a risk-neutral world, that the option will be exercised, that is, that \(S_T>K\). The term \(Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)\) is the present value of the strike price multiplied by the probability that it will be paid.
  • \(S_0N(d_1)\) is the present value, in a risk-neutral world, of receiving the share if the option is exercised and nothing otherwise. It exceeds \(S_0N(d_2)\) because, in the outcomes in which the option is exercised, the share is worth more than average.
  • \(N(d_1)\) is also the delta of the call: the number of shares in the replicating portfolio of Chapter 10. The formula states that a call is equivalent to \(N(d_1)\) shares financed by borrowing \(Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)\). In Worked example 12.1 the call is replicated by 0.4238 shares, worth $11.87, and borrowing of $10.35.

The formula behaves sensibly at its limits. When the share price is very large relative to the strike, \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) are large, both probabilities approach 1, and \(c\) approaches \(S_0-Ke^{-rT}\), the value of a forward contract: exercise is nearly certain. When the volatility approaches zero, the share grows at the risk-free rate with certainty, and the call is worth \(\max(S_0-Ke^{-rT},0)\), the lower bound of Result 8.1.

For a European call, \(d_1=0.60\) and \(d_2=0.40\), so that \(N(d_1)=0.7257\) and \(N(d_2)=0.6554\). Which statement is correct?

12.5  ★ The formula as a risk-neutral expectation

Optional section. This section outlines the derivation of the formula for the call from Principle 10.1 and Result 11.2.

In a risk-neutral world the expected return on the share is \(r\), so that by Result 11.2 \(\ln S_T\) is normal with mean \(m=\ln S_0+(r-\sigma^{2}/2)T\) and standard deviation \(s=\sigma\sqrt{T}\). The value of the call is \(c=e^{-rT}\hat E[\max(S_T-K,0)]\), where \(\hat E\) denotes the expectation in that world. Write the expectation as \(\hat E[S_T\,\mathbf 1_{S_T>K}]-K\,\hat P(S_T>K)\), where \(\mathbf 1\) equals 1 when the condition holds and 0 otherwise.

Second term. \(\hat P(S_T>K)=\hat P(\ln S_T>\ln K)=N\!\left(\dfrac{m-\ln K}{s}\right)\), and \(\dfrac{m-\ln K}{s}=\dfrac{\ln(S_0/K)+(r-\sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T}=d_2\).

First term. For a lognormal variable, a standard integration (completing the square in the exponent) gives \(\hat E[S_T\,\mathbf 1_{S_T>K}]=e^{m+s^{2}/2}\,N\!\left(\dfrac{m+s^{2}-\ln K}{s}\right)\). Here \(e^{m+s^{2}/2}=S_0e^{rT}\) and \(\dfrac{m+s^{2}-\ln K}{s}=d_2+\sigma\sqrt T=d_1\).

Combining the two, \(c=e^{-rT}\left[S_0e^{rT}N(d_1)-KN(d_2)\right]=S_0N(d_1)-Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)\). \(\blacksquare\)

12.6  Volatility

Of the five inputs to the formula, four can be observed: the share price, the strike, the time to expiration, and the risk-free rate. The fifth, the volatility of the share over the life of the option, cannot. Two approaches are used.

Historical volatility is the estimate obtained from past prices by the method of Section 11.7. It describes the past, and its use assumes that the future will resemble it.

Implied volatility is the volatility that, when substituted into the formula, gives the price at which the option trades in the market. It is found by reversing the usual calculation: the price is known and the volatility is the unknown. The formula cannot be inverted algebraically, but because the price of an option increases steadily with volatility, the implied volatility is easily found by trial. The simplest systematic method is bisection: choose a low volatility and a high one whose model prices lie on either side of the market price; test the midpoint; discard the half of the interval that cannot contain the answer; and repeat.

Worked example 12.2 — An implied volatility
The Northwind call of Worked example 12.1 trades at $1.80 and not at $1.52. Find the implied volatility to the nearest percentage point.
1
Bracket. At \(\sigma=40\%\) the formula gives $1.572, which is too low; at \(\sigma=50\%\) it gives $2.125, which is too high. The implied volatility lies between 40 and 50 percent.
2
Midpoint. At \(\sigma=45\%\) the formula gives $1.848, which is too high. The answer lies between 40 and 45 percent.
3
Continue. At 42.5 percent: $1.710, too low. At 43.75 percent: $1.779, too low. At 44.4 percent: $1.815, too high.
4
Result. The implied volatility is 44 percent; to two decimal places it is 44.14 percent.

Implied volatility is the market's assessment of the future volatility of the share, as expressed in the price that traders are willing to pay for options. It is forward-looking where historical volatility is backward-looking, and traders use it as the unit in which option prices are compared. A price of $1.52 for one option and $4.84 for another conveys little; implied volatilities of 39 percent for both convey that the two are priced consistently. In the opening exercise, the disagreement between the colleague and the market was a disagreement between a volatility of 25 percent and an implied volatility of 39 percent.

The best-known measure of implied volatility is the VIX index published by Cboe Global Markets, which is computed from the prices of options on the S&P 500 index expiring in about thirty days. Since 1990 it has usually stood between 12 and 25, and it exceeded 80 in October 2008 and in March 2020.

Concept check 12.2

Two call options on different shares both expire in three months. Option A costs $2.00 and has an implied volatility of 25 percent; option B costs $0.80 and has an implied volatility of 45 percent. In what sense can one be called more expensive than the other?

12.7  Dividends

The formulas of Result 12.2 assume that the share pays no dividend. For a European option on a share that will pay known dividends, a simple adjustment suffices. The share price may be regarded as the sum of two components: a riskless component equal to the present value of the dividends to be paid during the life of the option, and a risky component consisting of the remainder. By the time the option expires the dividends will have been paid and the riskless component will no longer exist. The formulas therefore apply with \(S_0\) replaced by

\[ S_0-D, \]

where \(D\) is the present value of the dividends, discounted from their ex-dividend dates at the risk-free rate. This is the adjustment that Section 8.6 made to the bounds and to put–call parity. The volatility in the formula is, strictly, that of the risky component, which is slightly higher than the volatility of the share price as a whole.

Worked example 12.3 — A call on a share that pays a dividend
Northwind will pay a dividend of $0.40 with an ex-dividend date in two months. Revalue the three-month European call with a strike of $30 of Worked example 12.1.
1
Present value of the dividend. \(D=0.40e^{-0.05\times2/12}=\$0.3967\).
2
Adjusted share price. \(28-0.3967=\$27.6033\).
3
Formula. \(d_1=\dfrac{\ln(27.6033/30)+0.03151}{0.195}=-0.2654\); \(d_2=-0.4604\); \(N(d_1)=0.3954\); \(N(d_2)=0.3226\).
4
Call. \(c=27.6033\times0.3954-29.6273\times0.3226=10.913-9.558=\$1.35\). The dividend of $0.40 reduces the value of the call by $0.17 and, by parity, raises the value of the put by \(0.40e^{-0.0083}-0.17=\$0.23\).

American options

By Result 8.3, an American call on a share that pays no dividend is worth the same as the European call, and the formula of Result 12.2 applies to it. When the share pays dividends, early exercise of the call may be optimal immediately before an ex-dividend date. A simple approximation due to Fischer Black is to compute the values of two European calls, one expiring at the original expiration date and one expiring immediately before the last ex-dividend date, and to take the greater of the two.

For American puts there is no exact formula, with or without dividends, because early exercise may be optimal at any time. They are valued numerically, by the binomial trees of Chapter 10 or by the methods of Chapter 16.

12.8  What the model does and does not claim

The model is the foundation of the modern derivatives industry, and it is used daily in forms little changed from those of 1973. Its claim should be stated precisely. It does not predict the price of a share, and it does not assert that the assumptions of Section 12.1 hold exactly. It asserts that if the share price follows geometric Brownian motion with a known volatility, an option can be replicated by trading in the share, and is therefore worth the cost of doing so.

In practice volatility is neither constant nor known, share prices occasionally jump, and trading is neither continuous nor free. Practitioners accommodate these facts within the framework of the model, principally by using a different implied volatility for each strike and expiration. That practice, and what it reveals about the distribution of share prices that the market in fact assumes, is the subject of Chapter 15.

Concept check 12.3

Analysts revise their forecast of the return on a share from 8 percent to 14 percent per year. The share price, its volatility, and the risk-free rate are unchanged. What happens to the Black–Scholes–Merton value of a call on the share?

Historical note

Fischer Black and Myron Scholes completed their paper in 1970. It was rejected by two journals before it was published in the Journal of Political Economy in the spring of 1973, within weeks of the opening of the Chicago Board Options Exchange. Robert Merton, whose paper appeared in the same year, supplied the argument based on continuous replication and showed that the result did not depend on the equilibrium model of asset prices that Black and Scholes had originally used. Within two years traders on the exchange floor were using calculators programmed with the formula.

Scholes and Merton were awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1997; the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences recorded that Black, who had died in 1995, would have shared it. In 1998 the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management, of which Scholes and Merton were partners, lost $4.6 billion, as recorded in Table 1.3. The loss arose from leverage and from the assumption that past relations between markets would persist, and not from the formula, but it has served since as a reminder of the distance between a model and the markets it describes.

Summary

  • The model assumes a share price that follows geometric Brownian motion with constant volatility, continuous trading without costs, and a constant risk-free rate.
  • A portfolio of the option and the share can be made riskless for an instant and must earn the risk-free rate. The resulting value of the option does not depend on the expected return on the share.
  • \(c=S_0N(d_1)-Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)\) and \(p=Ke^{-rT}N(-d_2)-S_0N(-d_1)\), with \(d_1=[\ln(S_0/K)+(r+\sigma^{2}/2)T]/(\sigma\sqrt T)\) and \(d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt T\).
  • \(N(d_2)\) is the risk-neutral probability of exercise; \(N(d_1)\) is the delta of the call, the number of shares in its replicating portfolio.
  • Implied volatility is the volatility at which the formula reproduces a market price. It is found by trial and is the unit in which option prices are compared.
  • For known dividends, \(S_0\) is replaced by \(S_0-D\). American puts, and American calls on shares that pay dividends, have no exact formula.

Exercises

12.1 A share that pays no dividend trades at $50 and has a volatility of 30 percent. The risk-free rate is 4 percent. Find the prices of six-month European options with a strike of $50.

\(\sigma\sqrt T=0.30\times0.7071=0.2121\). \(d_1=[0+(0.04+0.045)\times0.5]/0.2121=0.2003\); \(d_2=-0.0118\). \(N(d_1)=0.5794\); \(N(d_2)=0.4953\). \(Ke^{-rT}=50e^{-0.02}=49.010\). \(c=50\times0.5794-49.010\times0.4953=28.970-24.275=\$4.70\). \(p=4.70+49.01-50=\$3.71\).

12.2 A share that pays no dividend trades at $40 and has a volatility of 25 percent. The risk-free rate is 6 percent. Find the price of a nine-month European put with a strike of $45.

\(\sigma\sqrt T=0.25\times0.8660=0.2165\). \(d_1=[\ln(40/45)+(0.06+0.03125)\times0.75]/0.2165=(-0.11778+0.06844)/0.2165=-0.2279\); \(d_2=-0.4444\). \(N(-d_1)=0.5901\); \(N(-d_2)=0.6716\). \(Ke^{-rT}=45e^{-0.045}=43.020\). \(p=43.020\times0.6716-40\times0.5901=28.893-23.606=\$5.29\).

12.3 For a one-year European call with a strike of $95 on a share at $100 with a volatility of 20 percent and a risk-free rate of 5 percent, find (a) the price, (b) the risk-neutral probability of exercise, and (c) the composition of the replicating portfolio.

\(d_1=[\ln(100/95)+(0.05+0.02)\times1]/0.20=(0.05129+0.07)/0.20=0.6065\); \(d_2=0.4065\). \(N(d_1)=0.7279\); \(N(d_2)=0.6578\). \(Ke^{-rT}=95e^{-0.05}=90.367\). (a) \(c=72.79-59.44=\$13.35\). (b) 65.8 percent. (c) 0.7279 shares, worth $72.79, financed by borrowing $59.44.

12.4 Verify that the prices of the call and the put in Exercise 12.1 satisfy put–call parity, and explain why the call is worth more than the put although the option is at the money.

\(c+Ke^{-rT}=4.70+49.01=53.71\); \(p+S_0=3.71+50.00=53.71\). By parity \(c-p=S_0-Ke^{-rT}=50-49.01=\$0.99\): the holder of the call defers payment of the strike and earns interest on it, while the holder of the put defers its receipt.

12.5 The Northwind call of Worked example 12.1 trades at $1.03. Using the fact that the formula gives $1.029 at a volatility of 30 percent, state the implied volatility, and say what a trader who believes the true volatility to be 39 percent should do.

The implied volatility is 30 percent. On the trader's view the call is worth $1.52 and is cheap at $1.03. The trader should buy the call and, to profit from volatility and not from the direction of the share price, sell \(N(d_1)\) shares against it and adjust the hedge as the price changes, as Chapter 14 describes.

12.6 A share trades at $28 and will pay a dividend of $0.40 with an ex-dividend date in two months. Using the result of Worked example 12.3 and put–call parity, find the value of the three-month European put with a strike of $30.

\(p=c+D+Ke^{-rT}-S_0=1.35+0.397+29.627-28.00=\$3.38\), against $3.14 without the dividend.

12.7 Show that as \(\sigma\) approaches zero the Black–Scholes–Merton price of a call approaches \(\max(S_0-Ke^{-rT},0)\).

Write \(d_1=[\ln(S_0/K)+rT]/(\sigma\sqrt T)+\sigma\sqrt T/2\). The numerator \(\ln(S_0/K)+rT\) is positive when \(S_0>Ke^{-rT}\) and negative when \(S_0<Ke^{-rT}\). As \(\sigma\to0\), \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) therefore tend to \(+\infty\) in the first case, so that \(N(d_1)=N(d_2)=1\) and \(c\to S_0-Ke^{-rT}\); and to \(-\infty\) in the second, so that both probabilities are zero and \(c\to0\).

12.8 ★ Show that \(f=S\) and \(f=e^{rt}\) are both solutions of the Black–Scholes–Merton differential equation, and interpret each.

For \(f=S\): \(\partial f/\partial t=0\), \(\partial f/\partial S=1\), \(\partial^{2}f/\partial S^{2}=0\); the left-hand side is \(rS=rf\). The share is itself a derivative of the share. For \(f=e^{rt}\): \(\partial f/\partial t=re^{rt}\) and the derivatives with respect to \(S\) are zero; the left-hand side is \(re^{rt}=rf\). This is a risk-free deposit. The equation is satisfied by every traded asset whose value depends on \(S\) and \(t\), and since it is linear, by every portfolio of them; the forward contract \(S-Ke^{-r(T-t)}\) is such a portfolio.

Further reading

  • Black, F. (1989). How we came up with the option formula. Journal of Portfolio Management, 15(2), 4–8.
  • Black, F., and Scholes, M. (1973). The pricing of options and corporate liabilities. Journal of Political Economy, 81(3), 637–654.
  • Hull, J. C. (2022). Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (11th ed.). Pearson. Chapter 15.
  • MacKenzie, D. (2006). An Engine, Not a Camera: How Financial Models Shape Markets. MIT Press.
  • Merton, R. C. (1973). Theory of rational option pricing. Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science, 4(1), 141–183.

Chapter 12 Check — The Black–Scholes–Merton Model

8 questions · pass at 70%
Chapter 13 · Part IV: Valuation

Options on Indices, Currencies, and Futures

The extension of the Black–Scholes–Merton model to assets that provide a yield; index options and portfolio insurance; currency options; and options on futures contracts and Black's model

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. modify the bounds, put–call parity, and the Black–Scholes–Merton formulas for an asset that provides a known yield;
  2. value European options on a stock index and design a portfolio insurance strategy with index puts;
  3. value European options on a currency and use them to hedge a currency exposure;
  4. describe the mechanics of options on futures and value them with Black's model;
  5. state the single formula that covers all four cases and identify the parameter that distinguishes them.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

How much protection should the pension fund buy?

The Northwind pension fund holds a $12,000,000 equity portfolio that moves with a stock index, now at 6,000. The trustees wish to limit the loss over the next three months without selling the portfolio. Put options on the index are available at any strike; each contract pays $100 for every index point by which the index finishes below the strike, and twenty contracts cover the portfolio. Select the level of the index below which the fund is to be protected.

Protection against a fall of more than 10 percent costs less than half of one percent of the portfolio; protection against any fall at all costs more than 3 percent for a single quarter. The choice of strike is a choice of how much risk to retain, exactly as the deductible is in an insurance policy. The prices in the figure come from a formula that differs from that of Chapter 12 in one respect only: the index pays dividends. This chapter develops that modification and applies it to three kinds of underlying asset.

13.1  Options on an asset that provides a known yield

Chapter 12 valued options on a share that pays no dividend. Stock indices, currencies, and futures contracts all differ from such a share in one respect: the holder of the underlying asset receives income, or its equivalent, during the life of the option. Section 4.4 introduced the appropriate description. An asset provides a yield at the rate \(q\) per year, with continuous compounding, if income is paid continuously at the rate \(q\) multiplied by the current price.

The key to all the results of this chapter is a single observation. Consider two assets with the same price at time \(T\): asset A, which provides a yield at the rate \(q\) and is now worth \(S_0\), and asset B, which provides no income. An investor who holds one unit of asset A and reinvests the income in the asset will hold \(e^{qT}\) units at time \(T\). To hold exactly one unit at \(T\) it is sufficient to buy \(e^{-qT}\) units today, at a cost of \(S_0e^{-qT}\). Asset B, which delivers the same thing at \(T\), must therefore be worth \(S_0e^{-qT}\) today.

Principle 13.1

A European option on an asset with price \(S_0\) that provides a yield at the rate \(q\) has the same value as the corresponding European option on an asset with price \(S_0e^{-qT}\) that provides no income. Every result for options on a share that pays no dividend therefore applies, with \(S_0\) replaced by \(S_0e^{-qT}\).

Applying the principle to the results of Chapter 8 gives the lower bounds

\[ c\ \ge\ \max\!\left(S_0e^{-qT}-Ke^{-rT},\,0\right),\qquad p\ \ge\ \max\!\left(Ke^{-rT}-S_0e^{-qT},\,0\right), \]

and put–call parity in the form

\[ c+Ke^{-rT}=p+S_0e^{-qT}. \]

Applying it to Result 12.2, and noting that \(\ln(S_0e^{-qT}/K)=\ln(S_0/K)-qT\), gives the pricing formulas.

Result 13.1 — European options on an asset that provides a yield

\[ c=S_0e^{-qT}N(d_1)-Ke^{-rT}N(d_2),\qquad p=Ke^{-rT}N(-d_2)-S_0e^{-qT}N(-d_1), \] \[ d_1=\frac{\ln(S_0/K)+(r-q+\sigma^{2}/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T},\qquad d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt T . \]

These formulas were first given by Merton in 1973. In terms of risk-neutral valuation, the total return on every asset in a risk-neutral world is \(r\); if the asset provides income at the rate \(q\), its price must grow at the rate \(r-q\), which is the quantity that appears in \(d_1\). This is the same adjustment that Table 10.1 made to the binomial tree. For an American option the formulas do not apply, and the tree of Chapter 10 with \(a=e^{(r-q)\Delta t}\) is used.

13.2  Options on stock indices

Options on stock indices trade in very large volume on exchanges and over the counter. The most active are the options on the S&P 500 index listed by Cboe Global Markets, which are European and are settled in cash: on exercise, the holder of a call receives \((S-K)\times100\) dollars and the holder of a put \((K-S)\times100\) dollars, where \(S\) is the level of the index at settlement. No shares change hands. Options on the EURO STOXX 50, the FTSE 100, and the Nikkei 225 are designed in the same way, with their own multipliers.

An index is treated as an asset that provides a yield equal to the dividend yield on its constituent shares during the life of the option, and Result 13.1 applies with \(q\) set to that yield.

Worked example 13.1 — A put on a stock index
A stock index stands at 6,000 and has a volatility of 18 percent and a dividend yield of 1.2 percent. The risk-free rate is 4 percent. Value a three-month European put with a strike of 5,700.
1
Preliminaries. \(\ln(6{,}000/5{,}700)=0.05129\); \(\sigma\sqrt T=0.18\times0.5=0.09\); \(S_0e^{-qT}=6{,}000e^{-0.003}=5{,}982.03\); \(Ke^{-rT}=5{,}700e^{-0.01}=5{,}643.28\).
2
\(d_1\) and \(d_2\). \(d_1=\dfrac{0.05129+(0.04-0.012+0.0162)\times0.25}{0.09}=\dfrac{0.05129+0.01105}{0.09}=0.6927\); \(d_2=0.6927-0.09=0.6027\).
3
Normal probabilities. \(N(-d_1)=0.2442\); \(N(-d_2)=0.2734\).
4
Put. \(p=5{,}643.28\times0.2734-5{,}982.03\times0.2442=1{,}542.61-1{,}461.10=81.51\) index points. One contract costs \(81.51\times100=\$8{,}151\).

Portfolio insurance

The principal use of index puts by institutions is to limit the loss on an equity portfolio, as in the opening exercise. The strategy, a protective put on a portfolio, is called portfolio insurance.

Consider first a portfolio whose beta is 1.0, so that its value moves in proportion to the index. If the portfolio is worth \(V\) and the index stands at \(S_0\), the portfolio is equivalent to \(V/S_0\) units of the index, and each put contract protects 100 units. The number of contracts required is

\[ \frac{V}{100\,S_0}. \]

For the pension fund, \(12{,}000{,}000/(100\times6{,}000)=20\) contracts. With a strike of 5,700 they cost \(20\times100\times81.5114=\$163{,}023\), or 1.36 percent of the portfolio. If the index finishes below 5,700, the portfolio is worth \(12{,}000{,}000\times S_T/6{,}000=2{,}000\,S_T\) and the puts pay \(20\times100\times(5{,}700-S_T)=2{,}000\times(5{,}700-S_T)\); the total is \(2{,}000\times5{,}700=\$11{,}400{,}000\) whatever the level of the index.

When the beta of the portfolio is not 1.0, two adjustments are needed. The number of contracts becomes \(\beta V/(100S_0)\), since the portfolio moves \(\beta\) times as far as the index. And the strike must be chosen so that the puts begin to pay at the level of the index at which the portfolio reaches the value to be protected, which is found from the relation between the return on the portfolio and the return on the index used in Section 5.5.

⚙ Interactive figure 13.1 — Portfolio insurance at expiration

The insured portfolio has a floor; the uninsured portfolio does not

The fund holds 20 puts with a strike of 5,700, bought for $163,023. Set the level of the index in three months and examine the value of the portfolio, the payoff of the puts, and the net result.

Concept check 13.1

A fund manager holds a portfolio worth $30,000,000 with a beta of 1.0. The index stands at 5,000 and each index option contract has a multiplier of $100. How many put contracts insure the portfolio, and which position is taken?

13.3  Options on currencies

A currency option gives the right to buy or sell a specified amount of a foreign currency at a specified exchange rate. Most are traded over the counter, where corporations buy them from banks with strikes, amounts, and dates of their own choosing. As in Section 4.6, let \(S_0\) be the price of one unit of the foreign currency in the domestic currency, and \(r_f\) the foreign risk-free rate. A holding of foreign currency earns interest at \(r_f\); the currency is an asset that provides a yield, and Result 13.1 applies with \(q=r_f\). In this form the formulas are known as the Garman–Kohlhagen model.

The formulas may be written more compactly in terms of the forward exchange rate. From Result 4.5, \(F_0=S_0e^{(r-r_f)T}\), so that \(S_0e^{-r_fT}=F_0e^{-rT}\), and

\[ c=e^{-rT}\left[F_0N(d_1)-KN(d_2)\right],\qquad p=e^{-rT}\left[KN(-d_2)-F_0N(-d_1)\right],\qquad d_1=\frac{\ln(F_0/K)+\sigma^{2}T/2}{\sigma\sqrt T}. \]

Worked example 13.2 — Hedging a payment in euros with a call
Northwind must pay €5,000,000 to a German supplier in six months. The exchange rate is $1.1000 per euro; the risk-free rates are 4.5 percent in dollars and 2.5 percent in euros; and the volatility of the exchange rate is 9 percent. Northwind wishes to limit the dollar cost without giving up the benefit of a fall in the euro. Value a six-month European call on the euro with a strike of $1.1200, and describe the result of the hedge.
1
Preliminaries. \(\ln(1.10/1.12)=-0.01802\); \(\sigma\sqrt T=0.09\times0.7071=0.06364\); \(S_0e^{-r_fT}=1.10e^{-0.0125}=1.08634\); \(Ke^{-rT}=1.12e^{-0.0225}=1.09508\).
2
\(d_1\) and \(d_2\). \(d_1=\dfrac{-0.01802+(0.045-0.025+0.00405)\times0.5}{0.06364}=\dfrac{-0.01802+0.01203}{0.06364}=-0.0942\); \(d_2=-0.1578\).
3
Call. \(N(d_1)=0.4625\); \(N(d_2)=0.4373\). \(c=1.08634\times0.4625-1.09508\times0.4373=0.50242-0.47888=\$0.02353\) per euro.
4
Cost of the hedge. \(5{,}000{,}000\times0.02353=\$117{,}650\), or 2.1 percent of the amount due at the spot rate.
5
Result. If the euro is above $1.12 in six months, Northwind exercises and pays \(5{,}000{,}000\times1.12=\$5{,}600{,}000\). If it is below, the option expires and Northwind buys euros at the lower market rate. The dollar cost cannot exceed $5,600,000 plus the premium. A forward contract at \(1.10e^{0.01}=\$1.1111\) would have fixed the cost at $5,555,300 with no premium, and with no benefit from a fall in the euro.

A call on one currency is a put on the other. The right to buy €5,000,000 for $5,600,000 is the right to sell $5,600,000 for €5,000,000: a call on the euro with a strike of $1.12 is a put on the dollar with a strike of \(1/1.12=\)€0.8929. The two descriptions refer to the same contract and must give the same value when it is expressed in a common currency.

Concept check 13.2

A Japanese exporter will receive $10,000,000 in three months and will convert it into yen. It wishes to be protected against a fall in the dollar while retaining the benefit of a rise. Which contract is appropriate?

13.4  Options on futures

A futures option, or option on futures, is the right to enter a futures contract at a specified futures price. Futures options are American and are traded on the exchange that lists the underlying futures contract. They are the principal form of exchange-traded option on commodities and on interest rates.

Mechanics

When a call futures option is exercised, the holder acquires a long position in the underlying futures contract together with a cash amount equal to the excess of the most recent settlement futures price over the strike price. When a put futures option is exercised, the holder acquires a short position in the futures contract together with cash equal to the excess of the strike price over the most recent settlement futures price. The futures position has zero value when it is acquired and may be closed at once, so that the effective payoff from a call is \(\max(F-K,0)\) and from a put \(\max(K-F,0)\), where \(F\) is the futures price at the time of exercise.

Suppose that Northwind holds a call on one copper futures contract of 25,000 pounds with a strike of $4.20, and exercises when the settlement futures price is $4.45 and the current futures price is $4.47. Northwind receives a long futures position and cash of \((4.45-4.20)\times25{,}000=\$6{,}250\). If it closes the futures position immediately at $4.47, it gains a further \((4.47-4.45)\times25{,}000=\$500\), for a total of \((4.47-4.20)\times25{,}000=\$6{,}750\).

Reasons for their use

Options on futures are often preferred to options on the underlying asset itself. The futures contract is usually more liquid than the asset and its price is known at every moment from trading on the exchange, whereas the spot price of a commodity may be available only from dealers. Exercise does not ordinarily lead to delivery of the asset, since the futures position is closed beforehand; this is of particular value for commodities. And the option and the futures contract trade on the same exchange, which facilitates hedging and arbitrage between them.

Valuation: Black's model

A futures contract requires no investment. In a risk-neutral world its expected gain must therefore be zero, and the futures price has an expected growth rate of zero. An asset that provides a yield at rate \(q\) has a price that grows at \(r-q\) in a risk-neutral world; the futures price behaves as such an asset with \(q=r\). Setting \(q=r\) and \(S_0=F_0\) in Result 13.1 gives the following.

Result 13.2 — Black's model for European futures options

\[ c=e^{-rT}\left[F_0N(d_1)-KN(d_2)\right],\qquad p=e^{-rT}\left[KN(-d_2)-F_0N(-d_1)\right], \] \[ d_1=\frac{\ln(F_0/K)+\sigma^{2}T/2}{\sigma\sqrt T},\qquad d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt T, \] where \(F_0\) is the current futures price and \(\sigma\) the volatility of the futures price. Put–call parity takes the form \(c+Ke^{-rT}=p+F_0e^{-rT}\).

The model was published by Fischer Black in 1976. Its formulas are identical to those obtained for currency options in terms of the forward rate, and the agreement is general: whenever a European option expires at the same time as a futures or forward contract on the same asset, the option may be valued as an option on that contract, because the futures price and the spot price coincide at expiration. Practitioners value most European options in this way, since the forward price summarizes the interest rate, the income on the asset, and the storage cost in a single observable number.

Worked example 13.3 — A cap on the price of copper
The six-month copper futures price is $4.10 per pound, with a volatility of 22 percent. The risk-free rate is 5 percent. Northwind, which will buy 500,000 pounds in six months, considers buying European calls on the futures with a strike of $4.20 in place of the futures themselves. Value the call and the corresponding put, and state the maximum price that Northwind will pay for its copper.
1
Preliminaries. \(\ln(4.10/4.20)=-0.02410\); \(\sigma\sqrt T=0.22\times0.7071=0.15556\); \(\sigma^{2}T/2=0.0121\); \(e^{-rT}=0.975310\).
2
\(d_1\) and \(d_2\). \(d_1=(-0.02410+0.0121)/0.15556=-0.0771\); \(d_2=-0.2327\). \(N(d_1)=0.4693\); \(N(d_2)=0.4080\).
3
Call. \(c=0.975310\times(4.10\times0.4693-4.20\times0.4080)=0.975310\times0.2104=\$0.2052\) per pound.
4
Put, by parity. \(p=c+(K-F_0)e^{-rT}=0.2052+0.10\times0.975310=\$0.3027\).
5
The hedge. Calls on 500,000 pounds cost \(500{,}000\times0.2052=\$102{,}600\). Northwind will pay no more than $4.20 per pound, or $4.405 including the premium, and will pay the market price if copper falls. The futures hedge of Chapter 1 fixed the price at $4.10 at no cost; the call costs $0.2052 and preserves the benefit of a fall.

American futures options

Traded futures options are American, and Result 13.2 gives only an approximation to their value. Unlike a call on a share that pays no dividend, an American call on a futures contract may be worth exercising early: when the call is deep in the money, exercise releases cash of \(F-K\) at once, on which interest can be earned, and nothing is given up in exchange, since the futures position costs nothing to hold. American futures options are therefore always worth more than the corresponding European options, and are valued on a binomial tree with \(a=1\), as in Table 10.1.

13.5  A single formula

The four cases treated in Chapters 12 and 13 are special cases of Result 13.1, distinguished only by the value of \(q\).

Table 13.1  European options: the parameters of Result 13.1 for four underlying assets
Underlying asset\(S_0\)\(q\)Growth rate of the price in a risk-neutral worldPut–call parity
Share paying no dividendShare price0\(r\)\(c+Ke^{-rT}=p+S_0\)
Stock indexIndex levelDividend yield\(r-q\)\(c+Ke^{-rT}=p+S_0e^{-qT}\)
CurrencyExchange rate\(r_f\)\(r-r_f\)\(c+Ke^{-rT}=p+S_0e^{-r_fT}\)
Futures contractFutures price \(F_0\)\(r\)0\(c+Ke^{-rT}=p+F_0e^{-rT}\)

In every case the option is discounted at \(r\), and the only quantity that changes is the rate at which the underlying price is expected to grow in a risk-neutral world. That rate is the cost of carry of Section 4.7, net of any convenience yield: the same quantity that determines the forward price of the asset determines the adjustment to its options.

⚙ Interactive figure 13.2 — One formula, four underlying assets

European options on a share, an index, a currency, and a futures contract

Select an underlying asset to load the example of this chapter or of Chapter 12, then vary the inputs. Prices are expressed as percentages of the strike so that the four cases may be compared. For a futures contract the yield is held equal to the risk-free rate.

Concept check 13.3

A European call and a European put on the same futures contract have the same strike and expiration, and the strike equals the current futures price. How do their prices compare?

Historical note

Trading in options on a stock index began in Chicago in March 1983 with a contract on what is now the S&P 100; options on the S&P 500 followed in July of that year. Portfolio insurance became a large business within a few years, though most of it was conducted not with traded puts but by replicating a put through sales of index futures as the market fell, in the manner of the dynamic hedge of Chapter 10. On 19 October 1987 the index fell by more than 20 percent in a single day. The sales required by these programs could not be executed at the prices assumed, the protection failed when it was needed, and the selling itself contributed to the fall. The episode remains the principal illustration of the difference between owning an option and attempting to manufacture one.

Mark Garman and Steven Kohlhagen published the currency form of the model in 1983, shortly after the Philadelphia Stock Exchange had listed the first options on currencies. Black's model of 1976 was devised for options on commodity futures, and became in the following decade the standard for interest rate options, a use that its author had not anticipated.

Summary

  • A European option on an asset that provides a yield \(q\) is valued by replacing \(S_0\) with \(S_0e^{-qT}\) in the results for a share that pays no dividend; in the formulas, \(r-q\) replaces \(r\) in \(d_1\).
  • A stock index is treated as an asset with a yield equal to its dividend yield. A portfolio with a beta of 1.0 is insured with \(V/(100S_0)\) put contracts.
  • A currency is an asset with a yield equal to the foreign risk-free rate. A call on one currency is a put on the other.
  • A futures option, when exercised, gives a futures position and cash. European futures options are valued by Black's model, which is Result 13.1 with \(q=r\); American futures options are worth more, and early exercise of both calls and puts may be optimal.
  • Any European option that expires when a forward or futures contract on the same asset matures may be valued by Black's model, using the forward price.

Exercises

13.1 A stock index stands at 5,000, with a volatility of 20 percent and a dividend yield of 2 percent. The risk-free rate is 5 percent. Value a six-month European call with a strike of 5,000.

\(\sigma\sqrt T=0.1414\). \(d_1=[0+(0.05-0.02+0.02)\times0.5]/0.1414=0.1768\); \(d_2=0.0354\). \(N(d_1)=0.5702\); \(N(d_2)=0.5141\). \(S_0e^{-qT}=5{,}000e^{-0.01}=4{,}950.25\); \(Ke^{-rT}=5{,}000e^{-0.025}=4{,}876.55\). \(c=4{,}950.25\times0.5702-4{,}876.55\times0.5141=315.4\) index points.

13.2 Use put–call parity to find the value of the put with the same terms as the call of Exercise 13.1.

\(p=c+Ke^{-rT}-S_0e^{-qT}=315.4+4{,}876.55-4{,}950.25=241.7\) index points.

13.3 The pound trades at $1.2500. The risk-free rates are 4 percent in dollars and 3 percent in sterling, and the volatility of the exchange rate is 10 percent. A United States company will receive £1,000,000 in three months. Find the cost of European puts on the pound with a strike of $1.2500 that protect the whole amount.

\(\sigma\sqrt T=0.05\). \(d_1=[0+(0.04-0.03+0.005)\times0.25]/0.05=0.075\); \(d_2=0.025\). \(N(-d_1)=0.4701\); \(N(-d_2)=0.4900\). \(Ke^{-rT}=1.25e^{-0.01}=1.23756\); \(S_0e^{-r_fT}=1.25e^{-0.0075}=1.24066\). \(p=1.23756\times0.4900-1.24066\times0.4701=\$0.0232\) per pound; total \(\$23{,}200\).

13.4 A trader holds a put option on one crude oil futures contract (1,000 barrels) with a strike of $74. The trader exercises when the most recent settlement futures price is $69.50. What does the trader receive?

A short position in one futures contract and cash of \((74.00-69.50)\times1{,}000=\$4{,}500\).

13.5 A futures price is $75 and its volatility 30 percent. The risk-free rate is 4 percent. Value a three-month European call on the futures with a strike of $70, and find the put by parity.

\(\sigma\sqrt T=0.15\); \(\sigma^{2}T/2=0.01125\). \(d_1=[\ln(75/70)+0.01125]/0.15=(0.06899+0.01125)/0.15=0.5350\); \(d_2=0.3850\). \(N(d_1)=0.7037\); \(N(d_2)=0.6499\). \(c=e^{-0.01}\times(75\times0.7037-70\times0.6499)=0.99005\times7.284=\$7.21\). \(p=c-(F_0-K)e^{-rT}=7.21-5\times0.99005=\$2.26\).

13.6 A fund holds a portfolio worth $12,000,000 with a beta of 1.5. The index stands at 6,000; the risk-free rate is 1 percent per quarter and the dividend yield on the index 0.3 percent per quarter. The fund wishes to ensure that the portfolio is worth at least $10,800,000 in three months. Find the number of put contracts (multiplier $100) and their strike.

Contracts: \(1.5\times12{,}000{,}000/(100\times6{,}000)=30\). The floor corresponds to a portfolio return of −10 percent. From Section 5.5, the return on the portfolio is \(1+1.5\times(R_M-1)\) percent, where \(R_M\) is the return on the index including dividends; setting this to −10 gives \(R_M=-6.33\) percent. Excluding the dividend of 0.3 percent, the index falls by 6.63 percent, to \(6{,}000\times0.9337=5{,}602\). The fund buys 30 puts with a strike of about 5,600.

13.7 Explain why it can be optimal to exercise an American call on a futures contract early, whereas it is never optimal to exercise early an American call on a share that pays no dividend.

Exercising a call on a share requires payment of the strike, on which interest is then forgone; the lower bound \(S_0-Ke^{-rT}\) exceeds the exercise value \(S_0-K\). Exercising a call on a futures contract requires no payment: the holder receives \(F-K\) in cash and a futures position that costs nothing. The lower bound for the European futures call is \((F_0-K)e^{-rT}\), which is less than the exercise value \(F_0-K\). When the call is deep in the money and has little time value, receiving the cash at once is worth more than waiting.

13.8 Show that the Garman–Kohlhagen formula for a currency call and Black's formula for a call on the corresponding forward contract give the same price.

With \(F_0=S_0e^{(r-r_f)T}\): \(S_0e^{-r_fT}=F_0e^{-rT}\), so the first term \(S_0e^{-r_fT}N(d_1)\) equals \(e^{-rT}F_0N(d_1)\). In \(d_1\), \(\ln(S_0/K)+(r-r_f)T=\ln(F_0/K)\), so \(d_1=[\ln(F_0/K)+\sigma^{2}T/2]/(\sigma\sqrt T)\), which is the \(d_1\) of Black's model. The second term, \(Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)\), is common to both. Hence \(c=e^{-rT}[F_0N(d_1)-KN(d_2)]\) in each case.

Further reading

  • Black, F. (1976). The pricing of commodity contracts. Journal of Financial Economics, 3(1–2), 167–179.
  • Garman, M. B., and Kohlhagen, S. W. (1983). Foreign currency option values. Journal of International Money and Finance, 2(3), 231–237.
  • Hull, J. C. (2022). Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (11th ed.). Pearson. Chapters 17–18.
  • Leland, H. E., and Rubinstein, M. (1988). The evolution of portfolio insurance. In D. L. Luskin (Ed.), Portfolio Insurance: A Guide to Dynamic Hedging. Wiley.
  • Merton, R. C. (1973). Theory of rational option pricing. Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science, 4(1), 141–183.

Chapter 14 · Part V: Risk Management

The Greeks and Dynamic Hedging

The sensitivities of an option position to the price of the underlying, the passage of time, volatility, and the interest rate; the hedging of a written option by continual adjustment; and the limits of that procedure

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. explain why neither a naked nor a covered position is a satisfactory hedge for a written option;
  2. define delta, gamma, theta, vega, and rho, and compute each for a European option;
  3. construct a delta-neutral position and describe how it is maintained through time;
  4. use delta and gamma to approximate the change in the value of a position;
  5. make a portfolio neutral with respect to gamma and vega by means of traded options;
  6. describe the creation of an option synthetically and the risks of that procedure;
  7. ★ relate the profit of a delta-hedged position to the difference between the volatility assumed and the volatility realized.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

How should a dealer hedge an option that it has sold?

A dealer has sold to a client European calls on 100,000 Northwind shares, with a strike of $30 and three months to expiration, for $170,000. The share price is $28. The Black–Scholes–Merton value of the calls, at a volatility of 39 percent and a risk-free rate of 5 percent, is $151,700. The dealer wishes to retain the difference of $18,300 whatever happens to the share price. Which course of action serves that purpose?

Select a policy.

14.1  The position of an option writer

A financial institution that sells an option to a client in the over-the-counter market has acquired a risk. If an identical option is traded on an exchange, the institution can buy it and the risk is removed. More often the option has been tailored to the client and has no traded counterpart. The institution must then manage the risk by other means. This chapter describes those means. The dealer of the opening decision serves as the example throughout.

Two simple policies are available, and both are unsatisfactory.

A naked position consists in doing nothing. If the share price is below $30 in three months, the calls are not exercised and the dealer keeps the $170,000. If the price is $40, the dealer must deliver shares worth $4,000,000 for $3,000,000, a cost of $1,000,000 that greatly exceeds the premium.

A covered position consists in buying 100,000 shares at once, for $2,800,000. If the calls are exercised, the shares are delivered and the dealer has done well. If the price falls to $20, the calls expire unexercised and the dealer has lost $800,000 on the shares.

Neither policy secures the profit of $18,300. By put–call parity the covered position is equivalent to a written put, so that the dealer has merely exchanged an exposure to rising prices for an exposure to falling prices. A satisfactory hedge must ensure that the cost of meeting the obligation is close to $151,700 in every case.

Common error

It is tempting to hold the shares only when they are needed: buy 100,000 shares whenever the price rises above $30 and sell them whenever it falls below. This stop-loss strategy appears to ensure that the dealer holds the shares in exactly those cases in which the calls are exercised, and at no cost, since every purchase and every sale is made at $30. It fails for two reasons. The purchases are made at a price slightly above $30 and the sales at a price slightly below, and the price may cross $30 many times. And the cash flows occur at different dates and cannot be added without discounting. Simulation shows that the cost of the strategy is highly variable and on average exceeds the value of the option.

14.2  Delta

The delta of an option, \(\Delta\), is the rate of change of its price with respect to the price of the underlying asset: \[ \Delta=\frac{\partial f}{\partial S}. \] It is the slope of the curve that relates the price of the option to the price of the underlying, and it is the quantity \(\Delta\) of Chapter 10, the number of shares in the portfolio that replicates the option. A delta of 0.42 means that when the share price changes by a small amount, the price of the option changes by about 42 percent of that amount.

Result 14.1 — Delta of European options

For European options on a share that pays no dividend, \[ \Delta_{\text{call}}=N(d_1), \qquad \Delta_{\text{put}}=N(d_1)-1, \] where \(d_1\) is defined in Result 12.2. The delta of a call lies between 0 and 1, and the delta of a put between \(-1\) and 0. For an asset that provides income at the rate \(q\), both expressions are multiplied by \(e^{-qT}\).

The delta of a call is close to zero when the option is far out of the money, close to one when it is far in the money, and near one half when the share price is near the strike. The two deltas differ by exactly one, as put–call parity requires: a long call and a short put with the same strike together behave as one share.

Key terms

Delta of a portfolio: the sum of the deltas of its components, each multiplied by the quantity held; a share has a delta of 1, and a short position has the negative of the delta of the corresponding long position. Delta-neutral position: a position with a delta of zero, whose value does not change, to a first approximation, when the price of the underlying changes by a small amount. Delta hedging: the maintenance of a delta-neutral position by trading the underlying asset. Rebalancing: the adjustment of the hedge as delta changes.

Worked example 14.1 — The delta hedge of the dealer
Find the delta of the calls that the dealer has written and the holding of shares that makes the position delta neutral.
1
Delta of one call. From Worked example 12.1, \(d_1=-0.1922\), so that \(\Delta=N(-0.1922)=0.4238\).
2
Delta of the written calls. The dealer is short 100,000 calls: \(-100{,}000\times0.4238=-42{,}380\). The position behaves as a short position in 42,380 shares.
3
The hedge. The dealer buys 42,380 shares, at a cost of \(42{,}380\times28=\$1{,}186{,}640\). The delta of the whole position is \(-42{,}380+42{,}380=0\).
4
Verification. If the share price rises by $0.10, the shares gain \(42{,}380\times0.10=\$4{,}238\) and the calls rise in value by about \(100{,}000\times0.4238\times0.10=\$4{,}238\), which is a loss to the dealer. The two effects offset.

14.3  Dynamic delta hedging

The delta of an option does not remain constant. If the Northwind share price rises to $30 during the first week, the delta of the call rises to 0.562, and the dealer must buy a further 13,800 shares to remain delta neutral. If the price falls to $26, delta falls to 0.271 and 15,200 shares must be sold. The hedge is therefore adjusted repeatedly through the life of the option. A hedge of this kind is called a dynamic hedge, in contrast with a static hedge, which is established once and left in place.

The procedure has a feature that explains its cost. Shares are bought after the price has risen and sold after it has fallen. Each round of buying high and selling low loses a small amount, and the accumulated losses are the cost of the hedge. The central result of Chapters 10 and 12 may be restated in these terms: if the volatility of the share is 39 percent throughout and the hedge is adjusted continuously, the present value of the cost of the hedge is exactly the Black–Scholes–Merton value, $151,700, whatever path the share price follows. The dealer who sold the calls for $170,000 is left with $18,300.

In practice the hedge is adjusted at intervals, and the cost varies from one path to another. Interactive figure 14.1 carries out the hedge along a simulated path and then repeats it over many paths to show how the variation depends on the frequency of adjustment.

⚙ Interactive figure 14.1 — Delta hedging along a path

The cost of hedging 100,000 written calls

The dealer holds \(100{,}000\times\Delta\) shares, with \(\Delta\) computed at a volatility of 39 percent, and finances the holding by borrowing at 5 percent. Choose the frequency of adjustment and the volatility that the share in fact exhibits, and generate new paths. The table records the hedge at the end of each week. The cost of the hedge is the amount borrowed at expiration, less the $3,000,000 received if the calls are exercised, discounted to the present.

Three observations should be drawn from the figure. First, when the realized volatility is 39 percent, the average cost of the hedge is close to $151,700 at every frequency of adjustment: the frequency affects the dispersion of the cost and not its average. Second, the dispersion falls as the hedge is adjusted more often, approximately in proportion to the square root of the interval between adjustments. Third, when the share proves more volatile than the dealer assumed, the hedge costs more than the value at which the calls were priced, and when it proves less volatile the hedge costs less. A dealer who has sold an option and hedged its delta is no longer exposed to the direction of the share price. The dealer remains exposed to its volatility.

Concept check 14.1

A trader has written 500 put options, each on one share, with a delta of −0.30. What position in the share makes the trader delta neutral?

14.4  Theta

The theta of an option, \(\Theta\), is the rate of change of its price with respect to the passage of time, all else remaining the same. It is also called the time decay of the option. The formulas are in Table 14.1. Theta is computed with time measured in years; it is usually quoted per day, by dividing by 365 for the decay per calendar day or by 252 for the decay per trading day.

The theta of an option held is usually negative: as expiration approaches and nothing else changes, the option loses value. For the Northwind call, \(\Theta=-4.794\) per year, or \(-4.794/365=-\$0.0131\) per calendar day. The 100,000 calls lose about $1,310 of value on each day on which the share price does not move, and this is a gain to the dealer who wrote them. Theta is greatest in magnitude for options that are at the money and close to expiration.

Theta differs in kind from delta. The future price of the share is uncertain; the passage of time is not. It makes sense to hedge against changes in the share price and none to hedge against the passage of time. Theta is nevertheless of interest, because of its relation to gamma, which Section 14.6 states.

14.5  Gamma

The gamma of an option, \(\Gamma\), is the rate of change of its delta with respect to the price of the underlying asset: \[ \Gamma=\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial S^{2}}. \] It measures the curvature of the relation between the price of the option and the price of the underlying. If gamma is small, delta changes slowly, and a delta-neutral position needs adjustment only occasionally. If gamma is large, delta changes rapidly, and a hedge that is left unadjusted soon ceases to be a hedge.

For a European call or put on a share that pays no dividend, \[ \Gamma=\frac{N'(d_1)}{S_0\sigma\sqrt{T}}, \qquad N'(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^{2}/2}, \] where \(N'(x)\) is the standard normal density. The gamma of a call equals the gamma of the put with the same strike and expiration. It is positive for an option held and negative for an option written. For the Northwind call, \(N'(-0.1922)=0.3916\) and \(\Gamma=0.3916/(28\times0.39\times0.5)=0.0717\): when the share price rises by $1, the delta of the call rises by about 0.072.

Gamma accounts for the error of a delta hedge when the price moves by more than a small amount. Expanding the value of a position \(\Pi\) to the second order in the change \(\Delta S\) of the share price over a short interval,

Result 14.2 — The delta–gamma approximation

\[ \Delta\Pi\approx\Delta\times\Delta S+\tfrac12\Gamma(\Delta S)^{2}+\Theta\,\Delta t . \] For a delta-neutral position the first term is zero, and the change in value over an interval in which the price moves by \(\Delta S\) is approximately \(\tfrac12\Gamma(\Delta S)^{2}+\Theta\,\Delta t\).

Worked example 14.2 — The error of the delta hedge
The dealer is short 100,000 calls and long 42,380 shares. The share price moves at once from $28 to $30. Find the change in the value of the position, and compare it with the delta–gamma approximation. Repeat for a fall to $26.
1
Exact change, rise to $30. The value of a call rises from $1.5173 to $2.5067, a change of $0.9895. The shares gain \(0.4238\times2=\$0.8476\) per call hedged. The dealer loses \(100{,}000\times(0.9895-0.8476)=\$14{,}190\).
2
Approximation. The position is short 100,000 calls, so its gamma is \(-100{,}000\times0.0717=-7{,}173\). By Result 14.2, \(\Delta\Pi\approx\tfrac12\times(-7{,}173)\times2^{2}=-\$14{,}346\).
3
Fall to $26. The value of a call falls by $0.7057, and the shares lose $0.8476 per call hedged. The dealer loses \(100{,}000\times(0.8476-0.7057)=\$14{,}190\). The approximation is again −$14,346.
4
Interpretation. A position with negative gamma loses when the price moves in either direction, and the loss increases with the square of the move. Delta hedging removes the exposure to the direction of the price and leaves an exposure to the size of its movements.

The sign of gamma thus divides option positions into two classes. A position that is long gamma, such as a purchased call, a purchased put, or the straddle of Section 9.4, gains from large movements once its delta has been hedged, and pays for this through time decay. A position that is short gamma, such as that of the dealer, collects time decay and loses from large movements.

14.6  The relation between delta, theta, and gamma

The Black–Scholes–Merton differential equation, Result 12.1, holds for every derivative on a share that pays no dividend, and therefore for every portfolio \(\Pi\) of such derivatives. Since \(\partial\Pi/\partial t=\Theta\), \(\partial\Pi/\partial S=\Delta\), and \(\partial^{2}\Pi/\partial S^{2}=\Gamma\), the equation states the following.

Result 14.3 — Delta, theta, and gamma

\[ \Theta+rS\Delta+\tfrac12\sigma^{2}S^{2}\Gamma=r\Pi . \] For a delta-neutral portfolio, \(\Theta+\tfrac12\sigma^{2}S^{2}\Gamma=r\Pi\).

For the Northwind call the three terms are \(-4.7942\), \(0.05\times28\times0.4238=0.5933\), and \(\tfrac12\times0.1521\times784\times0.07173=4.2768\). Their sum is 0.0759, which equals \(0.05\times1.5173\), as the result requires.

The result shows that theta and gamma are two aspects of one property. In a delta-neutral portfolio whose value is small, a large positive gamma is accompanied by a large negative theta, and conversely. The holder of options pays time decay each day and receives in return the gains of Worked example 14.2 when the price moves. The price of an option is such that, when the volatility is as assumed, the two are equal on average.

14.7  Vega and rho

The Black–Scholes–Merton model assumes that volatility is constant. In practice the implied volatilities at which options trade change from day to day, and the value of an option position changes with them. The vega of an option, \(\mathcal{V}\), is the rate of change of its price with respect to the volatility of the underlying asset. For a European call or put on a share that pays no dividend, \[ \mathcal{V}=S_0\sqrt{T}\,N'(d_1). \] Vega is the same for a call and for the put with the same strike and expiration, is positive for an option held, and is greatest for options that are at the money. Unlike gamma, it increases with the time to expiration. For the Northwind call, \(\mathcal{V}=28\times0.5\times0.3916=5.483\). The formula measures volatility as a decimal, so that an increase of one percentage point, from 39 to 40 percent, raises the price of the call by about \(5.483\times0.01=\$0.055\). The dealer, who is short 100,000 calls, loses about $5,480 for each percentage point by which implied volatility rises.

There is an inconsistency in computing vega from a model that assumes volatility to be constant. Practitioners accept it: the vega computed from the Black–Scholes–Merton formula has been found to be close to the vega computed from models in which volatility is itself uncertain.

The rho of an option is the rate of change of its price with respect to the risk-free rate. For a European call on a share that pays no dividend it is \(KTe^{-rT}N(d_2)\), which is positive; for a put it is \(-KTe^{-rT}N(-d_2)\), which is negative. For the Northwind call, rho is 2.587, so that an increase of one percentage point in the rate raises the price by about $0.026. For options on shares with a life of a few months, rho is the least important of the sensitivities.
