A delta-neutral position has a large negative gamma. Over the next day the share price does not move at all. What happens to the value of the position, and why?

14.8  Making a portfolio gamma neutral and vega neutral

A position in the underlying asset has a delta of one and a gamma and a vega of zero: its price is a linear function of itself and does not depend on its volatility. Trading the asset can therefore change the delta of a portfolio and nothing else. The gamma and the vega of a portfolio can be changed only by trading instruments whose value is not linear in the price of the asset, which in practice means other options.

Suppose that a delta-neutral portfolio has a gamma of \(\Gamma\), and that a traded option has a gamma of \(\Gamma_T\). Adding \(w_T\) of the traded options gives a gamma of \(w_T\Gamma_T+\Gamma\), which is zero when \[ w_T=-\frac{\Gamma}{\Gamma_T}. \] The traded options have a delta of their own, so that the portfolio is no longer delta neutral, and the position in the underlying asset must then be adjusted. Vega is neutralized in the same way, with \(w_T=-\mathcal{V}/\mathcal{V}_T\). A single traded option cannot in general neutralize gamma and vega together. Two traded options are needed, and the quantities are found from two simultaneous equations.

Worked example 14.3 — A portfolio neutral in delta, gamma, and vega
An options desk holds a portfolio of options on Northwind shares that is delta neutral, with a gamma of −6,000 and a vega of −6,000 per percentage point of volatility. Two options are traded: option A, a three-month call with a strike of $28 (delta 0.5642, gamma 0.0721, vega 0.0551 per percentage point), and option B, a six-month call with a strike of $30 (delta 0.4914, gamma 0.0517, vega 0.0790 per percentage point). Find the trades that make the portfolio neutral in all three respects.
1
The two conditions. Let \(w_A\) and \(w_B\) be the numbers of the two options bought. Gamma: \(0.0721w_A+0.0517w_B=6{,}000\). Vega: \(0.0551w_A+0.0790w_B=6{,}000\).
2
Solution. \(w_A=57{,}530\) and \(w_B=35{,}824\). Options are bought, as expected, because the portfolio is short both gamma and vega.
3
Restoring delta neutrality. The options bought have a delta of \(57{,}530\times0.5642+35{,}824\times0.4914=50{,}062\). The desk sells 50,062 shares.
4
Using option A alone. Gamma could be neutralized with \(6{,}000/0.0721=83{,}218\) of option A. The vega of the portfolio would then be \(-6{,}000+83{,}218\times0.0551=-1{,}415\), which is not zero. One instrument cannot satisfy two conditions.

The portfolio so constructed is neutral only at the present share price, volatility, and date. As these change, the sensitivities change, and the procedure must be repeated. In practice delta is restored to zero, or close to it, at least once a day, because the underlying asset can be traded at low cost. Gamma and vega are monitored and corrected only when they exceed limits set by the institution, because options are more costly to trade and a suitable option is not always available at a reasonable price.

14.9  ★ The profit and loss of a delta-hedged position

Optional section. This section combines Results 14.2 and 14.3 to show what a delta-hedged option position gains and loses. It explains the third observation drawn from Interactive figure 14.1.

Consider a position that is long one option and short \(\Delta\) shares, financed at the risk-free rate, and suppose for simplicity that \(r=0\). The option was valued at a volatility \(\sigma_{\text{imp}}\). Over a short interval \(\Delta t\) the share price changes by \(\Delta S\). By Result 14.2 the position gains \[ \tfrac12\Gamma(\Delta S)^{2}+\Theta\,\Delta t . \] By Result 14.3 with \(r=0\), \(\Theta=-\tfrac12\sigma_{\text{imp}}^{2}S^{2}\Gamma\). Substituting,

\[ \text{gain over the interval}=\tfrac12\Gamma S^{2}\left[\left(\frac{\Delta S}{S}\right)^{2}-\sigma_{\text{imp}}^{2}\,\Delta t\right]. \]

The term \((\Delta S/S)^{2}\) is the square of the return over the interval, and its expected value is \(\sigma_{\text{real}}^{2}\Delta t\), where \(\sigma_{\text{real}}\) is the volatility that the share in fact exhibits. The expected gain over the interval is therefore \(\tfrac12\Gamma S^{2}(\sigma_{\text{real}}^{2}-\sigma_{\text{imp}}^{2})\Delta t\), and the gain over the life of the option is the sum of such terms.

Three conclusions follow. A delta-hedged purchase of an option is profitable if the share proves more volatile than the volatility at which the option was bought, and unprofitable if it proves less volatile; for a delta-hedged sale the signs are reversed. The direction of the share price does not enter. And the gain depends on the path, because each interval is weighted by \(\Gamma S^{2}\): volatility that occurs while the share price is near the strike and expiration is near counts for more than volatility that occurs elsewhere. For the dealer, on any day the breakeven move in the share price is that for which \((\Delta S/S)^{2}=\sigma_{\text{imp}}^{2}\Delta t\), namely \(0.39/\sqrt{252}=2.46\) percent, or about $0.69 on a share price of $28. On days when the price moves by less, the dealer gains; on days when it moves by more, the dealer loses.

14.10  Synthetic options and portfolio insurance

Delta hedging can be read in the opposite direction. The dealer who buys \(100{,}000\times\Delta\) shares and adjusts the holding has created, by trading, a position whose value follows that of 100,000 purchased calls, and uses it to offset the calls that were written. An option that is produced by trading the underlying asset according to its delta is called a synthetic option.

Section 13.2 described a fund with a portfolio of $12,000,000 that follows an index standing at 6,000, and that buys three-month puts with a strike of 5,700 to place a floor under its value. The fund may instead create the put synthetically. From Table 14.1 the delta of the put is \(e^{-qT}[N(d_1)-1]=e^{-0.003}(0.7558-1)=-0.2435\). The portfolio together with the put has the exposure of \(1-0.2435=0.7565\) of the portfolio. The fund obtains the same exposure by selling 24.35 percent of the portfolio, $2,922,000, and investing the proceeds at the risk-free rate. If the index falls to 5,700 after one week, the delta of the put becomes −0.4518, and the proportion sold must be raised to 45.18 percent. If the index rises, shares are bought back. In practice the adjustment is made by selling and buying index futures, which is cheaper than trading the shares.

The procedure has the cost described in Section 14.3: the fund sells after prices have fallen and buys after they have risen. It also rests on two assumptions that fail when they are most needed. It assumes that the market moves by small steps, so that the fund can trade at each level on the way down, and it assumes that the fund's own sales do not move the price. A purchased put requires neither assumption. The difference is the subject of the historical note.

Concept check 14.3

A portfolio is delta neutral, with a gamma of −2,000 and a vega of −5,000 per percentage point. Which of the following reduces both exposures toward zero?

Historical note

In 1981 Hayne Leland and Mark Rubinstein, with John O'Brien, founded a firm to sell portfolio insurance of the kind described in Section 14.10 to pension funds. By the autumn of 1987 the strategy was applied to assets estimated at between $60 billion and $90 billion. In the week of 12 October 1987 the American stock market fell by about 10 percent, and the programs called for large sales of index futures. On Monday 19 October the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 22.6 percent, the largest fall in one day in its history. The commission appointed by the President to examine the event, chaired by Nicholas Brady, found that the sales of a small number of portfolio insurers accounted for a substantial part of the selling pressure in the futures market on that day. The insurers could not complete the sales that their programs required, and the floors that they had promised were not achieved.

The episode showed that a hedge which depends on trading in a falling market is not equivalent to an option that has been bought, and that a strategy which is sound for one investor may fail when many follow it together. It also changed the pricing of index options permanently, in a manner that Chapter 15 describes.

Summary

  • A written option cannot be hedged satisfactorily by a naked position, a covered position, or a stop-loss rule.
  • Delta is the sensitivity of the price of an option to the price of the underlying: \(N(d_1)\) for a call and \(N(d_1)-1\) for a put on a share that pays no dividend. A position is delta neutral when its delta is zero.
  • Delta changes with the share price and with time, so that a delta hedge must be rebalanced. With continuous rebalancing and volatility as assumed, the cost of hedging an option equals its Black–Scholes–Merton value.
  • Gamma is the sensitivity of delta to the price of the underlying. A delta-neutral position changes in value by about \(\tfrac12\Gamma(\Delta S)^{2}\) when the price moves by \(\Delta S\).
  • Theta is the sensitivity to the passage of time. \(\Theta+rS\Delta+\tfrac12\sigma^{2}S^{2}\Gamma=r\Pi\): positive gamma is paid for by negative theta.
  • Vega is the sensitivity to volatility and rho the sensitivity to the interest rate. Gamma and vega can be changed only by trading options.
  • An option can be created synthetically by trading the underlying asset according to delta. The procedure fails when prices move discontinuously or when the trading itself moves the price.

Exercises

14.1 A share that pays no dividend trades at $50 and has a volatility of 30 percent. The risk-free rate is 4 percent. A dealer has written six-month European calls on 20,000 shares with a strike of $50. Find the delta of one call and the delta hedge. (From Exercise 12.1, \(d_1=0.2003\).)

\(\Delta=N(0.2003)=0.5794\). The written calls have a delta of \(-20{,}000\times0.5794=-11{,}588\). The dealer buys 11,588 shares, at a cost of \(11{,}588\times50=\$579{,}400\).

14.2 A share that pays no dividend trades at $40 and has a volatility of 25 percent. The risk-free rate is 6 percent. An investor holds nine-month European puts on 10,000 shares with a strike of $45. Find the delta of one put and the trade in shares that makes the position delta neutral. (From Exercise 12.2, \(d_1=-0.2279\).)

\(N(d_1)=N(-0.2279)=0.4099\), so that \(\Delta_{\text{put}}=0.4099-1=-0.5901\). The puts held have a delta of \(10{,}000\times(-0.5901)=-5{,}901\). The investor buys 5,901 shares. The position is then a hedged put: it gains if the share price moves substantially in either direction.

14.3 For a one-year European call with a strike of $95 on a share at $100 with a volatility of 20 percent and a risk-free rate of 5 percent, \(d_1=0.6065\) and \(d_2=0.4065\). Find the gamma, the vega per percentage point, and the theta per calendar day.

\(N'(0.6065)=0.3989e^{-0.1839}=0.3319\). \(\Gamma=0.3319/(100\times0.20\times1)=0.0166\). \(\mathcal{V}=100\times1\times0.3319=33.19\), or $0.332 per percentage point. \(N(d_2)=0.6578\) and \(Ke^{-rT}=90.367\). \(\Theta=-100\times0.3319\times0.20/2-0.05\times90.367\times0.6578=-3.319-2.972=-6.291\) per year, or \(-6.291/365=-\$0.0172\) per calendar day.

14.4 A delta-neutral portfolio has a gamma of −4,000. Estimate the change in its value if the price of the underlying share moves at once (a) from $60 to $62 and (b) from $60 to $57.

By Result 14.2 with delta equal to zero and no passage of time, \(\Delta\Pi\approx\tfrac12\Gamma(\Delta S)^{2}\). (a) \(\tfrac12\times(-4{,}000)\times4=-\$8{,}000\). (b) \(\tfrac12\times(-4{,}000)\times9=-\$18{,}000\). The position loses in both cases; a move one and a half times as large produces a loss two and a quarter times as large.

14.5 A delta-neutral portfolio has a gamma of −3,000. A traded call has a delta of 0.62 and a gamma of 1.50. Find the trades that make the portfolio both gamma neutral and delta neutral.

\(w_T=-(-3{,}000)/1.50=2{,}000\): buy 2,000 of the traded calls. They add a delta of \(2{,}000\times0.62=1{,}240\), so that 1,240 shares are sold. The portfolio then has a delta of zero and a gamma of zero.

14.6 A delta-neutral portfolio on a share priced at $80, with a volatility of 30 percent, is worth $200,000 and has a gamma of −500. The risk-free rate is 5 percent. Find its theta per year and per trading day, and state what the result means.

By Result 14.3, \(\Theta=r\Pi-\tfrac12\sigma^{2}S^{2}\Gamma=0.05\times200{,}000-\tfrac12\times0.09\times6{,}400\times(-500)=10{,}000+144{,}000=\$154{,}000\) per year, or \(154{,}000/252=\$611\) per trading day. If the share price does not move, the portfolio gains $611 in a day. This is the compensation for the losses that negative gamma produces when the price does move.

14.7 A delta-neutral portfolio has a gamma of −5,000 and a vega of −8,000 per percentage point. Option 1 has a delta of 0.60, a gamma of 0.50, and a vega of 2.00 per percentage point; option 2 has a delta of 0.50, a gamma of 0.80, and a vega of 1.20 per percentage point. Find the trades that make the portfolio neutral in delta, gamma, and vega.

Gamma: \(0.50w_1+0.80w_2=5{,}000\). Vega: \(2.00w_1+1.20w_2=8{,}000\). Multiplying the first by 4 and subtracting the second, \(2.00w_2=12{,}000\), so that \(w_2=6{,}000\) and \(w_1=(5{,}000-4{,}800)/0.50=400\). Buy 400 of option 1 and 6,000 of option 2. Their delta is \(400\times0.60+6{,}000\times0.50=3{,}240\); sell 3,240 shares.

14.8 A pension fund holds a portfolio of $50,000,000 that follows a stock index. It wishes to create synthetically a six-month put on the portfolio, for which \(N(d_1)=0.68\); the dividend yield on the index is 2 percent. (a) What proportion of the portfolio should be sold at the outset? (b) Explain why the fund might prefer a purchased put, although the synthetic put has no initial cost.

(a) \(\Delta_{\text{put}}=e^{-0.02\times0.5}(0.68-1)=0.9900\times(-0.32)=-0.3168\). The fund sells 31.68 percent of the portfolio, $15,840,000, and invests the proceeds at the risk-free rate. (b) The synthetic put is not free: its cost is incurred through time, by selling after falls and buying after rises, and on average equals the value of the put. The cost is uncertain and is larger if the market proves more volatile than expected. The protection also depends on the ability to trade at each price as the market falls. If the market falls abruptly, or if many funds sell together, the floor is not achieved. A purchased put fixes both the cost and the floor in advance.

Further reading

  • Brady, N. F., et al. (1988). Report of the Presidential Task Force on Market Mechanisms. U.S. Government Printing Office.
  • Hull, J. C. (2022). Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (11th ed.). Pearson. Chapter 19.
  • Leland, H. E. (1980). Who should buy portfolio insurance? Journal of Finance, 35(2), 581–594.
  • Rubinstein, M., and Leland, H. E. (1981). Replicating options with positions in stock and cash. Financial Analysts Journal, 37(4), 63–72.
  • Taleb, N. N. (1997). Dynamic Hedging: Managing Vanilla and Exotic Options. Wiley.

8 questions · pass at 70%
Chapter 15 · Part V: Risk Management

Volatility Smiles and the Volatility Surface

The pattern of implied volatilities across strike prices and maturities, what it reveals about the distribution that the market assigns to future prices, and how the Black–Scholes–Merton model is used when its central assumption does not hold

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. define a volatility smile and explain why European calls and puts with the same strike and maturity have the same implied volatility;
  2. describe the smiles observed for currency options and for equity options, and the departures from the lognormal distribution to which each corresponds;
  3. read a volatility surface and use it to value an option;
  4. infer probabilities from the prices of options with neighbouring strikes;
  5. explain how the Black–Scholes–Merton model is used in practice when volatility is not constant;
  6. interpret the VIX index;
  7. ★ derive the risk-neutral density of the future price from the prices of options.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

Which option carries the higher implied volatility?

A stock index stands at 6,000. Two three-month European options are traded: a put with a strike of 5,400, which pays if the index falls by more than 10 percent, and a call with a strike of 6,600, which pays if it rises by more than 10 percent. The Black–Scholes–Merton model assumes one volatility for the index and therefore assigns the same implied volatility to both. Which pattern is observed in the market?

Select a pattern.

15.1  Implied volatility across strike prices

Section 12.6 defined the implied volatility of an option as the volatility at which the Black–Scholes–Merton formula reproduces its market price. If the model described the market exactly, every option on one asset would have the same implied volatility, whatever its strike price and maturity, because the model assumes that the asset has one constant volatility. This is not what is observed. A plot of the implied volatilities of options with one maturity against their strike prices is called a volatility smile, from the shape that it takes in some markets. The shape differs from one market to another, and it is the subject of this chapter.

A preliminary result simplifies the discussion. Put–call parity, Result 8.2 as extended in Chapter 13, is \(p+S_0e^{-qT}=c+Ke^{-rT}\). It rests on an arbitrage argument alone and holds whatever the distribution of the future price. It therefore holds for the market prices \(p_{\text{mkt}}\) and \(c_{\text{mkt}}\), and it holds for the prices \(p_{\text{BS}}\) and \(c_{\text{BS}}\) that the model produces at any one volatility. Subtracting one equation from the other,

Result 15.1 — Calls and puts share one implied volatility

\[ p_{\text{BS}}-p_{\text{mkt}}=c_{\text{BS}}-c_{\text{mkt}} . \] The amount by which the model misprices a European put equals the amount by which it misprices the European call with the same strike and maturity. At the volatility for which the model matches the price of the call, it matches the price of the put. The two options have the same implied volatility.

The smile may therefore be drawn without stating whether calls or puts were used. In practice the implied volatilities for low strikes are taken from puts and those for high strikes from calls, because options that are out of the money are the more actively traded.

Key terms

Volatility smile: the relation between implied volatility and strike price for options with one maturity. Volatility skew: a smile in which implied volatility falls, or rises, steadily as the strike increases. At-the-money volatility: the implied volatility of the option whose strike equals the current price or the forward price of the asset. Moneyness: the strike expressed in relation to the price of the asset, commonly as the ratio \(K/S_0\).

15.2  Currency options

For options on the major currencies, implied volatility is lowest when the strike is near the forward exchange rate and rises on both sides. The smile is approximately symmetric. An option far out of the money in either direction is priced at a higher volatility than an option at the money.

The pattern is explained by the distribution of exchange rate changes. An option far out of the money pays only if the exchange rate moves a long way. If the market prices such options above their Black–Scholes–Merton values at the at-the-money volatility, it assigns to large movements a greater probability than the lognormal distribution does. The distribution that the market uses has heavier tails than the lognormal distribution, in both directions.

The evidence supports the market. Under the model, daily changes in the logarithm of an exchange rate are normally distributed. Table 15.1 gives the frequency with which a normally distributed change exceeds a given number of standard deviations. Studies of exchange rates find that changes of more than three standard deviations occur on about 1 percent of days and not on 0.27 percent, and that changes of more than four or five standard deviations, which under the normal distribution should be seen once in decades or in millennia, are seen every few years.

Table 15.1  Frequency of large daily changes under the normal distribution (changes in either direction; 252 trading days per year)
Size of the changePercentage of daysExpected frequency
More than 1 standard deviation31.73One day in 3
More than 2 standard deviations4.55One day in 22
More than 3 standard deviations0.27One day in 370 (about 1.5 years)
More than 4 standard deviations0.0063One day in 15,800 (about 63 years)
More than 5 standard deviations0.000057One day in 1,740,000 (about 6,900 years)

Two of the assumptions of the model are responsible. The volatility of an exchange rate is not constant: periods of calm alternate with periods of disturbance, and a mixture of the two produces more very small and more very large changes than one normal distribution with the average volatility. And exchange rates do not always move continuously: an announcement by a central bank may move a rate by several percent in a moment. Both effects produce heavy tails. The effect of non-constant volatility is more pronounced for long maturities and that of jumps for short maturities.

15.3  Equity options

For options on shares and on stock indices the pattern is different, and it answers the opening question. Implied volatility decreases as the strike price increases. A put with a low strike is priced at a much higher volatility than a call with a high strike. This pattern is called a volatility skew, or sometimes a smirk.

The corresponding distribution has a heavier left tail and a lighter right tail than the lognormal distribution with the at-the-money volatility. The market assigns to a large fall in the index a greater probability than the lognormal distribution does, and to a large rise a smaller probability. Three explanations are offered, and they are not exclusive.

  1. Leverage. When the shares of a company fall in value, its debt is unchanged, and the ratio of debt to equity rises. The shares become riskier, and their volatility increases. When the shares rise, the reverse occurs. Volatility is therefore a decreasing function of the share price, as the skew implies.
  2. Volatility feedback. An increase in the volatility of the market raises the return that investors require, and prices fall to provide it. Falls in the index and rises in volatility are therefore observed together.
  3. The demand for protection. Investors as a group hold shares and wish to insure them against large falls. They buy puts with low strikes. Those who sell such puts cannot hedge them reliably in a market that falls abruptly, as Section 14.10 showed, and require a premium. The term crashophobia was applied to this explanation by Mark Rubinstein.

The third explanation is supported by the history of the pattern, which the historical note recounts: the skew in index options has been present since the fall in share prices of October 1987 and was not present before it.

⚙ Interactive figure 15.1 — From the smile to the distribution

The distribution of the future price that a smile implies

The upper figure shows the implied volatility of three-month options against the strike, which is stated as a percentage of the current price. The lower figure shows the risk-neutral distribution of the price in three months that these volatilities imply, together with the lognormal distribution at the at-the-money volatility. Select a market, then vary the slope and the curvature of the smile and observe the tails of the distribution.

Concept check 15.1

In a certain market, options with strikes far above the current price have higher implied volatilities than options at the money, and options with strikes far below have lower implied volatilities. What does this imply about the distribution that the market assigns to the future price, relative to the lognormal distribution?

15.4  The term structure of volatility and the volatility surface

Implied volatility varies with maturity as well as with strike. The relation between the at-the-money implied volatility and the maturity of the option is the volatility term structure. When recent volatility has been low by historical standards, the term structure tends to slope upward, because volatility is expected to rise toward its normal level; when recent volatility has been high, it tends to slope downward. Volatility, unlike a share price, is drawn back toward a long-run average.

The smile and the term structure are combined in a volatility surface, which gives the implied volatility for each strike and each maturity. Table 15.2 is a surface for options on the index of the opening decision. It is illustrative, with the features that such surfaces commonly have: a skew at every maturity, steeper for short maturities than for long, and an at-the-money volatility that rises with maturity. Some entries of a surface correspond to options that are actively traded, and their implied volatilities are observed directly. The remainder are obtained by interpolation.

Table 15.2  A volatility surface for options on a stock index at 6,000 (implied volatility, percent per year)
Strike \(K/S_0\)1 month3 months6 months1 year2 years
0.90 (5,400)27.924.023.323.222.9
0.95 (5,700)21.720.821.121.721.9
1.00 (6,000)16.818.019.320.420.9
1.05 (6,300)13.015.717.619.220.1
1.10 (6,600)10.213.816.218.119.3

The skew flattens as maturity increases when it is measured against \(K/S_0\), as in the table. A strike 10 percent below the index is a remote level for an option with one month to run and an ordinary level for an option with two years to run. For this reason the smile is often expressed against a measure that allows for maturity: the strike in relation to the forward price, \(K/F_0\); the number of standard deviations by which the strike differs from the forward price, \(\ln(K/F_0)/(\sigma\sqrt{T})\); or the delta of the option. Smiles expressed in these ways are more nearly the same from one maturity to the next.

Worked example 15.1 — Valuing an option from the surface
A client asks for the price of a nine-month European put on the index with a strike of 5,550. The risk-free rate is 4 percent and the dividend yield on the index is 1.2 percent. Value the put from Table 15.2.
1
Locate the option. \(K/S_0=5{,}550/6{,}000=0.925\), midway between the rows for 0.90 and 0.95. Nine months is midway between the columns for six months and one year.
2
Interpolate across strikes. Six months: \((23.3+21.1)/2=22.2\) percent. One year: \((23.2+21.7)/2=22.45\) percent.
3
Interpolate across maturities. \((22.2+22.45)/2=22.3\) percent, to one decimal place.
4
Apply Result 13.1. \(\sigma\sqrt{T}=0.223\times0.8660=0.1931\). \(d_1=[\ln(6{,}000/5{,}550)+(0.04-0.012+0.223^{2}/2)\times0.75]/0.1931=(0.07796+0.03965)/0.1931=0.6090\); \(d_2=0.4159\). \(N(-d_1)=0.2713\); \(N(-d_2)=0.3388\). \(p=5{,}550e^{-0.03}\times0.3388-6{,}000e^{-0.009}\times0.2713=1{,}824.5-1{,}613.0=211.5\) index points.
5
Comparison. At the nine-month at-the-money volatility, \((19.3+20.4)/2=19.85\) percent, the same formula gives 170.3. A dealer who ignored the skew would sell the put for about 20 percent less than the price at which it could be bought back in the market.
Worked example 15.2 — The cost of ignoring the skew
Value the two three-month options of the opening decision, first at the at-the-money volatility of 18.0 percent and then at the volatilities of Table 15.2.
1
Put with a strike of 5,400. At 18.0 percent the put is worth 25.8 index points. At its own implied volatility of 24.0 percent it is worth 63.7, about two and a half times as much.
2
Call with a strike of 6,600. At 18.0 percent the call is worth 48.5 index points. At its own implied volatility of 13.8 percent it is worth 20.5, less than half as much.
3
Interpretation. Differences of a few points of implied volatility correspond to large proportional differences in the prices of options far out of the money. These are the options whose prices depend most on the tails of the distribution, about which the lognormal assumption is least reliable.

15.5  Probabilities implied by option prices

The interpretation of the smile in terms of the tails of a distribution can be made exact. Consider two European puts with strikes slightly below and slightly above a level \(K\), at \(K-\delta\) and \(K+\delta\). A position that is long the put with the higher strike and short the put with the lower strike, a bear spread in the terms of Section 9.3, pays \(2\delta\) if the price ends below \(K-\delta\), nothing if it ends above \(K+\delta\), and an intermediate amount between the two. When \(\delta\) is small, the position is close to a contract that pays \(2\delta\) if the price ends below \(K\) and nothing otherwise. By risk-neutral valuation the value of such a contract is \(2\delta e^{-rT}\) multiplied by the risk-neutral probability of that event. Hence

Result 15.2 — The probability implied by a spread

\[ \Pr(S_T<K)\approx e^{rT}\,\frac{p(K+\delta)-p(K-\delta)}{2\delta}, \] where \(p(K)\) is the market price of a European put with strike \(K\) and the probability is that of a risk-neutral world.

Worked example 15.3 — The probability of a fall of 20 percent
Three-month puts on the index with strikes of 4,750 and 4,850 trade at 28.11 and 30.79 index points. The risk-free rate is 4 percent. Find the risk-neutral probability that the index is below 4,800 in three months, and compare it with the probability under a lognormal distribution with a volatility of 18.0 percent, at which the same puts would be worth 0.56 and 1.18.
1
From market prices. \(e^{0.01}\times(30.79-28.11)/100=1.01005\times0.0268=0.0271\), or 2.7 percent.
2
From the lognormal distribution. \(1.01005\times(1.18-0.56)/100=0.0063\), or 0.6 percent.
3
Interpretation. The market prices options as though a fall of 20 percent within three months were more than four times as probable as the model, at the at-the-money volatility, indicates. The probability is a risk-neutral one. It reflects the price that investors will pay for protection against such a fall, as well as their estimate of its likelihood, and it should not be read as a forecast.

15.6  ★ The implied density

Optional section. This section obtains the whole risk-neutral distribution from option prices. It uses differentiation under the integral sign.

Let \(g(S_T)\) be the risk-neutral probability density of the price at time \(T\). By Principle 10.1 the price of a European call with strike \(K\) is \[ c=e^{-rT}\int_{K}^{\infty}(S_T-K)\,g(S_T)\,dS_T . \] Differentiating once with respect to \(K\) gives \(\partial c/\partial K=-e^{-rT}\int_K^\infty g(S_T)\,dS_T\), which is \(-e^{-rT}\) multiplied by the probability that the call is exercised. Differentiating again,

Result 15.3 — The implied density

\[ g(K)=e^{rT}\frac{\partial^{2}c}{\partial K^{2}}\approx e^{rT}\,\frac{c(K-\delta)-2c(K)+c(K+\delta)}{\delta^{2}} . \] The same expression holds with put prices in place of call prices.

The numerator is the cost of a butterfly spread, Section 9.3: long one option at each of the outer strikes and short two at the middle strike. The butterfly pays a triangle of height \(\delta\) centred on \(K\), and its price measures the probability that the price ends near \(K\). Since the payoff of a butterfly is never negative, its price cannot be negative, and the density that a smile implies must be positive at every strike. A smile that is too steep or too sharply curved violates this condition and would permit arbitrage. The lower panel of Interactive figure 15.1 was drawn by applying Result 15.3 at each strike.

For example, the three-month puts on the index with strikes of 4,750, 4,800, and 4,850 trade at 28.111, 29.372, and 30.786. The butterfly costs \(28.111-2\times29.372+30.786=0.153\). The density at 4,800 is \(1.01005\times0.153/50^{2}=0.0000618\) per index point, and the probability that the index ends within 25 points of 4,800 is approximately \(0.0000618\times50=0.31\) percent.

15.7  The role of the model

If the implied volatility of every option is different, in what sense is the Black–Scholes–Merton model used? The answer is that practitioners use it as a means of quotation and interpolation and not as a statement about the behaviour of the asset. The prices of actively traded options are observed. They are converted into implied volatilities, which vary far less across strikes and maturities than the prices do, and a surface is fitted to them. The price of an option that is not actively traded is then found by reading its volatility from the surface and applying the formula, as in Worked example 15.1. The procedure ensures that the option is priced consistently with those that are traded. The model serves as the instrument by which prices are compared and interpolated, and the surface carries the information that the model omits.

The procedure is reliable for European options, whose prices depend only on the distribution of the price at one date. It is less reliable for the exotic options of Chapter 18, whose values depend on the path of the price, and for these, models that allow the volatility to vary are required.

The smile also affects hedging. The delta of Chapter 14 assumes that the implied volatility of an option is unchanged when the price of the asset changes. For equity options this is not so: implied volatilities tend to rise when the index falls and to fall when it rises. The price of a call therefore responds to a rise in the index by less than its Black–Scholes–Merton delta indicates, because the accompanying fall in volatility offsets part of the gain. Traders allow for this by using a delta somewhat lower than \(N(d_1)\) for equity options. Two rules of thumb describe how the surface is assumed to move. Under the sticky strike rule the implied volatility of an option with a given strike is unchanged from day to day. Under the sticky delta rule the smile moves with the price of the asset, so that the implied volatility is unchanged for a given moneyness.

Common error

An option with a high implied volatility is not thereby shown to be overpriced, and the skew is not an opportunity for arbitrage. Implied volatility is the price of the option in other units. A put far out of the money has a high implied volatility because the market assigns to large falls a greater probability, or a greater price, than the lognormal distribution does. To sell such puts and hedge their delta is to sell insurance against a fall in the market, which earns a premium in most periods and incurs a very large loss in a few.

15.8  An anticipated jump

The smiles described so far are those of ordinary conditions. The method of Section 15.5 applies equally to special conditions, and one case is instructive. Suppose that a single announcement, such as the outcome of a regulatory decision or of litigation, is expected shortly and will move the price of a share sharply in one direction or the other. The distribution of the price after the announcement has two peaks and little probability between them. The smile that corresponds is the reverse of that for currencies: implied volatility is highest at the money and falls on both sides. It is sometimes called a volatility frown.

Worked example 15.4 — A share awaiting an announcement
A share trades at $50. In one month an announcement will move its price to either $58 or $42. The risk-free rate is 4 percent. Value one-month European calls with strikes from $44 to $56 and find their implied volatilities.
1
Risk-neutral probability. By Result 10.1, \(p=(50e^{0.04/12}-42)/(58-42)=(50.1669-42)/16=0.5104\).
2
Call values. A call with a strike \(K\) between 42 and 58 pays \(58-K\) with probability 0.5104 and nothing otherwise: \(c=e^{-0.04/12}\times0.5104\times(58-K)\).
3
Implied volatilities. Each value is converted to an implied volatility by the method of Section 12.6.
Strike ($)44464850525456
Call value ($)7.126.105.094.073.052.031.02
Implied volatility (%)58.266.469.669.566.660.850.9
4
Interpretation. Implied volatility is greatest near the current price and falls away on both sides. A lognormal distribution wide enough to reach $42 and $58 assigns substantial probability to prices beyond them, which the true distribution excludes; options with strikes near those levels are therefore worth less than the model indicates.

15.9  The VIX index

The implied volatilities of options on the S&P 500 index are summarized in one number, the VIX index, published by the Cboe. It was introduced in 1993 and has been computed since 2003 from the prices of calls and puts across a wide range of strikes, weighted so that the result measures the volatility of the index that the market expects over the following 30 days. It does not depend on the Black–Scholes–Merton model or on any single strike. The index is stated in percent per year.

A VIX of 20 corresponds to a standard deviation of the return on the S&P 500 over the next 30 days of \(20\times\sqrt{30/365}=5.7\) percent, and to a daily standard deviation of \(20/\sqrt{252}=1.26\) percent. The index has been close to 20 on average over its history. It rises sharply when share prices fall, as the skew would suggest, and for this reason it is sometimes called a gauge of fear. Its closing value exceeded 80 in November 2008 and again in March 2020. Futures and options on the VIX have been traded since 2004 and 2006, and allow volatility itself to be bought and sold.

Concept check 15.2

On a certain day the implied volatility of a three-month call on a share with a strike of $60 is 30 percent. A three-month put on the same share with the same strike is quoted at a price that corresponds to an implied volatility of 35 percent. Both are European and the share pays no dividend. What follows?

Concept check 15.3

A bank values all its three-month index options at the at-the-money implied volatility. Relative to the market, how does it value puts far out of the money and calls far out of the money?

Historical note

Before October 1987 the implied volatilities of options on American stock indices were nearly the same at all strikes, as the Black–Scholes–Merton model requires, and a slight symmetric smile was the most that could be detected. On 19 October 1987 the S&P 500 index fell by 20.5 percent. At a volatility of 20 percent per year the standard deviation of a daily change is 1.26 percent, so that the fall was one of about 16 standard deviations. Table 15.1 does not extend so far; under the normal distribution such an event should not occur once in the life of the universe.

Mark Rubinstein, who had been among the founders of portfolio insurance, documented what followed. From that time the prices of index puts with low strikes have been persistently higher, in relation to other options, than before, and the skew of Section 15.3 has been present in every year since. The market had learned that the distribution of index returns has a left tail that the lognormal distribution does not describe, and it has not since allowed the fact to go unpriced. In 1994 Rubinstein, and independently Emanuel Derman and Iraj Kani and Bruno Dupire, showed how a model of the price of the asset could be constructed to agree with the whole of an observed volatility surface.

Summary

  • A volatility smile is the relation between implied volatility and strike for options with one maturity. By put–call parity, European calls and puts with the same strike and maturity have the same implied volatility.
  • For currency options implied volatility rises on both sides of the money, which corresponds to a distribution with heavier tails than the lognormal distribution.
  • For equity options implied volatility falls as the strike rises, which corresponds to a heavier left tail and a lighter right tail. Leverage, volatility feedback, and the demand for protection against large falls are the explanations offered.
  • A volatility surface gives implied volatility by strike and maturity. Options are valued by reading the volatility from the surface and applying the Black–Scholes–Merton formula.
  • The prices of options with neighbouring strikes reveal risk-neutral probabilities: a spread gives the probability of ending below a level, and a butterfly gives the density.
  • The VIX index measures the volatility of the S&P 500 that option prices imply for the following 30 days.

Exercises

15.1 At a volatility of 25 percent the Black–Scholes–Merton prices of a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity are $4.20 and $3.10. The call trades in the market at $4.50. At what price must the put trade, and what can be said of the implied volatilities of the two options?

By Result 15.1, \(p_{\text{mkt}}-p_{\text{BS}}=c_{\text{mkt}}-c_{\text{BS}}=4.50-4.20=0.30\), so that the put must trade at \(3.10+0.30=\$3.40\). Both options are priced above their values at 25 percent, and both have the same implied volatility, which is higher than 25 percent.

15.2 Three-month options on a share priced at $100 have implied volatilities of 22 percent at a strike of $95 and 19 percent at a strike of $100. Estimate by linear interpolation the implied volatility at a strike of $97, and state the type of smile.

The strike of $97 lies two fifths of the way from $95 to $100: \(22-\tfrac25\times(22-19)=20.8\) percent. Implied volatility falls as the strike rises, which is the skew typical of equity options.

15.3 A share that pays no dividend trades at $100, and the risk-free rate is 3 percent. The at-the-money implied volatility of six-month options is 20 percent, and that of options with a strike of $90 is 28 percent. Find the value of a six-month European put with a strike of $90 at each volatility. By what proportion would a dealer who used the at-the-money volatility undervalue the put?

At 20 percent: \(\sigma\sqrt T=0.1414\); \(d_1=[\ln(100/90)+(0.03+0.02)\times0.5]/0.1414=0.9218\); \(d_2=0.7804\); \(p=90e^{-0.015}\times0.2176-100\times0.1783=\$1.46\). At 28 percent: \(\sigma\sqrt T=0.1980\); \(d_1=[0.10536+(0.03+0.0392)\times0.5]/0.1980=0.7069\); \(d_2=0.5089\); \(p=88.660\times0.3054-100\times0.2398=\$3.10\). The dealer would value the put at $1.46 against a market price of $3.10, an undervaluation of 53 percent.

15.4 The volatility of a stock index is 16 percent per year. (a) Find the standard deviation of its daily change, taking 252 trading days in a year. (b) The index falls by 5 percent in one day. By how many standard deviations has it moved, and how often would Table 15.1 lead one to expect a change of at least that size?

(a) \(16/\sqrt{252}=1.008\) percent. (b) \(5/1.008=4.96\) standard deviations. Under the normal distribution a change of more than 4 standard deviations is expected about once in 63 years and one of more than 5 about once in 6,900 years, so that a change of 4.96 should be seen roughly once in several thousand years. Falls of this size in major indices have occurred several times in a decade, which is the evidence for heavy tails.

15.5 Six-month puts on a share with strikes of $78 and $82 trade at $2.10 and $3.30. The risk-free rate is 4 percent. Estimate the risk-neutral probability that the share price is below $80 in six months.

By Result 15.2 with \(\delta=2\): \(e^{0.02}\times(3.30-2.10)/4=1.0202\times0.30=0.306\), or about 31 percent.

15.6 ★ Six-month calls on a share with strikes of $95, $100, and $105 trade at $7.90, $4.60, and $2.30. The risk-free rate is 4 percent. Find the cost of the butterfly spread, the implied density at $100, and the approximate probability that the share price ends between $97.50 and $102.50.

The butterfly costs \(7.90-2\times4.60+2.30=\$1.00\). By Result 15.3, \(g(100)=e^{0.02}\times1.00/5^{2}=0.0408\) per dollar. The probability of ending in a band of width $5 centred on $100 is approximately \(0.0408\times5=0.204\), or about 20 percent.

15.7 A share trades at $80. In two months the result of a clinical trial will move its price to either $92 or $70. The risk-free rate is 3 percent. (a) Find the values of two-month European calls and puts with a strike of $80, and verify put–call parity. (b) The implied volatilities of the calls with strikes of $72, $80, and $88 are 31.4, 41.9, and 34.7 percent. Describe the smile.

(a) \(p=(80e^{0.005}-70)/22=(80.401-70)/22=0.4728\). Call: \(e^{-0.005}\times0.4728\times12=\$5.645\). Put: \(e^{-0.005}\times0.5272\times10=\$5.246\). Parity: \(c-p=0.399\) and \(S_0-Ke^{-rT}=80-79.601=0.399\). (b) Implied volatility is highest at the money and lower on both sides, a frown, which reflects a distribution with two peaks and thin tails beyond them.

15.8 The VIX index stands at 24. (a) What standard deviation of the return on the S&P 500 over the next 30 days does this represent? (b) What daily standard deviation? (c) Explain why the VIX tends to rise on days when the S&P 500 falls.

(a) \(24\times\sqrt{30/365}=6.9\) percent. (b) \(24/\sqrt{252}=1.51\) percent. (c) The volatility of share prices tends to increase when prices fall, for the reasons given in Section 15.3, and the demand for puts as protection increases at the same time. Both raise the prices of index options and therefore the volatility that those prices imply.

Chapter 16 · Part V: Risk Management

Numerical Methods: Trees, Simulation, and Finite Differences

Three procedures for valuing derivatives that have no formula: the binomial tree as it is used in practice, Monte Carlo simulation and the control of its error, and the solution of the pricing equation on a grid

Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

  1. state which numerical method is suited to a given derivative;
  2. estimate delta, gamma, and theta from a binomial tree, and improve the accuracy of a tree by the control variate technique;
  3. value a derivative by Monte Carlo simulation and state the standard error of the result;
  4. determine the number of trials that a required accuracy demands, and describe methods that reduce it;
  5. apply the explicit finite difference method at a node of a grid and state the condition for its stability;
  6. ★ derive the explicit finite difference method from the Black–Scholes–Merton differential equation.
⚙ Decision — choose first; the theory follows

How many more trials?

An analyst values an option by simulation. With 10,000 simulated outcomes the estimate of the value has a standard error of $0.04. The trading desk requires a standard error of $0.01. How many outcomes must be simulated?

Select a number.

16.1  The need for numerical methods

The Black–Scholes–Merton formulas value European calls and puts. Most other derivatives have no formula. The American put of Chapter 10 has none, because the holder may exercise at any time and the value depends on when it is optimal to do so. An option whose payoff depends on the average price over a period has none. An option on several assets has none. Such derivatives are valued by numerical methods, which are procedures that produce an approximate value and can be made as accurate as required by additional computation.

Three methods are in general use. All three apply the principle of risk-neutral valuation, Principle 10.1, and differ in how they represent the uncertain future.

  • A tree represents the possible prices of the asset at a sequence of dates and works backward from expiration to the present.
  • Monte Carlo simulation draws a large number of possible paths of the price at random, computes the payoff on each, and averages. It works forward from the present to expiration.
  • A finite difference method solves the Black–Scholes–Merton differential equation, Result 12.1, on a grid of prices and dates. Like a tree, it works backward.

The direction in which a method works determines what it can value. At each date the holder of an American option compares the value of exercising with the value of continuing. The value of continuing is known only when later dates have been dealt with, so that a method that works backward handles early exercise naturally. A payoff that depends on the path of the price, such as an average, is known only when the path has been followed from the start, so that a method that works forward handles it naturally. Table 16.1 summarizes.

Table 16.1  The three numerical methods compared
 Binomial treeMonte Carlo simulationFinite differences
DirectionBackwardForwardBackward
Early exerciseHandled directlyRequires special techniquesHandled directly
Payoff depending on the pathDifficultHandled directlyDifficult
Several underlying variablesImpractical beyond two or threeCost rises only in proportion to their numberImpractical beyond two or three
ErrorFalls roughly in proportion to the number of stepsFalls with the square root of the number of trials; it is random and can be measuredFalls with the fineness of the grid
SensitivitiesDelta, gamma, and theta from the tree itselfRequire repeated simulationDelta, gamma, and theta from the grid itself

16.2  Binomial trees in practice

Chapter 10 developed the binomial tree. With a time step of \(\Delta t\), the tree of Cox, Ross, and Rubinstein, Result 10.2, sets \[ u=e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}, \qquad d=\frac1u, \qquad p=\frac{a-d}{u-d}, \qquad a=e^{(r-q)\Delta t}, \] where \(q\) is the rate of income on the asset: zero for a share that pays no dividend, the dividend yield for an index, the foreign interest rate for a currency, and \(r\) for a futures contract, in which case \(a=1\). The value at each node is the discounted risk-neutral expectation of the values at the two nodes that follow, or the value of immediate exercise if the option is American and that value is greater. In practice thirty or more steps are used, and the calculation is done by computer. Two refinements are in general use.

Sensitivities from the tree

The tree that values an option also supplies its sensitivities. Let \(f_{i,j}\) be the value of the option at the node reached after \(i\) steps of which \(j\) were upward, where the price of the asset is \(S_0u^{j}d^{\,i-j}\). Delta is the change in the value of the option between the two nodes at the first step, divided by the change in the price: \[ \Delta=\frac{f_{1,1}-f_{1,0}}{S_0u-S_0d}. \] Gamma is the change in delta. The three nodes at the second step provide two estimates of delta, one over the interval from \(S_0\) to \(S_0u^{2}\) and one over the interval from \(S_0d^{2}\) to \(S_0\), whose midpoints are separated by \(h=\tfrac12(S_0u^{2}-S_0d^{2})\): \[ \Gamma=\frac{1}{h}\left[\frac{f_{2,2}-f_{2,1}}{S_0u^{2}-S_0}-\frac{f_{2,1}-f_{2,0}}{S_0-S_0d^{2}}\right]. \] Theta is obtained from the middle node at the second step, at which the price is again \(S_0\) and the time is later by \(2\Delta t\): \[ \Theta=\frac{f_{2,1}-f_{0,0}}{2\Delta t}. \] Vega and rho are found by valuing the option again with a slightly different volatility or interest rate and taking the difference.

Worked example 16.1 — The sensitivities of an American put
A six-month American put on Northwind shares has a strike of $30. The share price is $28, the volatility 39 percent, and the risk-free rate 5 percent. A tree with five steps gives the values below. Estimate delta, gamma, and theta.
Node \((i,j)\)(0,0)(1,0)(1,1)(2,0)(2,1)(2,2)
Share price ($)28.000024.751231.675221.879428.000035.8327
Value of the put ($)3.94825.78812.06978.12063.41470.6880
1
Delta. \((2.0697-5.7881)/(31.6752-24.7512)=-3.7184/6.9240=-0.537\).
2
Gamma. Upper delta: \((0.6880-3.4147)/(35.8327-28)=-0.3481\). Lower delta: \((3.4147-8.1206)/(28-21.8794)=-0.7689\). \(h=\tfrac12(35.8327-21.8794)=6.9767\). \(\Gamma=(-0.3481+0.7689)/6.9767=0.0603\).
3
Theta. \(\Delta t=0.1\), so that \(\Theta=(3.4147-3.9482)/0.2=-2.668\) per year, or \(-\$0.0073\) per calendar day.
4
Accuracy. A tree with 500 steps gives a value of $3.911, a delta of −0.529, a gamma of 0.0557, and a theta of −2.38. Five steps give the value within 1 percent and the sensitivities within about 10 percent. At the node (2,0) the value of the put, $8.1206, is its intrinsic value: early exercise is optimal there.

The control variate technique

The error of a tree with a given number of steps is much the same for an American option as for the corresponding European option, because the two are valued on the same tree and differ only where early exercise occurs. The error for the European option is known exactly, since the Black–Scholes–Merton formula gives its true value. The control variate technique uses this knowledge. Let \(f_A\) and \(f_E\) be the values of the American and the European option from the tree, and \(f_{\text{BSM}}\) the value of the European option from the formula. The improved estimate is \[ f_A+(f_{\text{BSM}}-f_E). \] The error that the tree is known to make on the European option is assumed to be the error that it makes on the American option, and is removed.

Worked example 16.2 — Correcting a tree of twenty steps
For the put of Worked example 16.1, a tree with 20 steps values the American option at $3.9460 and the European option at $3.8450. The Black–Scholes–Merton value of the European put is $3.8091. Find the improved estimate.
1
Error of the tree on the European put. \(3.8450-3.8091=0.0359\): the tree values it too high.
2
Correction. \(3.9460+(3.8091-3.8450)=3.9460-0.0359=\$3.9101\).
3
Comparison. A tree with 5,000 steps gives $3.9104. The uncorrected value is in error by $0.0356 and the corrected value by $0.0003. Twenty steps with the correction are more accurate than several hundred without it.
⚙ Interactive figure 16.1 — The control variate technique

The value of the American put against the number of steps

The figure shows the value of the six-month American put on Northwind shares from trees of 5 to 100 steps, without and with the control variate correction, and a reference value from a corrected tree of 2,000 steps. Vary the strike and the volatility. The uncorrected values oscillate about the reference; the corrected values lie close to it from the start.

The general principle is of wide application. Where a problem that cannot be solved exactly resembles one that can, the numerical method is applied to both, and its measured error on the second is used to correct the first. Section 16.3 applies the same principle to simulation.

16.3  Monte Carlo simulation

By Principle 10.1 the value of a derivative is the expected payoff in a risk-neutral world, discounted at the risk-free rate. An expected value can be estimated by sampling. Monte Carlo simulation values a derivative as follows.

  1. Generate at random a path for the price of the underlying asset in a risk-neutral world.
  2. Compute the payoff of the derivative on that path.
  3. Repeat the first two steps many times.
  4. Compute the mean of the payoffs.
  5. Discount the mean at the risk-free rate.

For a share that follows geometric Brownian motion, Result 11.2 supplies the price at a future date directly. In a risk-neutral world, \[ S_T=S_0\exp\!\left[\left(r-q-\tfrac12\sigma^{2}\right)T+\sigma\sqrt{T}\,\varepsilon\right], \] where \(\varepsilon\) is a random draw from the standard normal distribution. When the payoff depends on the price at one date only, one draw is needed for each trial. When it depends on the path, the life of the derivative is divided into intervals of length \(\Delta t\), and the same expression is applied to each interval in turn, with \(\Delta t\) in place of \(T\), the price at the start of the interval in place of \(S_0\), and a new draw for each interval.

Worked example 16.3 — Five trials by hand
Value the three-month European call on Northwind shares with a strike of $30 by simulation, using the five random draws 0.52, −1.13, 1.64, −0.27, and 0.88. The share price is $28, the volatility 39 percent, and the risk-free rate 5 percent.
1
The sampling formula. \((r-\sigma^{2}/2)T=(0.05-0.07605)\times0.25=-0.00651\) and \(\sigma\sqrt T=0.195\), so that \(S_T=28\exp(-0.00651+0.195\,\varepsilon)\).
2
Prices and payoffs.
Draw \(\varepsilon\)0.52−1.131.64−0.270.88
\(S_T\) ($)30.78722.31738.30226.39233.026
Payoff ($)0.78708.30203.026
3
Mean and discounting. The mean payoff is \((0.787+0+8.302+0+3.026)/5=2.423\). The estimate of the value is \(2.423e^{-0.0125}=\$2.39\).
4
Assessment. The true value is $1.52. Five trials are far too few: one large payoff, $8.30, dominates the mean. The usefulness of the method depends on a measure of how far such an estimate may be from the truth.

The standard error

The estimate from a simulation is the mean of a random sample, and the theory of sampling applies to it. Let \(M\) be the number of trials, \(\bar{f}\) the mean of the discounted payoffs, and \(s\) their standard deviation.

Result 16.1 — The standard error of a simulation

The standard error of the estimate \(\bar f\) is \[ \frac{s}{\sqrt{M}}, \] and a 95 percent confidence interval for the value of the derivative is \[ \bar f-\frac{1.96\,s}{\sqrt M}\;<\;f\;<\;\bar f+\frac{1.96\,s}{\sqrt M}. \] The error falls in proportion to the square root of the number of trials. To halve the error, the number of trials must be multiplied by four; to reduce it to one tenth, by one hundred.

This answers the opening question. To reduce a standard error from $0.04 to $0.01, a factor of 4, the number of trials must be multiplied by \(4^{2}=16\), from 10,000 to 160,000.

A simulation of 10,000 trials for the Northwind call illustrates the result. In one such simulation the mean of the discounted payoffs was $1.469 and their standard deviation $2.973. The standard error is \(2.973/\sqrt{10{,}000}=\$0.030\), and the 95 percent confidence interval runs from \(1.469-1.96\times0.030=\$1.41\) to $1.53. The true value, $1.52, lies within it. The standard deviation of the payoffs is about twice the value of the option. This is typical of options that are out of the money, which pay nothing on most paths and a large amount on a few, and it is the reason that simulation requires many trials.

Reducing the variance

Since the error falls only with the square root of the number of trials, methods that reduce the standard deviation \(s\) are valuable. They are called variance reduction procedures. Two are described here.

The antithetic variable technique uses each random draw twice. For each draw \(\varepsilon\) the payoff is computed with \(\varepsilon\) and again with \(-\varepsilon\), and the two are averaged. When one of the two payoffs is above the true value, the other tends to be below it, and the average of the pair varies less than the average of two independent trials. In a simulation of 10,000 pairs for the Northwind call, the standard deviation of the pair averages was $1.833 and the standard error $0.018. Twenty thousand independent trials, which require the same number of payoffs to be computed, would give a standard error of \(2.973/\sqrt{20{,}000}=\$0.021\). The gain is real and modest for this option; it is greater for options that are in the money, whose payoffs are more nearly linear in \(\varepsilon\).

The control variate technique of Section 16.2 applies to simulation as it does to trees. Suppose that derivative A, which has no formula, resembles derivative B, which has one. Both are valued with the same random draws, giving the estimates \(f_A^{*}\) and \(f_B^{*}\), and the estimate \(f_A^{*}+(f_B-f_B^{*})\) is used, where \(f_B\) is the known value of B. The errors of the two simulations are highly correlated, because the same paths produced both, and most of the error is removed.

Key terms

Trial: one simulated path and the payoff computed from it. Standard error: the standard deviation of the estimate, \(s/\sqrt M\). Path-dependent derivative: a derivative whose payoff depends on prices before expiration as well as at expiration. Asian option: an option whose payoff depends on the average price of the asset over a period; an average price call pays \(\max(S_{\text{ave}}-K,0)\).

⚙ Interactive figure 16.2 — A Monte Carlo valuation

The estimate and its confidence interval as trials accumulate

The figure values a three-month call on Northwind shares with a strike of $30. Select the European call, whose true value is known, or an Asian call on the average of the thirteen weekly closing prices, which has no formula. Choose the number of trials and the sampling method, and draw new samples. The solid line is the estimate as the trials accumulate and the dotted lines are the limits of the 95 percent confidence interval.

The figure shows the two properties of the method. The estimate wanders about the true value and the interval narrows slowly: the improvement from 100 trials to 10,000 is striking, and that from 10,000 to 50,000 is slight. And the Asian call is valued with no more difficulty than the European call, although no formula for it exists. Its value, about $0.66, is less than half that of the European call, because an average of prices varies less than the final price.

The cost of a simulation rises in proportion to the number of underlying variables, whereas the cost of a tree or a grid rises as a power of that number. For derivatives that depend on many variables, simulation is the only practical method. Its principal weakness is early exercise. On a simulated path the value of continuing is not known, since the simulation has not looked beyond the present path. The least-squares method of Francis Longstaff and Eduardo Schwartz overcomes the difficulty by estimating the value of continuing from a regression across all the paths, and is the standard approach for American options on several variables.

Concept check 16.1

A simulation of 2,500 trials gives a mean discounted payoff of $6.40 with a standard deviation of $10.00. Which statement is correct?

16.4  Finite difference methods

Result 12.1 states that the value \(f\) of every derivative on an asset satisfies the differential equation \[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+(r-q)S\frac{\partial f}{\partial S}+\frac12\sigma^{2}S^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial S^{2}}=rf , \] here written for an asset that provides income at the rate \(q\). A finite difference method solves the equation numerically. The life of the derivative is divided into \(N\) intervals of length \(\Delta t=T/N\), and prices from zero to a level \(S_{\max}\), high enough that the option is of negligible value or certain to be exercised there, are divided into \(M\) intervals of length \(\Delta S=S_{\max}/M\). The points \((i\Delta t,\,j\Delta S)\) form a grid, and \(f_{i,j}\) denotes the value of the derivative at the point \((i,j)\).

The values on three edges of the grid are known. For a put with strike \(K\), the values at expiration are \(f_{N,j}=\max(K-j\Delta S,0)\); the value when the price is zero is \(K\); and the value when the price is \(S_{\max}\) is zero. The method fills in the interior of the grid, one date at a time, from expiration back to the present. The simplest version is the explicit finite difference method, in which each value is computed directly from three values at the following date.

Result 16.2 — The explicit finite difference method

\[ f_{i,j}=a_j^{*}f_{i+1,j-1}+b_j^{*}f_{i+1,j}+c_j^{*}f_{i+1,j+1}, \] where \[ a_j^{*}=\frac{\tfrac12\sigma^{2}j^{2}\Delta t-\tfrac12(r-q)j\Delta t}{1+r\Delta t},\qquad b_j^{*}=\frac{1-\sigma^{2}j^{2}\Delta t}{1+r\Delta t},\qquad c_j^{*}=\frac{\tfrac12\sigma^{2}j^{2}\Delta t+\tfrac12(r-q)j\Delta t}{1+r\Delta t}. \] For an American option, \(f_{i,j}\) is replaced by the value of immediate exercise where that is greater.

The result has a familiar form. The three coefficients sum to \(1/(1+r\Delta t)\), which is a discount factor for one interval. The value at a node is therefore a discounted weighted average of the values at three nodes at the following date: the node below, the node at the same price, and the node above. The weights \(a_j^{*}(1+r\Delta t)\), \(b_j^{*}(1+r\Delta t)\), and \(c_j^{*}(1+r\Delta t)\) may be read as the risk-neutral probabilities that the price falls by \(\Delta S\), is unchanged, or rises by \(\Delta S\) over the interval. The explicit method is a trinomial tree, in which each node leads to three nodes and not two, laid out on a rectangular grid.

Worked example 16.4 — One step of the explicit method
The six-month American put on Northwind shares, with a strike of $30, is valued on a grid with \(\Delta S=\$2\) and 100 time steps, so that \(\Delta t=0.005\). Find the values one step before expiration at share prices of $28 and $30.
1
Coefficients at $28 (\(j=14\)). \(\tfrac12\sigma^{2}j^{2}\Delta t=\tfrac12\times0.1521\times196\times0.005=0.07453\); \(\tfrac12rj\Delta t=\tfrac12\times0.05\times14\times0.005=0.00175\); \(1+r\Delta t=1.00025\). \(a^{*}=(0.07453-0.00175)/1.00025=0.0728\); \(b^{*}=(1-0.14906)/1.00025=0.8507\); \(c^{*}=(0.07453+0.00175)/1.00025=0.0763\).
2
Value at $28. At expiration the put is worth $4, $2, and $0 at prices of $26, $28, and $30. \(0.0728\times4+0.8507\times2+0.0763\times0=1.9926\). The value of immediate exercise is $2.0000, which is greater. The value at the node is $2.0000: early exercise is optimal.
3
Value at $30 (\(j=15\)). \(a^{*}=(0.08556-0.00188)/1.00025=0.0837\). The values at expiration at $28, $30, and $32 are $2, $0, and $0, so that the value is \(0.0837\times2=\$0.1673\). Immediate exercise is worth nothing, and the option is held.
4
Continuation. The same calculation at every price gives the values one step before expiration, from which the values two steps before are found, and so on for 100 steps. The value at $28 at the present date is $3.888. A finer grid, with \(\Delta S=\$0.50\) and 2,000 time steps, gives $3.909, against $3.910 from the tree of Worked example 16.2.

Stability

The interpretation of the weights as probabilities fails if one of them is negative. The weight on the middle node, \(b_j^{*}\), is negative when \(\sigma^{2}j^{2}\Delta t>1\). This occurs first at the highest prices on the grid, where \(j\) is largest. When weights are negative, small errors are magnified at each step and alternate in sign from one node to the next. After a sufficient number of steps the computed values bear no relation to the solution. The method is then said to be unstable. All the weights are non-negative, and the method is stable, if \[ \Delta t\le\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}M^{2}}, \] where \(M=S_{\max}/\Delta S\) is the number of price intervals, provided also that \(\sigma^{2}\) exceeds \(r-q\), as is almost always the case.

The condition is demanding. For the grid of Worked example 16.4, with \(S_{\max}=\$60\) and \(\Delta S=\$2\), \(M=30\) and \(\Delta t\le1/(0.1521\times900)=0.0073\) years, so that at least 69 time steps are needed for a life of six months. If \(\Delta S\) is halved to improve the accuracy, \(M\) doubles and the largest permissible \(\Delta t\) falls to one quarter: the number of time steps must be multiplied by four, and the total amount of computation by eight. Interactive figure 16.3 shows what happens when the condition is ignored.

⚙ Interactive figure 16.3 — Three-dimensional view

The solution on the grid, and its destruction by instability

The surface is the value of the American put computed by the explicit method at every point of the grid, for share prices from $10 to $50. Expiration is at the front, where the surface is the payoff, and the present date is at the back. Select the price interval, then reduce the number of time steps and release the control: when the stability condition is badly violated, spikes appear at high share prices and grow toward the back of the grid. Table equivalent of this figure

Implicit methods

The explicit method computes each value from three known values at the following date. The implicit finite difference method instead relates three unknown values at one date to one known value at the following date. The values at each date are then found together, by solving a set of simultaneous linear equations. The equations have a simple structure and are solved quickly. The advantage of the implicit method is that it is stable for every choice of \(\Delta t\) and \(\Delta S\), so that the time step may be chosen for accuracy alone. The Crank–Nicolson method is an average of the explicit and the implicit methods. It is also stable, and it converges more rapidly than either as \(\Delta t\) is reduced. It is the method most often used in practice.

Common error

A numerical method always returns a number, and the number is not a value unless the method has converged. An unstable grid, a tree with too few steps, and a simulation with too few trials each produce a figure with as many decimal places as any other. The safeguards are those of this chapter: repeat the calculation with a finer step and confirm that the result changes little; state a standard error with every simulated value; and test the method on a derivative whose value is known.

16.5  ★ Derivation of the explicit method

Optional section. This section obtains Result 16.2 from the differential equation by replacing each derivative with a difference between neighbouring points of the grid.

At the point \((i,j)\) the derivative with respect to time is approximated by the difference between the values at the following date and at the present date, \[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\approx\frac{f_{i+1,j}-f_{i,j}}{\Delta t}. \] The explicit method evaluates the derivatives with respect to the price at the following date, where all values are known: \[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial S}\approx\frac{f_{i+1,j+1}-f_{i+1,j-1}}{2\Delta S},\qquad \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial S^{2}}\approx\frac{f_{i+1,j+1}-2f_{i+1,j}+f_{i+1,j-1}}{\Delta S^{2}}. \] The second of these is the butterfly of Result 15.3. Substituting in the differential equation, with \(S=j\Delta S\) and the right-hand side evaluated as \(rf_{i,j}\),

\[ \frac{f_{i+1,j}-f_{i,j}}{\Delta t}+(r-q)j\,\frac{f_{i+1,j+1}-f_{i+1,j-1}}{2}+\frac12\sigma^{2}j^{2}\left(f_{i+1,j+1}-2f_{i+1,j}+f_{i+1,j-1}\right)=rf_{i,j} . \]

The interval \(\Delta S\) has cancelled, since \(S/\Delta S=j\) and \(S^{2}/\Delta S^{2}=j^{2}\). Multiplying by \(\Delta t\) and collecting the terms in \(f_{i,j}\) on the left gives \[ (1+r\Delta t)f_{i,j}=\left[\tfrac12\sigma^{2}j^{2}-\tfrac12(r-q)j\right]\Delta t\,f_{i+1,j-1}+\left[1-\sigma^{2}j^{2}\Delta t\right]f_{i+1,j}+\left[\tfrac12\sigma^{2}j^{2}+\tfrac12(r-q)j\right]\Delta t\,f_{i+1,j+1}, \] which is Result 16.2. The implicit method differs only in evaluating the two derivatives with respect to the price at the present date \(i\), where the values are unknown; three unknowns then appear in each equation.

The three weights have a mean change in price of \((r-q)S\Delta t\) and a variance of approximately \(\sigma^{2}S^{2}\Delta t\), which are the mean and variance of the change in the price in a risk-neutral world over the interval. The explicit method and the trinomial tree are the same calculation reached from two directions.

16.6  The choice of method

For a European option on one asset the formula is used, and no numerical method is required. For an American option on one asset a tree with the control variate correction, or a Crank–Nicolson grid, is used. For a derivative whose payoff depends on the path, or on several assets, Monte Carlo simulation is used, with variance reduction. For a derivative with both early exercise and several underlying variables, simulation with the least-squares method is used. Where two methods are available, each serves as a check on the other, and agreement between them is the best evidence that a value is correct.

Concept check 16.2

An explicit finite difference grid for an option on a share with a volatility of 40 percent uses 50 price intervals. What is the largest time step for which every weight is non-negative, and what happens if the price interval is halved?

Concept check 16.3

A bank must value a European option that pays the amount by which the best-performing of eight share prices exceeds a strike. Which method is appropriate, and why?

Historical note

The Monte Carlo method was devised at Los Alamos in the 1940s by Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann for problems in the diffusion of neutrons that could not be solved analytically. Ulam is reported to have conceived the idea while estimating by repeated play the probability of winning a game of patience. Nicholas Metropolis proposed the name, after the casino. The finite difference methods of this chapter are older: the method of John Crank and Phyllis Nicolson was published in 1947 for the equation that governs the conduction of heat, to which the Black–Scholes–Merton equation can be reduced by a change of variables.

All three methods entered finance within a few years of the Black–Scholes–Merton paper. Phelim Boyle applied Monte Carlo simulation to options in 1977. Michael Brennan and Eduardo Schwartz applied finite differences to the American put in the same year. Cox, Ross, and Rubinstein published the binomial tree in 1979. The valuation of American options by simulation remained an open problem until the work of Longstaff and Schwartz in 2001.

Summary

  • Trees and finite difference methods work backward from expiration and handle early exercise. Monte Carlo simulation works forward and handles payoffs that depend on the path and derivatives on many variables.
  • A tree supplies delta, gamma, and theta from its first two steps. The control variate technique corrects the tree value of an American option by the known error of the same tree on the European option.
  • Monte Carlo simulation averages the discounted payoffs of randomly generated paths. Its standard error is \(s/\sqrt M\), so that four times as many trials are needed to halve the error.
  • Antithetic variables and control variates reduce the variance of a simulation.
  • The explicit finite difference method computes each value as a discounted weighted average of three values at the following date, and is a trinomial tree. It is stable only if \(\Delta t\le1/(\sigma^{2}M^{2})\). The implicit and Crank–Nicolson methods are stable for every time step.
  • A numerical result should be accepted only when refinement of the step, a stated standard error, or agreement with a second method shows that it has converged.

Exercises

16.1 A stock index has a volatility of 20 percent and a dividend yield of 2 percent. The risk-free rate is 5 percent. Find \(u\), \(d\), and \(p\) for a tree with a time step of three months.

\(u=e^{0.20\sqrt{0.25}}=e^{0.10}=1.1052\); \(d=1/u=0.9048\); \(a=e^{(0.05-0.02)\times0.25}=1.0075\); \(p=(1.0075-0.9048)/(1.1052-0.9048)=0.1027/0.2003=0.5126\).

16.2 A tree for an American call on a share priced at $60 has \(u=1.10\) and \(d=0.9091\), with a time step of one month. The values of the option are $5.20 at the initial node, $8.90 and $2.40 at the upper and lower nodes after one step, and $13.60, $4.90, and $0.70 at the three nodes after two steps. Estimate delta, gamma, and theta.

Prices after one step: $66.00 and $54.55. Delta: \((8.90-2.40)/(66.00-54.55)=6.50/11.45=0.568\). Prices after two steps: $72.60, $60.00, and $49.59. Upper delta: \((13.60-4.90)/12.60=0.6905\). Lower delta: \((4.90-0.70)/10.41=0.4035\). \(h=\tfrac12(72.60-49.59)=11.505\). Gamma: \((0.6905-0.4035)/11.505=0.0249\). Theta: \((4.90-5.20)/(2/12)=-1.80\) per year, or about \(-\$0.0049\) per calendar day.

16.3 A tree with 30 steps values an American put at $4.26 and the corresponding European put at $3.94. The Black–Scholes–Merton value of the European put is $3.99. Find the control variate estimate of the value of the American put.

The tree undervalues the European put by \(3.99-3.94=\$0.05\). The estimate is \(4.26+0.05=\$4.31\).

16.4 A simulation of 40,000 trials gives a mean discounted payoff of $5.84 and a standard deviation of $9.20. (a) Find the standard error and the 95 percent confidence interval. (b) How many trials would be needed for a standard error of $0.01?

(a) \(9.20/\sqrt{40{,}000}=9.20/200=\$0.046\). The interval is \(5.84\pm1.96\times0.046\), from $5.75 to $5.93. (b) \(M=(s/0.01)^{2}=920^{2}=846{,}400\) trials.

16.5 A share that pays no dividend trades at $50 and has a volatility of 30 percent. The risk-free rate is 4 percent. A random draw of 0.80 is obtained. Using the antithetic variable technique, find the two simulated prices in six months and the pair's estimate of the value of a six-month European call with a strike of $50.

\((r-\sigma^{2}/2)T=(0.04-0.045)\times0.5=-0.0025\); \(\sigma\sqrt T=0.2121\). With \(\varepsilon=0.80\): \(S_T=50e^{-0.0025+0.1697}=50e^{0.1672}=\$59.10\); payoff $9.10. With \(\varepsilon=-0.80\): \(S_T=50e^{-0.1722}=\$42.09\); payoff 0. The average payoff is $4.55, and the estimate is \(4.55e^{-0.02}=\$4.46\). The Black–Scholes–Merton value, from Exercise 12.1, is $4.70.

16.6 A one-year option on a share with a volatility of 30 percent is to be valued by the explicit finite difference method, on a grid that extends to a share price of $200 in intervals of $5. (a) Find the smallest number of time steps for which the method is stable. (b) Find the number if the interval is reduced to $2.50.

(a) \(M=200/5=40\). \(\Delta t\le1/(0.09\times1{,}600)=0.006944\) years, so that \(N\ge1/0.006944=144\) steps. (b) \(M=80\). \(\Delta t\le1/(0.09\times6{,}400)=0.001736\), so that \(N\ge576\) steps, four times as many.

16.7 In an explicit finite difference grid for an American put with a strike of $50, the coefficients at the node for a share price of $46 are \(a^{*}=0.12\), \(b^{*}=0.76\), and \(c^{*}=0.115\). The values at the following date at share prices of $44, $46, and $48 are $6.30, $4.60, and $3.20. Find the value at the node.

The value of continuing is \(0.12\times6.30+0.76\times4.60+0.115\times3.20=0.756+3.496+0.368=\$4.62\). The value of immediate exercise is \(50-46=\$4.00\). The value at the node is the greater, $4.62, and the option is held.

16.8 State, with a reason, the numerical method best suited to each of the following: (a) a one-year American put on a share that pays no dividend; (b) a one-year European option on the average of the daily closing prices of a share; (c) a European option on the lowest of the returns on five stock indices.

(a) A binomial tree with the control variate correction, or a Crank–Nicolson grid: there is one underlying variable and early exercise, which a backward method handles directly. (b) Monte Carlo simulation: the payoff depends on the path, which a forward method follows directly; the corresponding option on the geometric average, which has a formula, may serve as a control variate. (c) Monte Carlo simulation: there are five underlying variables, and the cost of a tree or a grid in five dimensions is prohibitive.
